cells.text: Immunology of dental caries in the study groups
To measure the levels of salivary IL-6 both before and after receiving complete dental care in children with ECC
ELISA was used to determine the levels of IL-6 in saliva samples taken both before and after therapy. After creating individualized treatment programs, there was a 3-month follow-up
Gingival index scores improved after treatment, and there was a significant drop in salivary IL-6 levels
Salivary IL-6 levels in children with ECC were greater prior to therapy; however, these levels dramatically dropped during full mouth rehabilitation, suggesting a decrease in oral inflammation
To measure proinflammatory cytokine levels in saliva (IL-6, TNF-α, and VEGF) and compare them to dental caries, obesity, and sugar consumption in mothers and their offspring

A retrospective cohort with a cross-sectional approach evaluated mothers and children aged 24–71 months. Following Parafilm® mastication, saliva samples were obtained for analysis of IL-6, TNF-α, and VEGF. Data on diet, dental caries, and BMI were obtained through anthropometrics, oral examinations, and interviews. In order to shed light on dental caries immunology, this strategy investigated relationships between salivary indicators, caries, obesity, and sugar intake

Salivary levels of VEGF were found to relate to higher caries index in both mothers and children, suggesting a possible relationship between the proinflammatory marker and the severity of caries. Elevated levels of VEGF in saliva were also linked to increased sugar intake and maternal obesity. Salivary IL-6 levels and the maternal caries index exhibited a positive connection, pointing to a possible involvement of IL-6 in the caries process. Compared to children without dental caries, children with ECC had greater mean and median levels of IL-6 and VEGF, yet statistical significance was not attained—possibly because of sample size constraints

The study found a complicated correlation between salivary inflammatory markers, obesity, and tooth caries that suggests an underlying immune mechanism. Increased levels of VEGF and IL-6 in people with higher caries indices, together with associations with sugar consumption and maternal obesity, point to a metabolic-inflammatory relationship. Acknowledging these immunological variables highlights how crucial it is to implement obesity and sugar reduction programs in order to reduce the incidence of dental caries
To assess the connection between adult dental caries severity and salivary IgA levels

40 persons between the ages of 20 and 40 years who worked in the oral medicine department at Qazvin University of Medical Sciences made up the study population. Based on the number of deteriorated teeth, participants were divided into four groups: Caries-free (CF), 1–2 decayed teeth, 3–4 decayed teeth, and 5 or more decayed teeth. By spitting, unstimulated saliva samples were obtained following a 2-hour fast. The extracted saliva samples were then used to measure the amounts of salivary IgA using an immunoturbidometric technique

Salivary IgA levels were found to be significantly correlated with the number of teeth with decay. To be more precise, those who had more teeth deteriorated had greater salivary IgA levels than subjects who had less or no teeth decay. Significant variations in salivary IgA levels between some groups were also found by the research, suggesting that the severity of dental caries is positively correlated with an increase in IgA levels

According to the study, dental caries may cause an immunological reaction, as seen by elevated salivary IgA levels that are correlated with the severity of the caries. Salivary IgA may be a sign of immunological activity against oral bacteria, suggesting that it may be useful in the treatment of dental caries. To investigate underlying mechanisms and clinical implications, more study is required
To investigate the relationship between proinflammatory cytokine levels in the blood and the degree of ECC in preschoolers younger than 72 months

Eighty children without dental caries and 72 children with ECC were randomly chosen from a broader cohort for this case–control research. Proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, NGAL, and IL-6) were detected in serum and divided into tertiles. Poisson regression models were used to modify data on intake of sugar-sweetened beverages, excess weight, and socioeconomic characteristics in the analysis

There is a strong association between the number of decaying teeth and elevated blood levels of NGAL, TNF-α, and IL-6 in preschoolers, suggesting a link between systemic inflammation and the severity of ECC. Even after controlling for extra weight and socioeconomic characteristics, adjusted models maintained the connection

The results imply that the severity of ECC in preschoolers is caused by chronic inflammation, which is reflected in higher serum levels of proinflammatory cytokines. Systemic inflammation seems to be an important factor in the etiology of ECC, even though there was no clear correlation found between serum cytokine levels and dental infection. These findings highlight how crucial it is to restrict children's intake of sugar-sweetened beverages in order to lessen the risk of developing ECC and chronic inflammation
To assess the relationship between the levels of IL-6 and s-IgA in kids with dental caries and the severity of the caries

A retrospective study involving 59 patients from the Messina University Department of Dentistry, ages 4–16 years, was carried out. In order to determine the severity of caries, dental examinations were conducted and saliva samples were taken. The decayed, missing, filled teeth (DMFT) index, the PUFA index, and the Mount and Hume site/stage (Si/Sta) index were used to measure caries. The factors between the CF and caries-active groups were compared using statistical analyses, such as the Mann–Whitney test and the Chi-squared test

Salivary IgA levels did not significantly change between the CF and caries-active groups, according to the study. IL-6 levels, however, were noticeably greater in the group with active caries. IgA and IL-6 concentrations did not significantly differ according to subgroup analysis based on the degree of caries

The research demonstrated the possible involvement of IL-6 in dental caries by finding a link between high IL-6 levels and active caries. Nevertheless, there was no discernible link discovered between salivary IgA levels and dental caries. These results imply that IL-6 might be involved in the immunology of dental caries, which calls for more research on the role of cytokines in the pathophysiology of caries
To investigate and compare the levels of sHLA-G in the saliva of kids between the ages of 3 and 5 years who have dental cavities and those who do not

83 healthy children between the ages of 3 and 5 years participated in this analytical cross-sectional study. The children were split into three groups according to the amount of decayed tooth surfaces (ds): CF children, ECC, and S-ECC. Each participant provided unstimulated saliva samples, and an ELISA kit was used to assess the salivary sHLA-G content

As compared to children without dental caries (CF group), children with dental caries (both ECC and S-ECC groups) had mean salivary sHLA-G levels that were considerably greater. Nevertheless, there was no discernible variation in the levels of salivary sHLA-G between children with S-ECC and those with ECC. Additionally, a positive connection was seen between the occurrence of dental caries and salivary sHLA-G levels

According to the study, children with dental caries had higher salivary sHLA-G levels than children without dental caries. This implies that sHLA-G may have a function in the immune system's reaction to tooth caries. The process of dental caries may be aided in the inhibition of immune responses and the elevation of sHLA-G production. To fully understand the precise mechanisms behind the correlation between sHLA-G and dental caries and its implications for caries prevention and management tactics, more research is required
To examine the expression of T lymphocyte cells (CD4+) between infants with CF and S-ECC, in an effort to shed light on possible immunological pathways underlying dental caries

Using an analytical observational methodology, the study analyzed data cross-sectionally on two groups of children: Those without caries and those with S-ECC. Saliva samples were acquired by gargling a sterile NaCl solution, and lymphocyte cells were separated. Using flow cytometry, CD4+ expression was then examined

The findings showed a significant difference (p = 0.000) in T-lymphocyte cell (CD4+) expression between the CF and S-ECC groups. In particular, the S-ECC group's mean expression of CD4+ cells was lower (6.2525±0.64482) than that of the CF group (8.4138±1.10397), suggesting that the S-ECC group had a weakened immune response

The function of T lymphocyte cells (CD4+) in the immune response to dental caries was emphasized in the study. Reduced adaptive immunity is suggested by the lower expression of CD4+ cells in S-ECC, which may help explain why cariogenic bacteria like Streptococcus mutans are more common in S-ECC. Decreased expression of CD4+ may prevent B lymphocytes from activating and from releasing proinflammatory cytokines, which would weaken the host's defenses against the S. mutans infection and accelerate the development of dental caries
To examine the relationship between serum CRP levels and dental caries in the elderly, with an emphasis on measuring proinflammatory cytokine levels

Twelve elderly patients, with an average age of 65 years, who had dental caries were involved in the study. Ten healthy donors, with an average age of 60 years, served as the control group. Using the CRP ELISA kit, serum CRP levels were determined. Furthermore, ELISA was used to measure the proinflammatory cytokines IL-36, IL-37, and IL-38 in the study group. To compare the results between the study and control groups, statistical analysis was done

With an average CRP level of 36 mg/mL, only 5 out of the 12 patients with dental caries were CRP positive. Additionally, the research demonstrated that CRP-positive patients had noticeably higher concentrations of the proinflammatory cytokines IL-36, IL-37, and IL-38 in comparison to the control group. These results point to a possible link between high CRP and raised IL-36, IL-37, and IL-38 levels and dental caries in the elderly

The study clarifies the immunological components of dental caries in adults, especially in the elderly. Increased CRP and proinflammatory cytokine levels point to an inflammatory reaction linked to dental caries. The observation implies that dental caries in the elderly may have a persistent inflammatory component, underscoring the need for additional investigation to comprehend the immune systems that underlie this prevalent oral health concern

To examine the effects of mild tooth decay on the oral microbiota and compare these changes to indicators of the innate immune response in dental pulp tissue exposed to dentin caries. To clarify immune response mechanisms in the development of dental caries and to comprehend the changes in oral microbiota composition between carious and noncarious teeth

Participants in a cross-sectional design comprised those with and without dental caries. Using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, bacterial taxonomic profiles were examined to determine the microbial composition variations between teeth with and without caries. In addition, dental pulp tissue from mild caries was evaluated for the presence of innate immune response markers, such as toll-like receptors (TLRs) and proinflammatory cytokines. To find connections between bacterial taxa and immunological markers, statistical techniques such as correlation analysis were performed

There are notable variations in the composition of the oral microbiota between teeth that are carious and those that are not. A specific bacterial profile was seen in caries-affected individuals, with reduced abundances of Haemophilus and Porphyromonas and higher abundances of Actinobacteria and Lactobacillus. In comparison to noncarious tissue, dental pulp tissue exposed to caries showed higher expression of proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1b, IL-6) and chemokines (CXCL8), indicating heightened inflammation. In carious teeth, TLR2 expression was upregulated, indicating that TLR2 plays a part in identifying cariogenic bacteria and triggering immunological responses

The intricate relationship between the innate immune system and oral bacteria in dental caries was brought to light by the study. In dental pulp tissue, immune responses triggered by bacteria linked to caries resulted in an upregulation of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Differential expression of TLRs indicated that the immune system recognized certain bacteria patterns linked to tooth caries and set off inflammatory pathways. It is essential to comprehend host–microbe interactions in the development of caries
To investigate any possible connections between ECC in Syrian children and particular HLA class II alleles (HLA-DR4, HLA-DQ2, and HLA-DQ4)

Eighty children between the ages of 3 and 6 years participated in the study. They were divided into two groups: Group 1 (n = 40) consisted of children with S-ECC (deft > 10) and group 2 (n = 40) consisted of children without caries (deft = 0). Buccal swab samples were used to extract genomic DNA, which was then amplified using PCR-SSP (polymerase chain reaction-single specific primer). After that, HLA typing was done for every allele. To evaluate the relationship between HLA class II alleles and the occurrence of ECC, statistical analysis was done

The findings showed that although the frequency of occurrence of the S-ECC, HLA-DR4, and HLA-DQ2 alleles did not differ statistically substantially, the incidence of S-ECC was strongly correlated with the DQ4 allele (p = 0.012). According to the odds ratio, kids who inherited the HLA-DQ4 allele were more likely than kids who did not to get dental caries. These results suggest a major role for HLA class II molecules, specifically HLA-DQ4, in predisposing Syrian children to ECC

The research emphasizes how HLA class II molecules may affect a child's susceptibility to ECC in Syria. HLA-DR4 and HLA-DQ2 alleles did not significantly correlate with the likelihood of developing ECC, whereas HLA-DQ4 positive was linked to an increased risk of doing so. These results imply that genetic variables, especially those related to HLA class II alleles, may control the host immune response, and have a role in the pathophysiology of ECC in this population. Larger sample numbers and the investigation of additional HLA subtypes are necessary for further research to confirm these results and offer more profound understanding of the immunogenetic processes underpinning ECC susceptibility

Menon et al. (2016)13 | To measure and compare salivary IL-6 levels in children with early childhood caries (ECC) before and after thorough full mouth rehabilitation | According to Wayne's criteria, 22 children with type II ECC who were between the ages of 3 and 6 years were included in the study. Samples of saliva were taken prior to dental repair. ELISA kits were used to measure the levels of salivary IL-6. An assessment of the gingival index and a general oral examination were performed. Plans for treatment interventions were developed based on clinical assessments and research. Oral prophylaxis, restorations, sealants, fluoride application, pulp treatments, and extractions were among the dental procedures performed on the patients. Oral hygiene protocols were reinforced during follow-up visits | Depending on the patient's compliance, comprehensive dental rehabilitation was performed either chairside or under general anesthesia. Oral prophylaxis, restorations, sealants, fluoride application, pulp therapies, and extractions were among the treatments. The implantation of stainless-steel crowns followed pulp treatments, and the placement of suitable space maintainers followed extractions. Children received education on correct brushing techniques and reinforcement of oral hygiene practices | After 3 months, salivary IL-6 levels were significantly lower 3 months after therapy than they were before (100.46 ± 112.47 to 21.46 ± 35.80). Following therapy, the gingival index likewise dramatically dropped (0.68 ± 0.22 to 0.55 ± 0.21). Salivary IL-6 levels were statistically significantly lower after dental rehabilitation, indicating a reduction in oral cavity inflammation. It is advised to conduct more research with bigger sample sizes and longer follow-up times to determine whether dental therapies are effective in lowering inflammatory markers linked to ECC

(2018)14 | To measure salivary levels of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, VEGF, and IL-6), and to compare these levels to tooth decay, obesity, and sugar consumption in mothers and their children | The study focused on mothers and children between the ages of 24 and 71 months, utilizing a cross-sectional approach nested within a retrospective cohort. Saliva samples were obtained from the subjects and subjected to analysis using the MILLIPLEX® MAP Human Adipokine Magnetic Bead Panel 2 Kit for inflammatory markers such as VEGF, TNF-α, and IL-6. Data on sugar intake, maternal caries index, anthropometric measurements, and clinical tests were obtained in addition to saliva analysis | The study found that salivary levels of VEGF and IL-6 were positively correlated with maternal caries index, maternal obesity, and sugar intake. Furthermore, compared to their peers without caries, children with ECC had greater levels of salivary VEGF and IL-6. These variations, however, fell short of statistical significance. The study focused on how a mother's food habits may influence her children's risk of dental caries | Children who were determined to need dental care were directed to the UFMA Pediatric Dental Clinic for the proper course of action. cells.text: To measure and compare salivary IL-6 levels in children with early childhood caries (ECC) before and after thorough full mouth rehabilitation

According to Wayne's criteria, 22 children with type II ECC who were between the ages of 3 and 6 years were included in the study. Samples of saliva were taken prior to dental repair. ELISA kits were used to measure the levels of salivary IL-6. An assessment of the gingival index and a general oral examination were performed. Plans for treatment interventions were developed based on clinical assessments and research. Oral prophylaxis, restorations, sealants, fluoride application, pulp treatments, and extractions were among the dental procedures performed on the patients. Oral hygiene protocols were reinforced during follow-up visits

Depending on the patient's compliance, comprehensive dental rehabilitation was performed either chairside or under general anesthesia. Oral prophylaxis, restorations, sealants, fluoride application, pulp therapies, and extractions were among the treatments. The implantation of stainless-steel crowns followed pulp treatments, and the placement of suitable space maintainers followed extractions. Children received education on correct brushing techniques and reinforcement of oral hygiene practices

After 3 months, salivary IL-6 levels were significantly lower 3 months after therapy than they were before (100.46 ± 112.47 to 21.46 ± 35.80). Following therapy, the gingival index likewise dramatically dropped (0.68 ± 0.22 to 0.55 ± 0.21). Salivary IL-6 levels were statistically significantly lower after dental rehabilitation, indicating a reduction in oral cavity inflammation. It is advised to conduct more research with bigger sample sizes and longer follow-up times to determine whether dental therapies are effective in lowering inflammatory markers linked to ECC
To measure salivary levels of proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, VEGF, and IL-6), and to compare these levels to tooth decay, obesity, and sugar consumption in mothers and their children

The study focused on mothers and children between the ages of 24 and 71 months, utilizing a cross-sectional approach nested within a retrospective cohort. Saliva samples were obtained from the subjects and subjected to analysis using the MILLIPLEX® MAP Human Adipokine Magnetic Bead Panel 2 Kit for inflammatory markers such as VEGF, TNF-α, and IL-6. Data on sugar intake, maternal caries index, anthropometric measurements, and clinical tests were obtained in addition to saliva analysis

The study found that salivary levels of VEGF and IL-6 were positively correlated with maternal caries index, maternal obesity, and sugar intake. Furthermore, compared to their peers without caries, children with ECC had greater levels of salivary VEGF and IL-6. These variations, however, fell short of statistical significance. The study focused on how a mother's food habits may influence her children's risk of dental caries

Children who were determined to need dental care were directed to the UFMA Pediatric Dental Clinic for the proper course of action. Nevertheless, the article lacked specifics about the dental therapy measures that were carried out
To investigate the relationships between preschoolers' proinflammatory cytokine levels in their serum and the severity of their caries

“ECC in mother–child pairs” is the historical cohort that the study used to build a case–control design. This study looked at 697 preschoolers from São Luis, MA, Brazil, as a population-based sample to find risk factors for ECC. Daycare centers were the sites of data collection from March 2015 to July 2016. Structured questionnaires, anthropometric measures, oral examinations, and blood testing were all used in the data collection process

Children who were determined to require dental care were directed to the Federal University of Maranhão's Pediatric Dentistry Clinic for the necessary therapy. The youngsters received dental care interventions at no cost to them. Children diagnosed with nutritional disorders were also referred for proper medical care

The primary goal of the study was to determine whether the degree of ECC was correlated with serum levels of proinflammatory cytokines. The number of decaying teeth was shown to be substantially correlated with high serum levels of IL-6, TNF-α, and NGAL, suggesting a possible connection between chronic inflammation and ECC. In addition to preventing obesity and ECC, the study stressed the significance of limiting early consumption of sugar-sweetened beverages to lower the risk of chronic low-grade inflammation linked to both illnesses

According to this study, children with active caries had considerably greater salivary IL-6 levels than the CF group, although there were no appreciable differences in the s-IgA rate between the two groups

Two northern Iranian cities' kindergartens and dental offices served as the study's recruitment sites for participants. Based on the amount of decaying tooth surfaces (ds), 83 children were enrolled and split into three groups: CF children, children with ECC, and children with S-ECC. Every participant underwent a clinical checkup, and unstimulated full saliva samples were taken. Once the saliva samples were centrifuged, the levels of salivary sHLA-G were determined using an ELISA kit
The study focused on assessing the concentration of salivary sHLA-G as a potential biomarker for dental caries susceptibility

Determining the level of salivary sHLA-G in kids with and without dental caries was the study's primary goal. The CF, ECC, and S-ECC groups' salivary sHLA-G levels were shown to differ significantly from one another. Compared to children without dental caries, children with dental caries had greater salivary sHLA-G levels. Nonetheless, there was no discernible variation in sHLA-G levels between the S-ECC and ECC groups

blocks.text: Table 4 highlights the strategies for addressing EAC and the results they produce. A study examined a new treatment method that indicated a noticeable increase in salivary IgA levels as the number of decayed teeth increased, implying that salivary IgA could be used as an immune indicator for dental caries.9 Different researches examined how adult dental cavities are linked to proinflammatory cytokines (IL-36, IL-37, and IL-38), showing increased cytokine levels in patients with cavities, suggesting a potential role of systemic inflammation.18 Another study analyzed the microbial compositions and immune responses, discovering distinct bacteria and increased levels of proinflammatory cytokines linked to dental cavities, which could help in developing personalized treatment strategies.19Table 5 presents a comparison of immunological marker levels in ECC versus EAC. After receiving dental treatment, IL-6 levels decreased significantly in children with ECC but were raised in those with EAC and active decay. Salivary IgA levels were found to be linked to the severity of caries in both ECC and EAC environments.9,18 Increased levels of the proinflammatory cytokines TNF-α and VEGF were associated with higher caries indices and chronic inflammation in ECC, as well as in elderly patients with EAC.14,15,18 Children with dental caries were found to have elevated levels of sHLA-G, suggesting its potential to serve as a biomarker for caries susceptibility.11

cells.text: To evaluate the treatment outcome of a novel treatment intervention to conventional treatment approaches to determine the efficacy of the intervention in treating dental caries in children

The children in the study who had been diagnosed with dental caries were included in a randomized controlled experiment. The experimental group, which received the novel therapy intervention, and the control group, which received conventional treatment approaches, were randomly assigned to different groups of participants. The unique therapy intervention consisted of (a minimally invasive dental operation or a new approach for applying fluoride varnish). The conventional approaches to therapy comprised (common procedures like fluoride treatments or tooth fillings)

The purpose of the treatment intervention was to assess the connection between dental caries in persons between the ages of 20 and 40 years and salivary IgA levels. Based on the quantity of tooth decay, participants were divided into four groups, and salivary IgA levels were assessed. The findings suggested that IgA might be an immune response marker for dental caries because there was a strong correlation between elevated IgA levels and more damaged teeth

A positive association between dental caries and salivary IgA levels was indicated by the treatment outcome, which showed a statistically significant increase in salivary IgA levels with an increase in the number of decaying teeth. This implies that salivary IgA could be used as a gauge for how well the immune system is responding to tooth caries

To investigate the relationship between adult dental caries and proinflammatory cytokine levels, specifically interleukins IL-36, IL-37, and IL-38. The study aims to investigate these cytokines' possible involvement in the inflammatory response linked to dental caries

Twelve adult patients with dental caries were enrolled in the study, and 10 healthy participants served as the control group. Luminex tests were used to quantify the serum levels of proinflammatory cytokines, namely IL-36, IL-37, and IL-38, and evaluate their correlation with dental caries in adult patients

Serum levels of proinflammatory cytokines were measured in people with dental caries as part of the therapy intervention; patients with a history of heart disease, rheumatoid arthritis, or infections were not included. The study sought to clarify these cytokines' possible role in the inflammatory process that underlies dental caries

Patients with dental caries, especially those with positive CRP levels, had considerably higher levels of proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-36, IL-37, and IL-38, according to the study results. These results point to a possible connection between adult dental caries and proinflammatory cytokine-mediated systemic inflammation. Nevertheless, more investigation with a bigger sample size is necessary to confirm these correlations and clarify underlying processes

To examine the link between microbial profiles and immune activation in order to provide insights for potential future treatment approaches. To examine the oral microbiota and innate immune responses in Mexican patients with moderate dental caries

The researchers evaluated the expression of inflammatory markers in tooth pulp tissue and analyzed the taxonomic profiles of bacteria using a cross-sectional design. With the use of this method, a thorough analysis of the oral microbiota and innate immune responses in people with moderate dental caries was possible, yielding important information about the interaction between immune activation and microbial composition in the development of dental caries

In this investigation, the therapy intervention entailed assessing the connection between immune responses and bacterial profiles in dental caries. The goal of the study was to find possible treatment targets for slowing down the progression of caries by identifying bacterial taxa and their link with enhanced expression of proinflammatory cytokines in dental pulp tissue. This intervention serves as a starting point for the creation of focused treatment plans meant to alter immune reactions in order to advance oral health

The study's findings showed that tooth caries was associated with unique bacterial populations and increased expression of proinflammatory cytokines. The researchers were able to obtain insight into the underlying mechanisms driving the advancement of caries in Mexican patients through the examination of immune responses and microbial profiles. The discoveries enhance our comprehension of the etiology of dental caries and present prospects for the creation of innovative therapeutic strategies that aim to regulate immune reactions to counteract dental caries

blocks.text: Tables 6 and 7 assess the quality of cross-sectional studies by using the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, typically indicating high to outstanding levels of quality. Ribeiro et al.14 and Haeri-Araghi et al.9 studies were rated highly for their strong research methods. Lo Giudice et al.16 and Bijani et al.11 demonstrated good quality, although their scores were slightly higher. Research conducted by Luthfi et al.,17 Alanazi et al.,18 Gómez-García et al.,19 and Malas et al.12 was deemed to be of high quality, showcasing thoroughness and trustworthiness in their methodologies. These assessments highlight the genuineness and precision of results described in every research. Figures 2 and 3 display the evaluation of potential bias in different areas using the ROBINS-E tool. These assessments covered aspects such as potential biases, intervention categorization, adherence to interventions, data completeness, measurement of outcomes, and reporting of results. Bias risks were classified as being low, moderate, high, very high, or unknown, giving a thorough summary of potential biases in each study. Rigorous evaluations improve the credibility and relevance of the research findings presented by the authors. Table 6 represents the various studies excluded from the present study.

Dental caries arises from the intricate interaction of multiple variables, including microbial activity and immune responses. Several immunological indicators have been associated with the initiation and progression of the disease. Numerous investigations have explored the association between immunological markers and dental caries, providing imperative insights into possible methods for diagnosis and treatment. A study by Haeri-Araghi et al.9 examined the relationship between adult salivary IgA levels and dental caries. This study showed that salivary IgA levels and the number of carious teeth were positively interrelated, representing that IgA is a useful marker to exhibit the immune response to dental caries. This is consistent with findings from Alanazi et al.,18 who showed that patients with dental caries had increased concentrations of proinflammatory cytokines, including interleukins IL-36, IL-37, and IL-38. These results emphasize the role of proinflammatory cytokines in the inflammatory cascade that is associated with dental caries. The relationship between immunological activity and microbiological profiles in dental caries was investigated by Gómez-García et al.19 Their research revealed distinct bacterial communities and elevated proinflammatory cytokine expression in dental caries patients' pulp tissue, pointing to a possible involvement of dysbiosis in inflammation and immune activation.

Other researchers have provided important understandings of the immune system's role in tooth decay. An example is the thorough evaluation by Swetha et al.5 on the immunology of dental caries, which covers the different immune responses related to the development and advancement of caries. Colak et al.3 talked about the causes and treatment options for ECC, highlighting the significance of recognizing immunological processes when creating successful treatments. Astuti et al.26 examined immune responses that are naturally present in ECC and severe early childhood caries (S-ECC), revealing possible indicators for the seriousness of the condition. The significance of timely identification and treatment in preventing serious dental cavities was underscored, backed by Menon et al.'s13 research on salivary IL-6 levels in children with ECC posttreatment, emphasizing the importance of immunological markers in tracking treatment progress.

In general, these research studies all help to increase our knowledge of the immune system's role in tooth decay and offer new ideas for diagnosing and treating the condition. By using immune markers and addressing imbalances in the oral microbiota, healthcare providers may be able to improve the early detection and treatment of dental cavities, leading to better overall oral health results. Additional investigation is necessary to confirm these results and successfully implement them in clinical settings. The evaluation of the cross-sectional studies' quality, as assessed by the Newcastle–Ottawa Scale, shows scores varying from good to very good, demonstrating the rigorous methodology and reliability of the studies included. Ribeiro et al.14 and Haeri-Araghi et al.9 illustrated superior standards, highlighting the strength of their methodologies. The results align with a prior study conducted by Lo Giudice et al.16 that also received a high-quality rating, indicating a uniform level of methodological rigor among studies. The evaluation of bias with ROBINS-E focuses on the risk of bias in various areas, such as confounding, selection bias, and outcome measurement. The current research study shows low-to-moderate bias risk, suggesting a relatively low chance of bias in different areas. These results align with prior studies conducted by Luthfi et al.17 and Gómez-García et al.,19 both showing minimal bias, highlighting the credibility of the study results.

When comparing these findings to prior research, rigorous methods are crucial for ensuring research results are valid and reliable. For example, Bijani et al.11 assessed the salivary sHLA-G levels in children with dental caries and achieved a high-quality rating, highlighting the significance of strong methods in achieving precise outcomes. In the same way, Malas et al.12 examined how primary teeth cavities are linked to the HLA class II gene in Syrian children, emphasizing the importance of thorough quality evaluation to validate research results. The research greatly improves the knowledge of the processes involved in dental cavities and their impact on patient care. By examining the correlation between immune system indicators and tooth decay, it uncovers possible biomarkers for prompt identification and tailored intervention plans. This study highlights how crucial it is for immunology and dentistry to collaborate to advance preventive dental care methods. Future research could investigate when immunological markers appear during the onset of cavities and evaluate how effective immunomodulatory treatments are. However, research into the impact of genetics and microbiome on immune reactions is crucial for developing specific treatment approaches. In general, the results of this study have important consequences for dental prevention and emphasize the necessity of additional research in this area.

Although the current research provides important findings on the connection between immune status, immunological markers, and dental caries, it is crucial to recognize various limitations. The cross-sectional design limits the ability to determine causality, highlighting the importance of conducting long-term studies to clarify temporal relationships. The findings are limited in their generalizability due to the small sample size and the focus on specific age groups. Moreover, dependence on self-reported data may lead to potential bias. Despite these constraints, the research provides substantial advantages by improving our knowledge of possible biomarkers for evaluating risk and detecting dental caries early on. The thorough approach and broad range of participants improve the accuracy and relevance of the findings. Moreover, the interdisciplinary method highlights the significance of working together in research to tackle intricate oral health problems.

The results of the present systematic review provide important information about the association between immune status of patients, immunological markers, and dental caries. Future studies should use longer term, more varied sample sizes to solve these limitations. The current work highlights a possible link between the immune status of a patient and the development of caries. Thus, this work has got great relevance to pediatric dentists. This study also suggests the potential clinical utility of immunological markers in the diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment of dental caries in both pediatric and adult patients, emphasizing the value of multidisciplinary cooperation and creative research strategies in expanding the knowledge of oral diseases and enhancing patient outcomes among the clinical practitioners and researchers. Thus, a multidisciplinary approach is needed to unravel the pathogenesis of oral diseases.

blocks.text: The national prevalence of dental caries in Nigeria is currently unknown. The objective of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to determine the prevalence of dental caries in the primary, mixed and permanent dentition among residents in urban, rural and semi-urban Nigeria.

A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL and Embase databases and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2001 and December 2023 reporting the prevalence of dental caries in Nigeria. The review was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42022362019) and conducted in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Data extracted included study design, sample size, age of participants, and study location. Study quality and risk of bias were assessed. A random-effects meta-analysis was performed to estimate pooled prevalence.

A total of 1,010 records were identified, of which 52 studies were included in the systematic review and 35 were eligible for meta-analysis. Most studies were conducted in Southwestern Nigeria. The overall pooled prevalence of dental caries in Nigeria was 17% (95% CI: 14%–21%; I² = 97%). The pooled prevalence was 16% (95% CI: 10%–24%; I² = 98%) in primary dentition, 16% (95% CI: 11%–23%; I² = 97%) in mixed dentition, and 20% (95% CI: 16%–26%; I² = 96%) in permanent dentition. By setting, the pooled prevalence was 22% (95% CI: 7%–52%; I² = 98%) in rural areas, 17% (95% CI: 14%–22%; I² = 97%) in semi-urban areas, and 14% (95% CI: 6%–29%; I² = 98%) in urban areas. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies.

Dental caries remains a significant public health concern in Nigeria, affecting approximately one in five individuals. Although variations were observed across dentition types and geographic settings, substantial heterogeneity indicates diverse epidemiological contexts across the country. Strengthened preventive strategies and improved access to oral healthcare services are needed to address the burden of dental caries nationwide.

Dental caries is a worldwide health issue [1–4], affecting approximately 2.3 billion people with caries in permanent teeth and 514 million children with caries in primary teeth worldwide [2]. Dental caries represent a lifelong health burden, beginning in childhood and potentially persisting into adulthood if untreated [3]. Among children, dental caries is one of the most common conditions affecting the deciduous dentition [5,6], and globally, approximately 34% of the population has untreated cavities in permanent teeth [2]. These figures underscore the need for coordinated global responses tailored to context-specific risk factors and health system capacities.

The burden of dental caries is particularly concerning in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where prevalence remains high and continues to increase [4,7]. Many LMICs face significant challenges, including limited access to dental care, inadequate resources, and disparities in oral health education [8,9]. Untreated dental caries has far-reaching consequences for health and well-being. It is associated with pain, difficulty chewing, and dietary restrictions, which may contribute to nutritional deficiencies [10–16]. Beyond physical health, dental caries also has psychosocial implications, including social stigma, reduced self-esteem, social withdrawal, and poorer mental health outcomes [17–19]. The economic burden is substantial as well, encompassing treatment costs, missed workdays, and reduced productivity [20]. These challenges are compounded in settings with limited oral health insurance coverage [4,21], low awareness of preventive oral healthcare [22], and a high prevalence of poor mental health and reduced quality of life [23].

Nigeria, as an LMIC, faces similar challenges. Reports indicate a considerable burden of untreated dental caries in both permanent and deciduous dentition [23]. Despite increasing recognition of oral health as an important component of overall health, comprehensive national data on the prevalence of dental caries in Nigeria remain limited [24]. Data from the Global Burden of Disease Study show that between 1990 and 2017, the number of persons with untreated caries in Nigeria increased by 22.5% in primary dentition and by 91.5% in permanent dentition [25]. Although Nigeria ranked as the 20th African country with the lowest percentage change in oral disease prevalence during this period [25], these increases highlight the need for updated and nationally synthesized epidemiological evidence. Establishing reliable baseline prevalence estimates is essential for informing strategic planning, prevention programs, and policy decisions related to caries control [26].

Given these gaps, a comprehensive synthesis of existing evidence is necessary to better understand the epidemiology of dental caries in Nigeria. By integrating data across different regions and examining variations by dentition type and geographical setting (urban, rural, and semi-urban), this study provides a clearer picture of the burden and distribution of dental caries in the country. Such evidence is critical for guiding targeted public health interventions, improving resource allocation, and strengthening oral health policies.

This systematic review and meta-analysis therefore aim to determine the pooled prevalence of dental caries in primary, mixed, and permanent dentition among the Nigerian population and to explore differences in prevalence by geographical location.

This systematic review and meta-analysis was registered with PROSPERO (CRD42022362019). The study was reported following the Preferred Reporting Item for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) statement and checklist [27] (See S1 File).

What is the prevalence and severity of dental caries in the primary, mixed, and permanent dentition among residents in Nigeria, and how does this vary by geographical location (urban, rural, semi-urban)?

sections.title: Search strategy and selection of studies
heading_path: Search strategy and selection of studies

blocks.text: PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, and Google Scholar were searched from January 2001 to December 2023. The search targeted studies focused on dental caries and tooth decay in various types of teeth, in the Nigerian population, with emphasis on epidemiological concepts such as prevalence, burden, incidence, severity, and demographics. The search terms used for the search from the databases with the Boolean operators “OR” and “AND” are:

(“dental caries,” OR “tooth decay,” OR “caries,” OR “tooth caries,” OR “tooth decay”) AND (“primary teeth,” OR “deciduous teeth,” OR “milk teeth,” OR “baby teeth,” OR “permanent teeth,” OR “mixed dentition”) AND (“Nigeria,” OR “Nigerian”) AND (“prevalence,” OR “burden of disease,” OR “severity of illness index,” OR “incidence,” OR “epidemiology,” OR “demography”). The detailed search strategy are described in S2 File.

The search outcomes in the database were downloaded to the reference management software EndNote X9 and duplicate items were sorted out and removed. Two authors (O.R.A. and M.T.O.) independently assessed the title and abstracts of each study to assess if it met the inclusion criteria. Studies that did not meet the inclusion criteria were excluded. Two authors (O.M.O. and I.E.A.) independently assessed the eligibility of the retrieved papers and resolved disagreements by discussion or recourse to a third author (A.C. or F.T.A.).

All published and unpublished studies, including grey literature reporting on the prevalence of dental caries in Nigeria’s permanent and deciduous dentition, were eligible for study inclusion. These included cross-sectional, cohort, and case-control studies. For non-cross-sectional studies, inclusion in the meta-analysis was limited to studies that reported extractable prevalence-related data at a defined assessment point relevant to the review objective. There was no language restriction.

Studies were excluded if they did not provide information on the sample size, had inaccurate or unavailable outcome data, had no data on the prevalence of dental caries, and featured duplicate samples. Furthermore, review articles, studies with overlapping data from other included studies, case reports, case series, editorials, laboratory investigations, or reviews devoid of primary data were also excluded. The detailed excluded studies and the reasons are reported in S3 File.

Four independent authors (I.E.A., M.T.O., A.C., and O.R.A.) used a pretested data extraction form prepared in Microsoft Excel to independently extract details of articles that met the inclusion criteria. The information was the author’s name, year of article publication, study design (cross-sectional, cohort-based), study location, and study setting were recorded. Information on the study participants (sample size and age range) was extracted. The prevalence of dental caries in each study was also extracted. Discrepancies among reviewers during the extraction process were resolved by a fifth author (F.T.A.).

sections.title: Quality and risk of bias assessment
heading_path: Quality and risk of bias assessment

blocks.text: The quality of all the included articles was assessed by two independents researchers (O.R.A. and M.T.O.). Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklist for prevalence studies was used to establish risk of biasness in included article [28]. JBI appraisal checklist for prevalence studies is based on 9 questions: (1) Was the sample frame appropriate to address the target population? (2) Were the study participants sampled in an appropriate way? (3) Was the sample size adequate? (4) Were the study subjects and the setting described in detail? (5) Was the data analysis conducted with sufficient coverage of the identified sample? (6) Were valid methods used for the identification of the condition? (7) Was the condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants? (8) Was there appropriate statistical analysis? (9) Was the response rate adequate, and if not, was the low response rate managed appropriately? [28]. Each of the question was analyzed by giving score 1 or 0 (yes = 1), (no = 0), and (unclear or not applicable = 0). The over-all score for each included study was presented as percentages and study was characterized according to different degrees of risk of bias (high risk of bias if 20–50% items scored yes, moderate risk of bias if 50–80% items scored yes, and low risk of bias if 80–100% items scored yes as per JBI checklist). (See S1 Table)

The GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach is a structured and transparent method for assessing the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations in healthcare research. This approach evaluates the quality of evidence based on several criteria, including study design, consistency of findings, directness of evidence, precision of estimates, and risk of bias. The evidence is then rated into four categories: high, moderate, low, or very low.

In this study, the GRADE approach was applied to assess the quality of evidence from the included studies critically. This involved a systematic review of each study, applying the GRADE criteria rigorously to ensure that the conclusions drawn are based on reliable evidence. GRADE ensures that any recommendations are supported by the highest quality evidence available and are relevant to real-world clinical settings. Further details about the GRADE methodology can be found in the GRADEpro software, which is freely accessible via Cochrane resources (http://tech.cochrane.org/revman/gradepro). (See S2 Table)

In this systematic review, no missing data were identified across the included studies. As a result, no additional efforts were required to contact primary authors or impute missing data. All data reported in the studies were complete and were analyzed as presented.

The data included in the studies were synthesized using qualitative and quantitative approaches. In the qualitative synthesis, key characteristics of the included studies, such as study design, population demographics, and geographic location, were summarized to provide an overview of dental caries prevalence in Nigeria. The studies were grouped by their settings (urban, rural, or semi-urban) and dentition types (primary, mixed, or permanent), and patterns were identified across different regions of the country. Participant characteristics, such as age groups and sample sizes, were also summarized. The synthesis helped identify gaps in the literature, including underrepresentation from certain regions, and provided a broader understanding of the factors influencing dental caries prevalence in Nigeria.

All statistical analyses were conducted using R software (RStudio environment). The pooled prevalence of dental caries was estimated using a random-effects meta-analysis based on the DerSimonian and Laird method. A random-effects approach was selected a priori due to anticipated clinical and methodological heterogeneity across studies, including differences in study populations, geographic regions, and diagnostic criteria [29,30].

For studies that did not report standard errors (S.E.), these were calculated from the reported prevalence and sample size using standard formulas. Prevalence estimates were logit-transformed where appropriate to stabilize variances prior to pooling. Pooled prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were then back-transformed for presentation.

Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q test (p < 0.10 indicating significant heterogeneity) and quantified using the I² statistic, with values of approximately 25%, 50%, and ≥75% interpreted as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity, respectively. The between-study variance (τ²) was also reported [29,30].
Subgroup analyses were conducted according to geographical setting and dentition type. Differences between subgroups were evaluated using the chi-square test for subgroup differences.
Meta-regression analysis was performed using publication year as a continuous moderator to evaluate potential temporal trends in prevalence estimates.

Publication bias and small-study effects were assessed through visual inspection of funnel plots and formally evaluated using Egger’s linear regression test. A p-value < 0.05 was considered indicative of statistically significant small-study effects.

Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the pooled prevalence estimate. First, a leave-one-out influence analysis was conducted by sequentially excluding each study and recalculating the pooled prevalence to determine whether any individual study disproportionately influenced the overall estimate. Second, a trim-and-fill analysis was performed in R to evaluate the potential impact of missing studies due to publication bias and to generate an adjusted pooled prevalence estimate. In addition, sensitivity analysis was used to evaluate the influence of study design on the pooled estimate, including the effect of excluding the single retrospective/cohort-type study included in the meta-analysis.
All statistical tests were two-sided, and statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 unless otherwise specified.
Ethical approval was not required for this systematic review as the research was based on information retrieved from published studies.

As shown in Fig 1, 1,010 records were retrieved. After removing duplicates, 995 records remained for eligibility screening based on title and abstract. Of these, 886 studies were excluded based on title and abstract. After reviewing the full-text records of 107 studies (106 from the search on databases and a study from a citation search), 52 met the inclusion criteria [20,31–97].

blocks.text: The sample size of the included studies ranged from 17 to 2,835 with an aggregated number of 38,253 study participants. There were 48 (92.3%) cross-sectional studies [13,20,25,26,31–53,55–76,78–83,85–92,94,95] and 4 cohort studies [36,43,54,77].

Most of the studies were conducted in Southwest Nigeria: 14 studies in Lagos State [31,32,34,35,48,54,65–68,73,77–80,92], 11 studies in Osun State [33,37,49–53,56,57,75–77,85–89,94,96], seven studies in Oyo State [20,43–46,55,58,72], and a study in Ogun State [38] respectively. Some other studies were conducted in South-south Nigeria: four in Edo State [36,40,42,59,60,82,83] and three in Rivers State [41,47,64,84]. Four studies were conducted in Enugu, in the southeastern part of Nigeria [62,69–71,91]. The remaining studies were conducted in the Northern Territory part of Nigeria: a study in Kwara State [81,90,95] in Northcentral Nigeria, and three studies in Northwestern Nigeria: two studies in Kano State [39,63], and a study in Sokoto State [61]. There is no data from Northeastern Nigeria.

In addition, 21 (40.4%) articles demonstrated a low risk of bias [20,32,34,38,40,42–45,49–52,57, 59,62,63,72,75,76,81,83–89,94,96], 30 (57.7%) articles had moderate-risk of bias category [33,35–37,39,41,46–48,53–56,58,60,61,64–71,73,74,77–80] and a study had high risk of bias [31,95].

Also, 49 (94.2%) of the studies used the Decayed, Missing, and Filled Teeth index for permanent teeth (dmft/DMFT) index to assess dental caries [20,31–35,37–61,64,65,67–81]. A study used the International Caries Detection and Assessment System (ICDAS) index to assess dental caries [36].

The studies were generally categorized into three quality levels: low, moderate, and high risk of bias. Most studies 40.4% (21/52) had low risk of bias [20,32,34,38,40,42–45,49–52,57,59,62,63,72,75,76,81] while 57.7% (30/52) had a moderate risk of bias [35–39,41,46–48,53–56,58,60,61,64–71,73,74,77–80]. Studies with low risk of bias generally met key criteria like adequate sample size, detailed descriptions of the population and setting, appropriate sampling techniques, and valid and reliable methods for measuring the condition of interest. On the other hand, a study had a high risk of bias [31] due to weaknesses in sample size adequacy and the use of less reliable condition identification methods. (See S3 File)

Table 3 shows the profile of the 35 studies included in the meta-analysis. These were 13 studies showing the prevalence of dental caries in primary dentition, with dental caries prevalence ranging from 1.37% [71] to 95.6% [65]. Twelve studies showed dental caries’ prevalence in mixed dentition, with dental caries prevalence ranging from 5.20% [50] to 29.2% [67]. Nineteen studies showed dental caries’ prevalence in permanent dentition, ranging from 1.16% [38] to 64.7% [43]. The sample size for the studies in the primary dentition was 7,932, for the mixed dentition was 9,223, and for the permanent dentition was 10,729.

blocks.text: In addition, 20 (38.5%) studies included were conducted in the urban setting [32,35,40–46,53,55,58,62,65–71], three (5.77%) were conducted in rural settings [38,61,64] and 12 (23.1%) were conducted in semi-urban settings [33,37,48,50–52,56,57,63,72,78,79]. The prevalence of dental caries ranged from 6.60% [53] to 82.1% [65] in the urban setting, 12.3% [38] to 35.6% [61] in the rural setting, and 3.3% [52] to 24.7% [72].in the semi-urban setting.

Furthermore, of the 13 studies [32,46,51–53,55,57,65–67,69,70,79] in the primary dentition, 9 were conducted in the urban setting with prevalence ranging from 1.37% to 95.60% [51,52,57,79], 4 were conducted in the semi-urban setting with prevalence ranging from 3.02% to 10.54% [32,46,53,55,65–67,69,70], and there were no studies conducted in the rural setting.

Of the 12 studies in the mixed dentition [35,37,38,44,50,56,57,61,63,67,68,70], 5 were conducted in the urban setting with prevalence ranging from 9.31% to 29.2% [35,44,67,68,70], 2 were conducted in the rural setting with prevalence ranging from 11.1% to 13.0% [38,61], and 5 were conducted in the semi-urban setting with prevalence ranging from 5.20% to 22.9% [37,50,56,57,63].

Of the 19 studies in the permanent dentition [33,37,38,40–43,45,48,58,61,62,64,67,68,70–72,78], 11 were conducted in the urban setting with prevalence ranging from 1.52% to 64.7% [40–43,45,58,62,67,68,70,71], 3 were conducted in the rural setting with prevalence ranging from 1.16% to 35.1% [38,61,64], and 5 were conducted in the semi-urban setting with prevalence ranging from 7.36% to 24.7% [33,37,48,72,78].

Fig 2 presents the forest plot of the pooled prevalence of dental caries in Nigeria. Based on a random-effects meta-analysis, the overall pooled prevalence was 17% (95% CI: 14%–21%). Substantial heterogeneity was observed among the included studies (I² = 97%, χ² = 1312.83, p < 0.01), indicating considerable variability in prevalence estimates across different study populations, geographic locations, and methodological characteristics. Given the high heterogeneity, the pooled estimate should be interpreted as an average prevalence across diverse study contexts rather than a single uniform national rate.
Fig 2 Prevalence of dental caries in Nigeria.

sections.title: Prevalence of dental caries in primary dentition Nigeria
heading_path: Prevalence of dental caries in primary dentition Nigeria

blocks.text: As shown in Fig 3, the pooled prevalence of dental caries in primary dentition was 16% (95% CI: 10%–24%) based on a random-effects model. Substantial heterogeneity was observed among the included studies (I² = 98%, p < 0.01), indicating considerable variability across study settings and populations. Also, the pooled prevalence of dental caries in mixed dentition was 16% (95% CI: 11%–23%). There was substantial heterogeneity across studies (I² = 97%, p < 0.01), reflecting differences in population characteristics and study methodology. Also, the pooled prevalence of dental caries in permanent dentition was 20% (95% CI: 16%–26%). High heterogeneity was also observed (I² = 96%, p < 0.01), suggesting notable between-study variability.
Fig 3 Prevalence of dental caries in primary, mixed and permanent dentition.
The test for subgroup differences was not statistically significant (χ² = 1.53, df = 2, p = 0.47), indicating that prevalence did not significantly differ across dentition types.

sections.title: Prevalence of dental caries by study setting in Nigeria
heading_path: Prevalence of dental caries by study setting in Nigeria

blocks.text: As shown in Fig 4, the pooled prevalence of dental caries varied across study settings. In urban settings, the pooled prevalence was 14% (95% CI: 6%–29%), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 98%, p < 0.01). In semi-urban settings, the pooled prevalence was 17% (95% CI: 14%–22%), with high heterogeneity (I² = 97%, p < 0.01). In rural settings, the pooled prevalence was 22% (95% CI: 7%–52%), also with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 98%, p < 0.01).
Fig 4 Prevalence of dental caries in study settings in Nigeria.

Despite apparent differences in point estimates, the test for subgroup differences was not statistically significant (χ² = 0.43, df = 2, p = 0.81), indicating that prevalence did not significantly differ across study settings.

Fig 5 present the funnel plots used to assess potential publication bias. Visual inspection suggested some degree of asymmetry. However, Egger’s linear regression test did not demonstrate statistically significant evidence of funnel plot asymmetry or small-study effects (t = –0.60, df = 33, p = 0.552).
Fig 5 Funnel plot of comparison.

Given the substantial heterogeneity observed across studies (I² ≈ 97–99%), the apparent asymmetry may reflect genuine between-study variability in population characteristics, study settings, and diagnostic criteria rather than true publication bias. Therefore, statistical evidence of publication bias was not detected..

Fig 6 presents the meta-regression analysis examining publication year as a continuous moderator of dental caries prevalence. The regression model demonstrated a positive but statistically non-significant association between year of publication and prevalence (coefficient = 0.0384, p = 0.139). Although the regression line indicates a slight upward temporal trend, the wide confidence band and non-significant p-value suggest that publication year did not significantly explain the observed between-study heterogeneity. Therefore, temporal variation was not a significant predictor of pooled prevalence in this analysis.
Fig 6 Meta-regression.

Fig 7 displays the random-effects meta-regression forest plot using logit-transformed prevalence estimates. The pooled logit prevalence was −1.74 (95% CI: −1.95 to −1.53), corresponding to a back-transformed prevalence of approximately 17%. Individual study weights ranged from 1.4% to 1.8%, indicating relatively similar precision across studies. Despite substantial heterogeneity, the pooled estimate remained stable within the confidence interval shown.
Fig 7 Random-effects meta-regression model.

Fig 8 presents the leave-one-out sensitivity analysis. Sequential exclusion of each individual study did not materially alter the pooled prevalence estimate. The pooled estimate remained stable across iterations, with only minimal fluctuations. Notably, exclusion of the only retrospective/cohort-type study included in the meta-analysis did not materially alter the pooled prevalence estimate, further supporting the robustness of the findings.
Fig 8 Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis.

Fig 9 illustrates the trim-and-fill analysis conducted to assess the potential impact of small-study effects. Although the method suggested the possible presence of missing studies, the adjusted pooled prevalence (0.22; 95% CI: 0.17–0.26) remained comparable to the original pooled estimate. This suggests that any potential small-study effects or publication bias did not meaningfully affect the overall conclusions of the meta-analysis.
Fig 9 Trim-and-fill analysis.

The findings of this study indicate that approximately one in five individuals in Nigeria has dental caries. The highest pooled prevalence was observed in primary dentition, followed by permanent dentition, while the lowest prevalence was recorded in mixed dentition. Dental caries were more common in rural areas than in urban settings and least common in semi-urban areas. Data were available from five of Nigeria’s six geopolitical zones, although publications were disproportionately concentrated in Southwestern Nigeria. Overall, studies were conducted in only 10 of the 36 Nigerian states. Over the past 18 years, there has been a steady increase in publications on dental caries prevalence in Nigeria, reflecting growing academic interest and recognition of oral health as a public health concern.

The burden of dental caries in Nigeria remains substantial. However, the pooled estimate should be interpreted in the context of the considerable heterogeneity observed across studies (I² > 95%). This variability likely reflects genuine differences in study populations, age distributions, geographic settings, diagnostic criteria, and access to dental services rather than methodological limitations alone. The meta-regression analysis demonstrated that publication year did not significantly explain this heterogeneity, suggesting that contextual and structural factors may be driving the observed variability. Therefore, the pooled estimate represents a summary of diverse epidemiological contexts across Nigeria rather than a single uniform national prevalence.

Similar to other emerging economies, Nigeria’s oral healthcare system remains largely curative, with limited implementation of sustained community-based oral health promotion programs [98,99]. Despite this, the pooled prevalence reported in this study is lower than that reported in Ethiopia (40.98%) [100], China (41.15% − 67%) [101], Gulf countries (64.7%) [102], Brazil (72.9%) [103], and Kosovo (72.0%) [104]. Previous reports have also suggested relatively low caries prevalence in primary dentition in Nigeria [50]. The reasons for this comparatively lower prevalence remain unclear, particularly given Nigeria’s similar socioeconomic context to other low- and middle-income countries. One possible explanation may be the reported high use of fluoridated toothpaste [86]. Nonetheless, further epidemiological studies are required to clarify contributory behavioral and environmental factors.

The analysis further showed that caries prevalence varied by dentition type, with the highest prevalence in primary dentition and the lowest in mixed dentition. Although the prevalence in primary dentition was slightly higher than in permanent dentition, the difference was not statistically significant. This contrasts with findings from Eastern Mediterranean countries [105] and East Africa [106], where caries prevalence increases with age. Age-related increases in caries may result from cumulative plaque accumulation, age-related reductions in salivary flow and buffering capacity, gingival recession exposing vulnerable root surfaces, increased lifetime exposure to sugary diets, and degradation of dental restorations over time [107–111]. The similarity between primary and permanent dentition in Nigeria therefore warrants further investigation to identify local determinants that may modify these patterns.

With respect to geographical setting, caries prevalence was higher in rural areas than urban areas and lowest in semi-urban settings. This aligns with evidence highlighting rural challenges, including limited access to dental services, lower oral health literacy, and restricted preventive care [105]. Urban populations may benefit from better access to healthcare facilities and oral health education, contributing to improved outcomes [105]. Similar patterns have been reported in Yemen [112].

Urban–rural disparities may reflect broader social inequalities influencing oral health behaviors and service access. Differences in access to fluoridated water, preventive services, restorative care, and community-level interventions likely contribute to these patterns. Although urbanization has been associated with increased caries risk in some settings, this effect often attenuates after adjusting for socioeconomic status [113]. While the present study indicates lower overall prevalence in urban areas, urban slum populations may remain particularly vulnerable [72]. Future research exploring intra-urban and intra-rural disparities would help identify high-risk subpopulations.

The relatively lower prevalence observed in semi-urban populations may partly reflect contextual factors or reporting bias. Many semi-urban studies were conducted in towns with relatively better access to tertiary dental services and ongoing oral health initiatives. Further research is needed to disentangle the effects of lifestyle, access to care, and socioeconomic conditions across rural, semi-urban, and urban populations in Nigeria.

This study represents the first comprehensive pooled prevalence analysis of dental caries in Nigeria, providing nationally synthesized evidence on disease burden. Strengths include an extensive multi-database search, systematic review and meta-analysis procedures, independent data extraction by four reviewers, absence of language restrictions, and formal quality assessment. Inclusion of low- and moderate-risk studies enhances the credibility and applicability of the findings [114,115].

Nonetheless, limitations should be acknowledged. The overrepresentation of studies from Southwestern Nigeria, where 35.3% of Nigeria’s 17 dental schools are located, may limit national generalizability. Although two authors contributed multiple studies, each was conducted in independent populations without overlapping samples, reducing the likelihood of clustering bias at the author level. Although one retrospective hospital-based study was included in the meta-analysis [43], leave-one-out sensitivity analysis demonstrated that its inclusion did not materially influence the pooled estimate; nevertheless, its clinical context differed from the predominantly cross-sectional studies and should be considered when interpreting the findings. Despite these limitations, this study provides important and updated evidence on the epidemiology of dental caries in Nigeria.

This systematic review and meta-analysis provides the first nationally synthesized estimate of dental caries prevalence in Nigeria. The pooled prevalence of approximately 17% indicates that dental caries remains a significant public health concern in the country. Although variations were observed across dentition types and geographical settings, these differences were not statistically significant, and substantial heterogeneity reflects the diverse epidemiological contexts across Nigeria. These findings underscore the need for strengthened preventive strategies, improved access to oral healthcare services, and context-specific public health interventions to address the burden of dental caries nationwide. Further high-quality epidemiological studies are required to better understand regional disparities and determinants of caries risk in Nigeria.

title: Parental Cognition Regarding Children’s Sugar Consumption and Its Implications for Dental Caries Prevention: A Systematic Review
