sections.title: First stage: Adherence and lag
heading_path: Dental plaque identified as a biofilm
Stages of biofilm formation in dental plaques

blocks.text: In the initial stage of oral biofilm formation, planktonic (free-floating) bacteria approach and attach to the tooth surface, specifically, to the acquired enamel pellicle. This adherence is initially reversible, mediated by weak physicochemical forces (such as van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions), and soon becomes irreversible as bacteria use surface structures such as pili and adhesins to secure their attachment. This phase also involves a genetic shift in bacteria, with the upregulation of genes related to biofilm survival and resistance. As a result, bacterial growth slows temporarily in what is termed a ‘lag phase’, allowing for the establishment of a stable colonising population.26,50,51

sections.title: Second stage: Accelerated growth
heading_path: Dental plaque identified as a biofilm
Stages of biofilm formation in dental plaques

blocks.text: Once securely attached, bacteria begin to proliferate rapidly. This accelerated growth phase is characterised by active cell division, the recruitment and coaggregation of additional bacterial species, and the secretion of abundant EPSs, primarily polysaccharides and proteins. These secretions form a robust matrix that encapsulates the cells, fostering structural stratification and further complexity within the biofilm. The matrix not only supports additional bacterial adhesion but also enhances resistance to environmental stresses and antimicrobial agents.50,52

sections.title: Third stage: Stable attachment
heading_path: Dental plaque identified as a biofilm
Stages of biofilm formation in dental plaques

blocks.text: In the steady-state or stable attachment phase, the biofilm matures into a dense and highly organised microbial community. The growth rates of bacteria are slow, with metabolic activity often downregulated deep within the biofilm. At this point, the matrix becomes more complex and protective, and the established biofilm exhibits increased tolerance to antimicrobials and host immune defenses. Channels and pores develop, allowing for nutrient circulation. The mature biofilm can remain stable for extended periods and may occasionally release clusters of cells or single bacteria, contributing to colonisation elsewhere in the oral cavity.26,50,52

sections.title: Different bacterial mechanisms in gum and dental plaque infection
heading_path: Different bacterial mechanisms in gum and dental plaque infection

blocks.text: The enamel surface predominantly contains negatively charged phosphate groups that interact directly or indirectly with positively charged components of salivary and crevicular fluid macromolecules. Within a few hours of pellicle formation, bacteria colonise the pellicle-coated tooth surface. These initial colonisers are mainly gram-positive microorganisms, such as Actinomyces viscosus and S. sanguinis. These primary colonisers adhere to the pellicle via specific surface molecules called adhesins, which interact with receptors in the dental pellicle. The major constituents of the pellicle include salivary glycoproteins, phosphoproteins, and lipids, such as statherin, amylase, and proline-rich peptides.53

For example, A. viscosus cells possess fibrous protein structures termed fimbriae, which extend from their surface. Protein adhesins on these fimbriae specifically bind to proline-rich proteins within the dental pellicle, facilitating bacterial attachment to the pellicle-coated enamel surface.45,54 Following initial colonisation, the plaque mass matures through the growth of these attached species and colonisation by additional microbial species. Microorganisms are predominantly transported passively to the tooth surface via saliva flow; few oral bacterial species are motile (eg, possessing flagella), mainly inhabiting subgingival sites. Dental plaque can typically be visualised on teeth after 1 to 2 days without oral hygiene measures. It appears white, grayish, or yellowish and has a globular morphology. Effective oral hygiene can remove these pellicle and plaque layers.55,56

Several treatment modalities aim to remove plaque and extrinsic stains; patient-friendly approaches are generally better accepted than clinical interventions are. Certain chemical toothpastes inhibit plaque adherence by altering the tooth surface environment. For example, hydrogen peroxide acts by releasing nascent oxygen, whereas abrasive agents such as baking soda or silica mechanically cleanse the tooth surface. Some toothpastes contain specific enzymes believed to degrade plaque and stains, thereby improving gingival health. These formulations are biocompatible with the tooth surface and surrounding soft tissues.57

The initial colonisers represent a highly selected subset of the oral microflora. Within minutes after pellicle formation, coccal bacteria primarily streptococci of the mitis group (eg, S. sanguinis, S. oralis, and S. mitis biovar) are detectable on the surface. S. sanguinis and S. oralis produce IgA1 protease, which may help these bacteria evade a key element of host immune defense during early plaque formation.58

Other species, such as Actinomyces spp., typically appear after approximately 2 hours, along with Haemophilus and Neisseria spp. Obligate anaerobic species are rarely detected at this stage and generally remain in low numbers.47 Mixed-cell aggregates may also attach concurrently. Once adhered, these pioneer populations initiate cell division and form microcolonies. These early colonisers become embedded within extracellular bacterial slimes and polysaccharides, mixed with additional layers of adsorbed salivary proteins and glycoproteins.59,60 The streptococcal mitis group possesses multiple glycosidase activities that enable them to interact with and utilise salivary glycoproteins as substrates. The highest rates of bacterial multiplication occur during these early stages of plaque development.47

In addition to maintaining good oral hygiene habits, several other effective measures are available to prevent dental plaque accumulation. These include reducing the intake of sugary and starchy foods and beverages, drinking sufficient amounts of water, and chewing sugar-free gum after meals to stimulate saliva production, which helps neutralise acids in the oral cavity.

The human oral cavity harbours over 500 distinct bacterial species spanning diverse phyla, such as Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Tenericutes, Actinobacteria, Proteobacteria, Euryarchaeota, Chlamydiae, and Spirochaetes. Many of these microorganisms colonise the gingival sulci and tooth surfaces, forming biofilms that lead to dental plaque formation. The metabolic activities of these bacteria result in acid production, which demineralises enamel and causes caries and potentially infections. The diagnosis of oral bacterial infections is largely clinical, and antibiotics are often prescribed empirically for treatment or prophylaxis. However, definitive characterisation, precise diagnosis, and antimicrobial susceptibility testing are essential for guiding appropriate therapy and preventing disease progression.61

Antimicrobial dental materials are critical for reducing bacterial adhesion and inhibiting biofilm formation, as the majority of oral infections originate from these biofilms. Significant research has focused on developing dental materials with antimicrobial properties through various mechanisms, including antimicrobial agent release, contact killing, and multifunctional capabilities.62 The antibiotics most frequently used to manage odontogenic and periodontal infections include β-lactams, macrolides, lincosamides, nitroimidazoles, and tetracyclines—antibiotics well-suited for treating dental pathologies.63, 64, 65

Macrolides such as erythromycin, clarithromycin, and azithromycin primarily exhibit bacteriostatic effects by inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis through binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit. At higher concentrations, they may exhibit bactericidal properties. Tetracyclines inhibit protein synthesis by binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit, preventing aminoacyl-tRNA binding to the ribosome’s acceptor site. They traverse bacterial outer membranes via porin channels and can cross the cytoplasmic membrane without requiring a lipophilic, dissociated form.66 Metronidazole, a nitroimidazole, exerts cytotoxicity by interacting with anaerobic bacterial DNA.67 Its nitro group undergoes intracellular reduction, producing reactive intermediates that specifically target anaerobic bacteria.65,67

Antiplaque agents such as essential oils (eg, eugenol and clove oils) and surfactants such as sodium lauryl sulphate have demonstrated efficacy in preventing and removing dental plaque. Additionally, antimicrobial agents, including bisbiguanides (eg, chlorhexidine), metal ions (such as silver and zinc), phenolic compounds, and quaternary ammonium compounds, have been successfully incorporated alongside antiplaque agents into toothpastes and mouthwashes to control and eradicate oral biofilms.47,62 Furthermore, the use of probiotics and prebiotics is emerging as a promising adjunct therapy to favourably modulate the oral microbiome, inhibit pathogenic biofilm formation, and enhance oral health.68

The contact-killing approach involves integrating wide-ranging antimicrobial agents, ranging from synthetic chemicals such as quaternary ammonium compounds and polycations to natural biomolecules, such as AMPs, directly into dental materials. These compounds are nontoxic, readily incorporated into dental composites or adhesives, and form covalent bonds to maintain long-term antimicrobial activity.62

These agents provide broad-spectrum activity against both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria upon contact with the material surface. This strategy has several advantages: it is nontoxic, offers long-lasting antimicrobial effects, and results in minimal irritation to oral tissues. However, limitations include predominantly bacteriostatic rather than bactericidal effects, which may allow some surviving bacteria and the development of surface biofouling characterised by roughness on tooth surfaces.47,62 Novel approaches are currently under investigation to overcome these drawbacks, including stimuli-responsive antimicrobial surfaces that release agents upon bacterial adhesion and combined therapies that integrate contact killing with controlled agent release for enhanced effectiveness.69

Tooth development is driven by inductive signalling between oral epithelial cells and ectomesenchymal cells, both of which are derived from migrating neurocristal cells. These interactions produce an outer layer of enamel, which is formed by epithelial cell-derived ameloblasts.70 The enamel covers the crown of the tooth, which is located in the oral cavity, and the cementum, a thin layer of bone-like tissue, covers the root surface of the tooth. The inner layer of living mineralised dentin, which is synthesised by odontoblasts and ultimately the pulp core, benefits these hard tissues. The dental pulp is a soft, connective tissue contained within a hard, mineralised cavity with a limited opening at the root end that allows blood and nerve elements to enter and vascularise and innervate the tissue. The pulp fills both the tooth cavity (cavity pulp) and the root canals of the tooth. The pulp is characterised by cellular diversity, sensory innervation, and rich microcirculation.71

The tissue contains different types of fibroblast populations and a ground substance rich in proteoglycans and glycolipids, collagen, and elastic fibres.72 Several distinct regions are visible as histological features within the pulp. The ‘cell-rich zone’ within the histological structure of the pulp constitutes the pulp core, which is the central part and main mass of the pulp and contains human dental pulp stem cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells.73 Part of the pulp core contains the neurovascular network, which is located medially in the coronal chamber and root canal of the tooth.74 The second histologically distinct zone is a pale layer called the Will zone, which contains single fibroblasts, collagen, and elastic fibres.75 The last zone is known as the ‘odontoblastic layer’, which is a layer of odontoblasts and is located peripherally at the pulp‒dentin boundary.76

Odontoblasts (OBs) are dentin-forming cells whose processes extend into dentin, and their function intensifies when the repair process is activated. The dental pulp consists of connective tissue, mesenchymal cells, nerve fibres, blood vessels, and lymphatics.

The main functions of dentin are to produce dentin and maintain its biological and physiological vitality. Blood vessels and nerve bundles enter the dental pulp through the apical foramen, providing nutrition and a responsive sensory nervous system. This complex structure provides rigidity and stability; blood vessels and nerve bundles enter the dental pulp through the apical foramen, providing nutrition and a responsive sensory nervous system. This complex structure provides rigidity and stability; however, teeth remain vulnerable to damage caused by mechanical trauma, chemicals, oral cancers, and bacterial infections. Unlike bone, which can be regenerated and repaired, teeth are not able to regenerate completely quickly, and their repair processes are limited

After the formation of the dental crown, ameloblasts undergo programmed cell death and lose the ability to repair the enamel in vivo. Although odontoblasts cannot repair dentin in vivo, their progenitor cells or stem cells are able to migrate to the dentin surface and differentiate into odontoblasts to form restorative dentin. Unlike primary dentin, this tertiary reparative dentin is irregularly organised and has irregular dentinal tubules in the dentin matrix, but it provides a protective barrier for the dental pulp.

The ability to generate new odontoblasts throughout life in response to injury suggests a source of stem cells in the dental pulp. Gronthos et al.79 isolated and characterised these stem cells and named them DPSCs. DPSCs are a heterogeneous population of cells isolated from the pulp of human permanent third molars. These stem cells share similar properties with mesenchymal stem cells, except that DPSCs can differentiate into dentin-like odontoblast cells.80 Dental tissues are commonly discarded as medical waste. Cells with MSC properties can be obtained from various tissues, such as dental pulp, and are known as DPSCs.81 The gingiva is a source of gingival mesenchymal stem cells.82 Stem cells from the apical papilla are obtained from the apical papilla of developing roots. Stem cells from human deciduous teeth (SHEDs) are isolated from the latter source and originate from the embryonic neural crest as ectodermal mesenchymal stem cells.83

PDLSCs,84 alveolar bone marrow stromal cells, and dental follicle progenitor cells are isolated from dental follicles.85 The inner region of the dental pulp chamber contains highly proliferative stem cells that have self-renewal and differentiation properties. DPSCs were first reported in 2000. DPSCs are ectoderm-derived stem cells that originate from neural crest cells because they express GFAP, HNK-1, Nestin, P75, and S-100, which are markers of neural crest stem cells.6,76

Compared with bone marrow MSCs (BM-MSCs), DPSCs exhibit greater proliferative capacity, enhanced neurovascular differentiation potential, and superior odontogenic commitment.6 Unlike PDLSCs, which primarily support periodontal ligament regeneration, DPSCs uniquely secrete elevated levels of β-defensins and LL-37, endowing them with direct antimicrobial activity against key periodontal pathogens, such as Porphyromonas gingivalis and Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans.10,86 These attributes position DPSCs as particularly suited for dual-pathway therapy in biofilm-driven gingivitis.

These cells differentiate into mesenchymal cells phenotypically upon migration to the oral cavity early in development. Compared with equal volumes of dental pulp and bone marrow, dental pulp contains a greater number of MSCs, and DPSCs also have greater proliferative potential. Compared with other somatic cells, SHED-derived stem cells require more time to form primary colonies. DPSCs can be differentiated into a variety of cell types, including odontoblasts, osteoblasts, chondrocytes, cardiomyocytes, neurons, and adipocytes, via the modulation of growth factors, transcription factors, extracellular matrix proteins, and receptor molecules. DPSCs exhibit gene expression profiles and differentiation potential similar to those of bone marrow stem cells. DPSCs may have advantages over other stem cell types because teeth are easier to access—extracted teeth routinely provide a source of dental pulp tissue in dental clinics.70

The patient’s own stem cells can be obtained from DPSCs without the need for procedures that may require approval by a bioethics committee. In their study, Gronthos et al. isolated a clonogenic and rapidly proliferating population of cells from adult dental pulp.79 These cells have important similarities and differences with human BM-MSCs. In addition, Shi and Gronthos87 reported that the majority of DPSCs express the pericyte marker 3G5, an expression that is less frequently observed in BM-MSCs.80 Recently, Karaöz et al.88 compared DPSCs and BM-MSCs to confirm the intrinsic neurostromal properties of DPSCs and their ability to differentiate into neural and vascular endothelial cells in vitro. Mitsiadis et al.89 examined the region surrounding DPSCs and investigated the importance of Notch signalling in dentin repair.80

Additionally, a comparison of DPSCs with human BM-MSCs, which are precursors of odontoblasts, revealed that DPSCs produce only scattered, calcified nodules and are unable to form adipocytes, whereas BM-MSCs routinely calcify throughout the adherent cell layer and form clusters of lipid-rich adipocytes. DPSCs can form a dentin-like structure in immunodeficient mice.90 In contrast, BM-MSCs formed lamellar bone containing odontocytes and superficial odontoblasts that surrounded fibrous vascular tissue that contained adipocytes. Sloan and Waddington demonstrated that adult dental pulp-derived stem cell populations have a similar ability to generate clonogenic adherent colonies when grown and expanded under the same conditions as BM-MSCs. A comparison of DPSCs, SHEDs, adult PDLSCs, and BM-MSCs revealed that DPSCs, SHEDs, and PDLSCs maintained greater growth potential than did BM-MSCs.91

Yu et al. compared the odontogenic potential of BM-MSCs and DPSCs. Stromal progenitor cell marker (STRO-1)-positive DPSCs and BM-MSCs were isolated from mouse dental pulp and bone marrow, respectively.76 The odontogenic capacity of these strains was compared under the same inductive microenvironment generated by apical bud cells. Compared with BM-MSCs, DPSCs have greater odontogenic potential under postnatal apical bud cell induction. Therefore, DPSCs could be more effective for tooth regeneration.92

DPSCs can be derived from various dental tissues, such as exfoliated human primary and permanent teeth, apical papilla, periodontal ligament, and dental follicle tissue. DPSCs are good tools for regenerative medicine because they have the ability to differentiate into various cell types and can be easily isolated and retransplanted into the same person by autologous transplantation, which does not raise ethical issues related to their isolation.93 Recently, it has been shown that dental pulp contains a site that protects DPSCs from the cumulative effects of genetic and environmental factors and allows the cells to show acceptable differentiation and activity in the appropriate environment.94,95

Other advantages include ease of tissue harvesting, high initial cell function, short population doubling time, high potential capabilities, and immune system modulation properties, which make DPSCs suitable candidates for various types of therapy.96 DPSCs also show greater immunomodulatory capacity than do bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells because of the suppression of T-cell-mediated responses and increased proliferation in vitro during the first week of culture.97 These studies hold great promise for the use of DPSCs in research.

DPSCs in the pulp have multidifferentiation potential and share the characteristics of MSCs.98 Hence, they play a vital role in maintaining homeostasis and tooth repair after birth by replenishing odontoblasts during dentin repair.99 Furthermore, they can play a vital role in the regeneration of damaged teeth.100 Dental stem cells share similarities with BM-MSCs, with similar surface markers and matrix proteins associated with mineralisation (alkaline phosphates, osteocalcin, and osteopontin).79,87,101

Compared with BM-MSCs, DPSCs have a greater proliferation rate (∼30%), which can be attributed to the expression of cell cycle mediators such as cyclin-dependent kinase-6 and insulin-like growth factor in DPSCs.102 Dental pulp-derived stem cells are able to differentiate into odontoblastic (dentin-forming), osteoblastic (bone-forming), neurogenic (nerve-forming), adipogenic (fat-forming), myogenic (muscle-forming), chondrogenic (cartilage-forming), and melanocytic (pigment-forming) cell lineages in vitro. They are also able to form a mineralised matrix resembling dentin or bone and exhibit neurotrophic (nerve-feeding) properties when transplanted into immunodeficient mice.79,101,103

SHEDs are distinguished from DPSCs by their relatively higher proliferation rate, ‘round’ cell morphology, and inducible osteogenic capacity in vivo. SHEDs also possess the capacity to differentiate into neural and adipogenic lineages. Moreover, studies have demonstrated their ability to survive within the microenvironment when transplanted into the hippocampus of immunodeficient mice.104,105

In addition, researchers have successfully reprogrammed DPSCs into induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs). These iPSCs derived from DPSCs are indistinguishable from embryonic stem cells (ESCs) in terms of their ability to form embryoid bodies and express similar pluripotency markers. This advancement presents the potential for DPSCs to serve as an alternative to ESCs, preserving pluripotency without the ethical and legal concerns commonly associated with ESC usage.106,107

The potential pluripotency of DPSCs and their trans-differentiation properties also make them ideal targets for medical research. However, for obvious reasons, it is essential to perform experiments to reliably reproduce the results in animal models before transferring them to human studies.107 Govindasamy et al. recently investigated and transdifferentiated DPSCs into islet cell clusters similar to pancreatic islet cells. DPSC-derived islet cell clusters exhibit positive staining for dithizone, C-peptide, Pdx-1, Pax4, Pax6, Ngn3, and Isl-1 and release insulin in a glucose-dependent manner, confirming their function in vitro. These preliminary results suggest a promising role for DPSCs in the treatment of diabetes.108

Nesti et al. reported that when DPSCs were cocultured with rat dopaminergic cells, dopamine uptake by rat mesencephalic (midbrain) cells was not impaired in the presence of rotenone (a pesticide linked to the development of Parkinson’s disease in humans). This has been attributed to factors such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor and nerve growth factor released by DPSCs.109 Gandia et al. used the multipotentiality of DPSCs to treat myocardial infarction. Myocardial infarction was induced in the nude mice. DPSCs expanded in culture, and improvement in cardiac function was observed within 4 weeks after intramyocardial injection of DPSCs.110

In vitro studies have shown that limbal stem cells and SHED cells express similar markers, and when corneal cells reprogrammed from dental stem cells were transplanted onto the injured surface of the eye, successful repair of scarred corneas was observed in rabbits. Transplanted dental stem cells may have potential for use in humans with bilateral corneal damage and/or a complete lack of limbal stem cells.111,112 Kerkis et al. reported that human SHED cells expanded in culture and injected into the peritoneal cavity of golden retrievers with muscular dystrophy (the closest model to Duchenne muscular dystrophy in humans) persist in the host, engraft into host tissue, and differentiate into muscle tissue. They concluded that SHED has potential in the management of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.113

sections.title: Use of DPSCs for in situ pulp regeneration
heading_path: Use of DPSCs for in situ pulp regeneration

blocks.text: Many studies have shown that DPSCs may be used to regenerate partially lost pulp and dentin. Nakashima’s group demonstrated partial pulp regeneration via porcine pulp cells cultured as three-dimensional (3D) pellets.98 Dentin sialophosphoprotein expression confirmed the differentiation of DPSCs into odontoblasts. Furthermore, autologous bone morphogenetic protein-2 grafting of the pellet culture onto the resected canine pulp stimulated regenerative dentin formation.114

When the entire pulp tissue is lost, regeneration requires the formation of de novo pulp. To create a functional pulp for clinical use, several issues must be considered. First, the regenerated pulp tissue must be vascularised, even through blood supply only from the apical foramen. Second, newly differentiated odontoblasts must form on the existing dentin wall of the root canal space. Finally, new dentin must be produced by the differentiated odontoblasts on the existing dentin.115 A number of research groups have attempted to engineer pulp tissue substitutes that are physiologically similar to natural pulp tissue and have the potential to be used in root restorative procedures.80

Prescott et al. measured the efficacy of DPSCs in association with collagen scaffolds and dentin matrix protein 1 to form dental pulp-like tissue in subcutaneous grafts in mice. Mineral trioxide aggregate, which is commonly used for cavity repair, was used as the control repair material. The organisation of newly obtained pulp tissue was observed only in the group containing all three components.116

Since adult DPSCs are derived from the neural crest, they are potential substitutes for the embryonic mesenchyme in the generation of tooth primordia. However, this application has not yet been demonstrated. Hung et al.117 used DPSCs to form tooth-like structures in rabbit alveolar sockets, but no visible tooth eruption was observed at any of the graft sites. Yu et al.76 reported that DPSC pellets reassociated with adult mouse apical germ cells formed crown-like structures in vivo that contained distinct regions of enamel, dentin, predentin, and ameloblast and odontoblast layers.80

Dental stem cells are a potential source for bone tissue engineering. A novel c-kit+/CD34+ population of DPSCs was selected from dental pulp, expanded, and cultured. This stem cell population, termed stromal bone-producing DPSCs (SBP/DPSCs), was differentiated into CD44+/Runx2+ osteoblast precursors and subsequently differentiated into osteoblasts by the addition of 20% fetal bovine serum. Osteogenic culture in vitro for 50 days produced fibrous bone-like tissue composed of a dense mineral matrix. In vivo transplantation of DPSCs into immunodeficient mice produced fibrous lamellar bone tissues containing osteocytes.118

sections.title: DPSCs as potential solutions for the treatment of oral bacterial infections
heading_path: DPSCs as potential solutions for the treatment of oral bacterial infections

blocks.text: The dental pulp is the tissue located in the central part of the tooth and is surrounded by dentin. This tissue plays a very important role in maintaining the life of the teeth, as it supplies essential factors through the apical foramen. The nerve network distributed in the pulp tissue through the apical foramen helps detect harmful stimuli and protects the teeth, and the blood vessels in the pulp tissue deliver nutrients to the teeth and remove waste products. Dental tissue has a high regenerative and functional capacity, as it is responsible for the maintenance and repair of periodontal tissue in response to various types of injuries. Dental pulp cells proliferate when periodontal tissue is damaged, migrate to the damaged site, and then differentiate into odontoblasts to produce reparative dentin.119

Dental caries is one of the most common diseases worldwide, and its prevalence and incidence have remained high over the past 2 decades.120 According to the latest epidemiological data, the overall prevalence of caries among young people in the United States is 45.8%.121 In the early stages of caries, there are no symptoms, and symptoms begin only when the carious lesion grows and reaches the dentin.122 When caries progresses, and an inflammatory reaction occurs in the dental pulp, ischaemia of the pulp tissue occurs with severe pain. Current clinical treatments include removing the affected pulp tissue, disinfecting, and then filling it with artificial dental root-filling material.123

Although primary root canal therapy has a high success rate and offers a predictable prognosis after treatment, the possibility of reinfection still exists.124 Even if the treatment is successful, pulp vitality is lost, and perception and immune function completely disappear, leading to a decrease in resistance to external stimuli and weakening of the teeth.125 Furthermore, when reinfection occurs and retreatment is performed, the success rate decreases, and repeated root canal therapy treatments make teeth more vulnerable and prone to root fractures or even fractures.126,127

To solve these problems, a tissue regeneration approach that replaces damaged pulp with healthy pulp is an ideal treatment option. Therefore, innovative strategies for functional pulp regeneration are essential, as pulp stem cells have emerged as promising candidates. MSCs are multipotent cells that can differentiate into all types of cells derived from the three embryonic germ layers, including osteoblasts, chondroblasts, and adipocytes. MSCs have been discovered in various tissues, such as bone marrow, adipose tissue, and dental tissues.128

Owing to these properties, MSCs have been recognised as promising sources of stem cells for regenerative therapies. However, their applications have limitations, such as safety and accessibility issues; therefore, MSC-like cells isolated from dental tissues have attracted much attention. MSC-like cells isolated from dental tissues have the advantage of being easily obtained from extracted teeth or from periodontal tissues associated with extracted teeth.104 Furthermore, these cells can differentiate into nerves and blood vessels, which are essential structures constituting pulp tissue, and can be cryopreserved for cell preservation. More importantly, they may not induce an immune response in allogeneic transplantations because they are nonimmunogenic and have strong immunosuppressive properties.129

With these advantages, DPSCs are the most important source of stem cells for pulp tissue regeneration because they are present in the original dental pulp and are susceptible to repairing damaged dental pulp.130

The pulp response to dental caries is a complex process aimed at arresting carious lesions and protecting the pulp from bacterial invasion. In slowly progressing lesions, subiodontoblastic cells may adequately respond to carious penetration by inducing reactive dentin formation and repair. However, in rapidly advancing carious lesions, odontoblast death may occur, necessitating the differentiation of new odontoblast-like cells from stem or progenitor cells to initiate repair, regeneration, and tertiary dentin formation.131
DPSCs exert antimicrobial effects through 3 synergistic mechanisms

list_items: (1) Direct antimicrobial action: via the secretion of β-defensins, LL-37, and nitric oxide (NO), which disrupt bacterial membranes and neutralise endotoxins;
(2) Immunomodulation: Promotion of M2 macrophage polarisation and regulatory T-cell (Treg) activation through IL-10, HGF, and TGF-β;

(3) Biofilm disruption and microbiome rebalancing: This occurs through the degradation of EPSs and the selective suppression of periodontal pathogens (eg, P. gingivalis) while promoting beneficial taxa such as Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium.

blocks.text: Given the critical importance of eliminating infection prior to repair and regeneration, constitutive expression of antibacterial factors within the dentin–pulp complex has been documented. Odontoblast-like cells express AMPs such as β-defensins, which not only directly kill microorganisms but also neutralise bacterial toxins such as lipopolysaccharides (LPS). Furthermore, neutrophils recruited to the carious site attempt to eradicate invading bacteria via neutrophil extracellular traps, which contain AMPs, including α-defensins, with broad-spectrum activity. These coordinated innate immune responses contribute to restoring tissue homeostasis and enable subsequent repair and regeneration processes essential for maintaining tooth structure and function.134,135

The oral pulp also contains AMPs that help defend against bacterial invasion. These peptides can disrupt bacterial membranes and neutralise bacterial toxins, enhancing the ability of the pulp to fight infections. Many AMPs have immunomodulatory functions that are similar to those traditionally described for growth factors and cytokines. Similarly, soluble factors, such as indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase, islet-derived haptoglobin III, and osteoprotegerin (which acts as a cytokine), have been reported to have direct bactericidal effects. AMPs can disrupt bacterial membranes and neutralise bacterial toxins, enhancing the ability of the pulp to fight infections.136,137

Compared with BM-MSCs and PDLSCs, DPSCs demonstrate a comparatively stronger intrinsic AMP profile, particularly in LL-37 and β-defensin secretion. While conventional periodontal therapies primarily focus on mechanical biofilm disruption and broad-spectrum antimicrobial approaches, DPSCs uniquely combine direct antimicrobial activity with immunoregulatory and regenerative effects. This multimodal capacity positions DPSCs as a potential adjunct or alternative to antibiotic-dependent strategies, particularly in the context of increasing antimicrobial resistance. However, unlike established periodontal regenerative approaches, clinical translation of DPSC-based therapy remains limited to preclinical evidence, underscoring the need for well-designed translational studies.91,138,139 This functional distinction positions DPSCs as uniquely suited for dual-pathway intervention in polymicrobial oral infections.
A variety of immune cells, including neutrophils and macrophages, respond to bacterial infections.
Neutrophils can produce reactive oxygen species and release extracellular traps that contain antimicrobial agents to capture and destroy bacteria

sections.title: Effects of pulp immune cells on dental pathogens
heading_path: Effects of pulp immune cells on dental pathogens

blocks.text: Odontoblasts have long cell processes that extend into the dentinal tubules, and their cell bodies are located on the surface of the dental pulp.142 Odontoblasts also form a layer along the interface between dental pulp tissue and dentin, acting as a natural barrier between the mineralised tissues, dentin, and soft tissues of the dental pulp in the living tooth. Odontoblasts are the main biologically active cells that maintain dentin and protect living pulp tissue by depositing reactive dentin in response to mild stimulation with bacterial products in the early stages of dental caries and play a role in the innate and adaptive immunity of the dental pulp to combat invading bacteria.143

The dental pulp beneath this odontoblast layer is a vascular tissue with a dense capillary network. When bacteria and their products penetrate deep into the dentinal tubules, odontoblasts are the first pulp cells to encounter these invading microorganisms of the dentin and sense the pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) shared by the microorganisms through specific pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) at the dentin‒pulp interface. This triggers host defense responses, such as inflammatory responses, which lead to the production of a variety of inflammatory mediators, including chemotoxins and cytokines. These attract various inflammatory cells and initiate antibacterial responses, such as the production of defensins to kill microorganisms in the vicinity of odontoblasts.143

When inflammation occurs at low levels, odontoblasts promote regenerative mechanisms, including angiogenesis and dentinogenesis, thereby enhancing pulp defense. This process ultimately leads to the formation of reactive dentin. However, in cases of severe and/or prolonged inflammation where dentin regenerative pathways are inhibited, odontoblasts and infiltrating inflammatory cells produce large amounts of inflammatory mediators. These mediators activate diverse molecular and cellular signalling pathways that culminate in the degradation of dental pulp tissue.144

The penetration of oral bacteria associated with dental caries progression, along with physical and chemical stimuli to the exposed dentin surface, initiates both acute and chronic activation of innate immune responses within the dentin‒pulp complex. These immune responses contribute to the development of pulpitis.145 As carious infection advances towards the pulp–dentin interface, shifts in the bacterial microflora occur, characterised by a decrease in aerobic gram-positive bacteria and an increase in anaerobic gram-negative bacteria. Consequently, the increase in anaerobes within deep carious lesions results in more complex polymicrobial infections and an overall increase in bacterial diversity.146

The innate immune system is the main cause of acute inflammation and effective defense against microbial infection and is also important in activating acquired immune responses.147,148 In general, the initial rapid sensing of invading microbial pathogens is carried out by PRRs specialised for PAMPs, which are conserved structures among microbial species. Recent studies have shown that PRRs also recognise damage-associated molecular patterns, which include endogenous molecules released from damaged cells.147

sections.title: PRR classification and localisation
heading_path: Effects of pulp immune cells on dental pathogens

blocks.text: PRRs are broadly classified into four primary families: Toll-like receptors (TLRs), nucleotide-binding oligomerisation domain (NOD)-like receptors (NLRs), C-type lectin receptors (CLRs), and retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I)-like receptors (RLRs). While TLRs and CLRs are found primarily on the plasma membrane or in endolysosomal compartments, NLRs and RLRs are cytoplasmic sensors. This arrangement enables the immune system to detect a wide array of PAMPs both on cell surfaces and within the cytosol.
These receptors are expressed at variable levels across different tissues and activate distinct signalling pathways and host immune responses upon ligand engagement (

sections.title: TLR numbers, structure, and ligand recognition
heading_path: Effects of pulp immune cells on dental pathogens
TLR numbers, structure, and ligand recognition

blocks.text: To date, 10 functional TLRs have been identified in humans (TLR1-TLR10), and 12 have been identified in mice (TLR1-TLR9, TLR11-TLR13). TLRs are type I transmembrane glycoproteins featuring extracellular leucine-rich repeat domains for PAMP recognition, a transmembrane region, and a cytoplasmic Toll/interleukin-1 receptor homology domain needed for dimerisation and the initiation of downstream signalling. TLRs have specialised localisation:

• The plasma membrane contains TLR1, TLR2, TLR4, TLR5, and TLR6, which mainly sense bacterial and fungal cell components.
• The endosomal membrane proteins, TLR3, TLR7, TLR8, and TLR9, predominantly detect nucleic acids from viruses and bacteria.157

blocks.text: For example, TLR2 forms heterodimers with TLR1 or TLR6 and is crucial for sensing a range of bacterial cell wall components (eg, lipoteichoic acid, lipoproteins), as well as molecules from mycobacteria, fungi, and viruses. TLR4 recognises LPS from gram-negative bacteria with the help of MD2, LBP, and CD14, whereas TLR5 detects bacterial flagellin. TLR3, TLR7, and TLR8 are central to viral RNA detection, and TLR9 binds unmethylated CpG DNA motifs, leading to the activation of downstream immune signalling.149

sections.title: TLR signalling pathways
heading_path: Effects of pulp immune cells on dental pathogens

blocks.text: The activation of most TLRs triggers the MyD88-dependent pathway, activating MAPK and NF-κB, and resulting in the production of proinflammatory mediators. TLR4 (after endosomal translocation) and TLR3 utilise a MyD88-independent pathway via TRIF, activating TBK1, which phosphorylates IRF3 and induces type I interferons. TLR7 and TLR9 can also induce proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines via NF-κB.150,157

sections.title: NOD-like receptors: NOD1 and NOD2
heading_path: Effects of pulp immune cells on dental pathogens

blocks.text: Not all NLRs are fully characterised, but NOD1 and NOD2 have been well studied. NOD1 detects γ-d-glutamyl-meso-diaminopimelic acid (iE-DAP), which is common in gram-negative bacteria, whereas NOD2 recognises muramyl dipeptide, which is present in both gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria. Upon ligand recognition, both NODs signal through RIPK2, activating the NF-κB and MAPK pathways and inducing inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β.158,159

sections.title: NLRP3 inflammasome activation
heading_path: Effects of pulp immune cells on dental pathogens

blocks.text: NLRP3 is a cytoplasmic NLR that, upon sensing diverse PAMPs such as LPS, muramyl dipeptide, and cytoplasmic viral/bacterial RNA, assembles into an inflammasome complex. This results in the activation of caspase-1, which processes and facilitates the secretion of IL-1β, IL-18, and key proinflammatory cytokines.160, 161, 162

sections.title: Odontoblasts and dental pulp innate immunity
heading_path: Effects of pulp immune cells on dental pathogens
Odontoblasts and dental pulp innate immunity

blocks.text: Odontoblasts, located at the periphery of the dental pulp, are the primary cells that recognise caries-associated pathogens, such as S. mutans. As caries progress and the bacterial profile shifts from primarily gram-positive to predominantly gram-negative species, odontoblasts respond accordingly. These cells express TLRs and produce chemokines and cytokines (eg, IL-8, CCL2, CXCL2, CXCL10, IL-1β, and TNF-α) following bacterial challenge, thereby recruiting immune cells and contributing to the defense against caries-derived pathogens. Odontoblasts also secrete AMPs and constitute a critical innate immune barrier in teeth.163, 164, 165 Other pulp-resident cells including fibroblasts, stem cells, endothelial cells, dendritic cells, and recruited immune cells coordinate a rapid inflammatory response via PRR-dependent detection of bacterial PAMPs, contributing to early pulp immune responses through autocrine and paracrine signalling.165

Together, these pathways and cell types provide dental pulp with a specialised, multilayered innate immune defense capable of rapid microbial detection and response. Odontoblasts, as the first line of defense, use PRRs (such as TLRs and NODs) to recognise pathogens, coordinate local inflammation, and initiate antibacterial responses essential for oral health
Figure 5

Fig. 5 Odontoblasts act as innate immune sentinels in the dentin‒pulp complex. Odontoblasts are the first line of defense against cariogenic bacteria. Their long processes extend into the dentinal tubules. They express pattern recognition receptors, such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and NOD-like receptors. Upon recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns from invading bacteria, they initiate an immune response by secreting chemokines (eg, IL-8 and CCL2) to recruit immune cells and AMPs (eg, β-defensins) to directly kill pathogens.

Biofilms form on nearly all surfaces exposed to the natural environment, including the human oral cavity.166 Recent advances in molecular techniques such as pyrosequencing have revealed that the bacterial diversity within an individual’s oral microbiome approximates 500 species, highlighting the complexity and dynamic nature of this polymicrobial ecosystem. Biofilms established on hard and soft dental tissues represent a primary aetiological factor for dental caries and periodontal diseases.167

Clinical treatments for the consequences of oral biofilm infections such as endodontic therapy, restorations, and implant therapy often rely on dental materials (eg, root canal sealers, resin composites, and titanium implants) placed in various oral zones to restore function. Despite advancements, none of these treatments ensures complete and immediate eradication of biofilms or prevents secondary infections, thereby positioning the antimicrobial properties of dental materials as crucial for long-term clinical success.168 Emerging evidence suggests that dental pulp tissue, particularly multipotent MSCs, possesses intrinsic antibiofilm capacities. Odontoblasts, which are localised at the pulp–dentin interface with cellular extensions penetrating dentinal tubules, are the first pulp cells to encounter invading pathogens and their byproducts. Consequently, they have been hypothesised to serve as the first biologically active line of host defense in the tooth, analogous to epithelial cells in other barrier tissues.169

TLRs, particularly TLR2 and TLR4, are key PRRs expressed on odontoblast membranes and are responsible for sensing gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, respectively. Studies have shown that TLR2 expression increases in odontoblasts beneath carious lesions, enhancing their ability to respond to bacterial invasion. The activation of these receptors regulates the expression of innate immune factors, including AMPs and proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which recruit and activate immune cells within the dental pulp to combat infection.170,171 One of the critical consequences of TLR activation is the regulation of downstream mediators, including AMPs and proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which collectively recruit and activate both tissue-resident and circulating immune cells.171,172

In this context, odontoblasts have been shown to produce several antibacterial agents, with particular attention to beta-defensins and NO. Beta-defensins are small, cationic peptides that exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity through mechanisms such as the formation of membrane-disruptive pores in bacterial cells. While BD-1 is constitutively expressed, BD-2, BD-3, and BD-4 are inducible upon microbial exposure. Recent studies have shown that BD-2 can inhibit pathogens such as S. mutans and Lactobacillus casei, whereas BD-3 is effective against mature biofilms containing various oral bacteria. Additionally, BD-2 has a proinflammatory effect, as it increases the production of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and chemokines such as CXCL8 (IL-8), possibly amplifying host responses via feedback with inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1α and TNF-α. Recent findings also suggest that BD-2 expression in odontoblasts is influenced by specific TLR activations, with BD-2 upregulated by TLR4 and BD-1/BD-3 downregulated by TLR2 stimulation, supporting differential antimicrobial strategies against diverse bacterial threats.173

Another essential antimicrobial system in odontoblasts is NO production. NO is a highly reactive free radical synthesised from L-arginine by nitric oxide synthase (NOS). Three NOS isoforms exist: NOS1 and NOS3 (constitutive, producing low NO levels under physiological conditions) and NOS2 (inducible, synthesising high NO concentrations during inflammatory responses). NOS2 is minimally expressed in healthy pulp but is rapidly upregulated in inflamed tissue, contributing to the recruitment of immune cells such as neutrophils and macrophages. Notably, NO produced by NOS2 in odontoblasts effectively inhibits the growth of cariogenic bacteria, such as S. mutans, highlighting the antibacterial role of this pathway in limiting intradental infection progression.174, 175, 176

Furthermore, odontoblasts exposed to gram-positive bacterial PAMPs—such as lipoteichoic acid—activate TLR2, resulting in the upregulation of TLR2 and NOD2 receptors. This activation triggers intracellular signalling cascades, including the NF-κB and p38 MAPK pathways, leading to the suppression of dentinogenesis and the induction of chemokines such as CCL2, CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL8, and CXCL10. These chemokines orchestrate the recruitment of immune cells (immature dendritic cells, T cells, macrophages, neutrophils, and B cells) to the pulp‒dentin interface, thus bolstering local immune defense as the carious lesion advances. Collectively, the above mechanisms enable odontoblasts to act as immune sentinels, enhancing the antibacterial milieu of the dental pulp. They further contribute to the secretion of various cytokines and growth factors, such as IL-6, IL-8, HGF, and ANGPT-1, all of which are crucial for inhibiting biofilm bacterial growth, amplifying immune responses, and facilitating tissue repair. IL-6, for example, is markedly upregulated in inflamed pulp tissues and regulates numerous aspects of immune cell differentiation and acute-phase protein production, thus playing a central role in pulpal immune regulation.172,177,178

DPSCs represent a promising and readily accessible source of multipotent cells for regenerative therapies aimed at restoring pulp vitality and rebuilding the pulp‒dentin complex. Despite significant progress in preclinical studies, challenges remain in translating these findings into effective clinical protocols for pulp regeneration. The innate antibacterial capacity of dental pulp, which is mediated primarily by odontoblasts through PRRs and AMPs, plays a critical role in the initial defense against caries-associated pathogens. However, excessive or dysregulated innate immune responses may contribute to irreversible pulp damage, underscoring the importance of elucidating the specific PRRs and molecular mechanisms involved in odontoblast-mediated immunity.

Collectively, DPSCs act via three synergistic axes1: direct killing via AMPs,2 immune reprogramming towards M2/Treg phenotypes, and3 microbiome rebalancing, offering a multifactorial alternative to single-target antimicrobial agents.

A deeper understanding of the complex interplay between the immune response to microbial invasion and tissue repair processes is essential for developing strategies that preserve or regenerate vital pulp tissue effectively. Continued interdisciplinary research, integrating molecular, cellular, and translational approaches, will be pivotal in advancing novel therapeutic modalities. Such advances are expected to optimise the balance between defense and repair in the dental pulp, ultimately improving clinical outcomes and patient care in dentistry.

Notably, the current body of evidence on DPSCs is derived primarily from in vitro monoculture models, which do not fully recapitulate the polymicrobial and spatially organised nature of oral biofilms in gingivitis. Future studies should prioritise coculture systems or multispecies biofilm models to better simulate the clinical microenvironment and enhance translational relevance.

While DPSC-based therapy holds promise, clinical translation faces challenges, including optimal delivery methods (eg, hydrogel carriers, scaffold integration), long-term safety, and scalability. Importantly, DPSCs can be harvested via minimally invasive, autologous extraction of discarded teeth, thus avoiding ethical concerns associated with embryonic sources. No current clinical trials specifically evaluate DPSCs for gingivitis; thus, evidence remains preclinical.

blocks.text: Gingivitis is the most prevalent periodontal disease in children and adolescents. Although reversible, its high prevalence highlights a significant public health concern, especially in underserved populations.

A narrative literature review was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar to identify English and French studies published between 2014 and 2024. Inclusion criteria focused on epidemiological studies reporting prevalence, risk factors, and preventive strategies of gingivitis in pediatric populations.

Gingivitis prevalence among children and adolescents varies widely across countries, ranging from 20% to over 90%. Higher rates were observed in socioeconomically disadvantaged populations. Key risk factors include poor oral hygiene, sugar-rich diets, low parental education, orthodontic appliances, and limited access to preventive care.

Gingivitis in pediatric populations remains a global concern. Multilevel strategies involving families, schools, and oral health professionals are essential to improve prevention, health education, and access to care in order to reduce disease burden.

Gingivitis, defined as inflammation of the gingival tissues without clinical attachment loss, is the most prevalent periodontal disease among children and adolescents (1). It is primarily caused by dental plaque accumulation at the gingival margin, leading to microbial dysbiosis. This shift—characterized by a reduction in gram-positive cocci and an increase in gramnegative anaerobic bacteria—triggers an inflammatory response that can result in gingival swelling, redness, and bleeding (2). Although gingivitis is considered reversible in its early stages, persistent inflammation may predispose individuals to periodontitis later in life (3).

Despite its clinical simplicity, pediatric gingivitis remains a major public health concern due to its high and variable prevalence worldwide. This variability is largely influenced by differences in diagnostic criteria, access to dental care, oral hygiene practices, and socioeconomic conditions (4–6). Recent epidemiological data from countries such as Nigeria (7), Myanmar (8), China (9), and Saudi Arabia (10) confirm that gingivitis is particularly prevalent in disadvantaged populations, where preventive services and oral health education are often lacking.

Several behavioral and contextual factors—such as poor brushing habits, high sugar intake, low parental education, and orthodontic appliances—have been consistently associated with gingival inflammation in youth (5, 9, 11). Although various studies have examined these determinants individually, no recent synthesis has focused specifically on gingivitis in pediatric populations across diverse regions.

This narrative review aims to provide an updated overview of the epidemiology and risk factors of gingivitis in children and adolescents, and to support the development of targeted preventive strategies in clinical and public health contexts.

This narrative review was conducted to synthesize recent epidemiological data on gingivitis in children and adolescents, and to identify associated sociodemographic, behavioral, and clinical risk factors. The review followed PRISMA-ScR guidelines for scoping literature reviews.

A structured search was performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar to identify relevant peer-reviewed articles published in English and French between January 2014 and March 2024. The search strategy combined terms such as “gingivitis,” “children,” “adolescents,” “prevalence,” “epidemiology,” “risk factors,” and “oral hygiene,” using Boolean operators (AND/OR). Only articles reporting epidemiological data on gingivitis among children and/or adolescents were considered. Systematic reviews, cross-sectional studies, and populationbased surveys were eligible.
Studies were included if they:

list_items: Focused on individuals aged 6–18 years;
Reported gingivitis prevalence or associated risk factors;
Were available in full text and published in English or French;
Concerned plaque-induced gingivitis.

blocks.text: Studies were excluded if they:

list_items: Focused exclusively on individuals aged 18 years and older;
Addressed periodontitis, genetic syndromes, or histological mechanisms without epidemiological data;
Were not accessible in full text.

This review included 12 studies published between 2014 and 2024, conducted in various regions including Africa, Asia, and Europe, and involving pediatric populations aged 6–18 years.
The prevalence of gingivitis reported in these studies ranged from approximately 20% to over 90%, depending on the age group, diagnostic criteria, and study location (4–6, 9, 13).

The highest prevalence rates were consistently found in low- and middle-income countries, where limited access to preventive dental care, poor oral hygiene habits, and lack of public health programs are prevalent (5–7, 10).
Adolescents, particularly those around puberty, appeared more susceptible to gingival inflammation—likely due to hormonal changes that modulate immune response in the gingival tissues (1–9).
Across the reviewed studies, the most commonly reported risk factors included:

Poor oral hygiene practices, including inadequate toothbrushing and infrequent dental visits (4–6),
Low socioeconomic status and low parental education (5–11),
Frequent sugar intake and unbalanced diet (8–12),
Orthodontic appliances and dental malocclusions, which favor plaque retention (9, 10),
Lifestyle and geographical disparities, such as urban vs. rural settings, brushing frequency, and gender differences (8, 13, 14).

blocks.text: Gingivitis in children and adolescents is a highly prevalent and preventable periodontal disease that reflects both individual behaviors and broader structural determinants. This discussion synthesizes the epidemiological patterns, risk factors, and preventive strategies identified in the literature to better inform future public health interventions.

The reviewed studies consistently report a high, yet heterogeneous, prevalence of gingivitis among pediatric populations. This variability is attributed to differences in diagnostic criteria, age ranges, and geographical locations (4–6, 9, 13–14). Notably, gingival inflammation tends to increase with age, reaching a peak during adolescence, likely due to hormonal changes that enhance the gingival inflammatory response (1–9). Disparities in disease burden are particularly pronounced in low- and middle-income settings, where socioeconomic inequalities limit access to dental services and preventive care (5–7, 10)

While the accumulation of dental plaque remains the primary etiological factor in gingivitis, multiple aggravating conditions influence its severity and progression. Poor oral hygiene practices, such as inadequate toothbrushing and infrequent dental visits, are consistently associated with increased gingival inflammation (4–6, 11). Socioeconomic disadvantage is a significant predictor, encompassing limited oral health education, dietary imbalances, and poor access to preventive services (5, 11, 12).

Orthodontic conditions and defective restorations also play a role by creating niches that promote plaque accumulation and hinder effective cleaning (9–13). Behavioral factors—including excessive consumption of refined sugars, adolescent smoking, and psychosocial stress—have been linked to higher susceptibility and severity of gingival disease (6–8).

Adolescents undergoing orthodontic treatment are particularly vulnerable to gingivitis. Fixed appliances such as brackets and wires complicate oral hygiene maintenance, leading to increased plaque retention and inflammation (10–13). Similarly, defective restorations can act as plaque-retentive factors, emphasizing the need for careful dental material selection and maintenance in pediatric patients (9).

A consensus across studies highlights the critical importance of early and sustained prevention. Effective daily oral hygiene—particularly twice-daily brushing with fluoridated toothpaste and flossing—is the cornerstone of gingivitis control (3–14). School-based oral health programs have shown promise in raising awareness and establishing positive habits among children and their families. Regular dental check-ups, combined with professional prophylaxis, enable the early identification and management of inflammation. The adjunctive use of antiseptic mouthwashes has also demonstrated efficacy in reducing bacterial load and gingival bleeding (3–13).

Optimal gingivitis prevention requires a coordinated, multidisciplinary approach. Families are central to fostering consistent hygiene behaviors at home, while schools serve as strategic platforms for health education and routine screening. Dental professionals must tailor their interventions to the developmental and social contexts of pediatric patients, delivering care that is both preventive and culturally sensitive (3–13).
This review is limited by its narrative design and the heterogeneity of the included studies.

Differences in methodology, diagnostic criteria, and reporting may affect the comparability of prevalence and risk factor data. In addition, restricting the search to English-language articles published between 2020 and 2024 may have excluded relevant findings.

Gingivitis remains the most common periodontal condition in children and adolescents, with prevalence ranging from 20% to over 90% depending on the population, diagnostic criteria, and access to care. The synthesis of recent literature confirms that biological changes during adolescence, behavioral habits such as inadequate toothbrushing and high sugar intake, and socioeconomic inequities are consistent drivers of disease burden. Orthodontic appliances and poor restorative dentistry further exacerbate plaque retention and inflammation, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where access to preventive care is limited.

This review emphasizes the urgent need for early, structured interventions targeting children and adolescents. Preventive strategies should prioritize school-based oral health education, parental involvement, and regular dental check-ups, complemented by the use of fluoride toothpaste and safe antimicrobial rinses. Policymakers should focus on reducing barriers to dental services and implementing culturally sensitive, community-based programs to promote equity in pediatric oral health.

Future research should explore longitudinal trends in gingivitis progression, investigate the microbiological and immunological mechanisms in youth, and evaluate the cost-effectiveness of preventive interventions at the community and school levels. By aligning clinical, educational, and public health efforts, gingivitis prevention can become an achievable goal to improve lifelong oral and systemic health outcomes in children and adolescents.

blocks.text: To preliminarily evaluate the clinical efficacy of Bletilla striata-Litsea cube-batoothpaste in patients with plaque-induced gingivitis and its impact on inflammatory factors in gingival crevicular fluid.

In a randomised clinical trial, 80 patients with plaque-induced gingivitis were randomly allocated to receive either Bletilla striata-Litsea cubeba toothpaste (experimental group) or negative control toothpaste (control group). Following a 2-week washout period, periodontal indices including the Turesky-modified Quigley–Hein Plaque Index (TmQHI) and Sulcus Bleeding Index (SBI), along with inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) quantified from gingival crevicular fluid (GCF) samples of the right mandibular first molars, were assessed at baseline (0 week), 4, 8, and 12 weeks. Statistical analyses employed repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) for longitudinal comparisons and independent samples t-tests for inter-group comparisons at identical time points, with statistical significance defined as α = 0.05.

The experimental group exhibited significant TmQHI and SBI reductions at 8 and 12 weeks (p < 0.05) versus delayed changes in controls. IL-1β decreased significantly at 8 and 12 weeks with lower levels than controls (p < 0.05); IL-6 declined earlier in the experimental group, while TNF-α reductions were comparable between groups.
Compared with control, the novel toothpaste achieved earlier and greater improvements in periodontal indices and specific inflammatory mediator levels in plaque-induced gingivitis.

Plaque-induced gingivitis represents the most prevalent chronic infectious condition among contemporary gingival diseases, exhibiting association with dysbiosis of the periodontal microbiome and dysregulated host immune responses.11 Periodontal pathogens such as Porphyromonas gingivalis trigger gingival microvasodilation and inflammatory cell infiltration by directly releasing toxins and indirectly inducing host immune responses, increasing the levels of inflammatory factors such as interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) in gingival crevicular fluid (GCF).23 The clinical manifestations are usually dark red gingival colour, bleeding on probing, and round and blunt gingival papilla.

The effectiveness of using toothpaste with brushing for oral cleaning to prevent gingivitis has been supported by research.12 As a fundamental oral hygiene intervention, the plaque-inhibitory capacity of toothpaste is contingent upon not merely the mechanical abrasion provided by compounds such as calcium carbonate, but also on its chemical constituents.1,30 For instance, triclosan in toothpaste can reduce dental plaque by interfering with bacterial fatty acid metabolism.19 Moreover, many traditional Chinese herbal ingredients, such as clove,9 Andrographis paniculata 18 and gallnut,6 have been proven to have significant antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and anti-sensitive effects, leading to their progressive integration into commercial toothpaste.4,28,34 Nevertheless, current commercially available herbal toothpastes often rely on single plant ingredients, leading to issues such as false advertising, insufficient synergistic effects, and unclear mechanisms of action. For example, Yunnan Baiyao toothpaste has a haemostatic effect, but its formula contains the haemostatic agent tranexamic acid.24 These issues highlight the urgent need for scientific optimisation in the formulation of herbal toothpastes and the exploration of new formulations to achieve better antibacterial and anti-inflammatory effects.

Bletilla striata is a perennial herb indigenous to traditional Chinese medicine systems and possesses polysaccharides as its primary bioactive constituents. These glucomannan polymers, characterised by β-1,4-glycosidic linkages between mannose and glucose units (molecular weights ranging from 10 to 150 kDa), demonstrate significant antibacterial efficacy, procoagulant activity, and tissue regenerative properties.14 Such pharmacological attributes have facilitated their integration into oral care formulations, including lyophilised wafers17 and microneedle patches,25 enhancing antibacterial performance and promoting oral tissue repair. Concurrently, Litsea cubeba, distinguished by its pungent organoleptic properties and warm medicinal nature, contains citral-dominated monoterpenoid compounds within its volatile oil fraction.8 Empirical studies validate its marked antibacterial,16 anti-inflammatory33 and antioxidant activities.3 In vitro studies indicate that Litsea cubeba volatile oil is non-toxic to human gingival fibroblasts and can be added to denture soft lining materials to maintain oral health by inhibiting bacteria.27 Given their pharmacological activities and the functional needs of oral care products, combining Bletilla striata and Litsea cubeba extracts in toothpaste may reduce plaque, stop bleeding, and promote gum healing, assisting in treating plaque-induced gingivitis. Additionally, these extracts can replace thickeners and flavourings in toothpaste, achieving a medicated and auxiliary integration.

Limited research has documented the fundamental physicochemical profiles and therapeutic efficacy of toothpaste incorporating co-extracts of Bletilla striata and Litsea cubeba. This study employs a randomised controlled trial approach to investigate the effects of the toothpaste on clinical periodontal parameters in patients with plaque-induced gingivitis, as well as changes in the concentration of inflammatory mediators in the GCF. The aim is to evaluate the potential anti-plaque and anti-inflammatory effects of the toothpaste, thereby providing scientific evidence for the application of these two herbal extracts in oral care.

The Bletilla striata-Litsea cubeba toothpaste (Fig 1a, Table 1) was developed by the College of Pharmaceutical Science, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University, and produced in the standardised workshop of Yiwu Aishang Daily Necessities Co. The extract of Bletilla striata (provided by Jiangshan Liuheshuo Chinese Medicinal Materials Co., China) is Bletilla striata polysaccharides (BSP) (Fig 1b), and the extract of Litsea cubeba (provided by Hangzhou Kanglun Chinese Medicine Decoction Pieces Co., China) is Litsea cubeba volatile oil (Fig 1c).

blocks.text: The negative control toothpaste, also developed by the College of Pharmaceutical Science, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University, matches the experimental toothpaste in packaging and non-drug trace components, differing only in the absence of Bletilla striata and Litsea cubeba extracts.

Deionised water, PBS buffer, and human high-sensitivity ELISA kits (IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α) were sourced from Hangzhou Lianke Biotechnology Co. (Hangzhou, China); plaque disclosing agent was provided by Ci Medical Co. (Osaka, Japan).

The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of Zhejiang Chinese Medical University (NO.ZCMUHSIRB-2024051407) and registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registration Centre (CTR2400086388). All patients provided informed consent.

Patients were recruited from the VIP Department of the Hospital of Stomatology, Zhejiang Chinese Medical University between June 2024 and April 2025. They presented with gingival bleeding and swelling and were clinically diagnosed with plaque-induced gingivitis. All patients signed informed consent before the experiment. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are listed in the table. The Turesky-modified Quigley–Hein Index (TmQHI) was used as the outcome measure. Based on a pre-experiment, the estimated TmQHI was 0.85 ± 0.33 for the experimental group and 1.03 ± 0.27 for the control group.
Using the formula

where σ is the estimated overall standard deviation and β is the difference between the two group means, the sample size was calculated. A two-sided test was used with α = 0.05, β = 0.10, Zα = 1.96, Zβ = 1.28, δ = 0.3 (from the pre-experiment), and σ = 0.24. Each group needed 33 subjects. Considering a 20% dropout rate, the sample size was increased.7 Eventually, 80 subjects were effectively enrolled (with two dropouts), meeting the requirement.

Patients received oral hygiene education, plaque removal, enamel polishing, and calculus cleaning, if needed.15 They learned the modified Bass brushing technique and used a negative control toothpaste for 2 weeks to standardise the baseline. Clinical assessments were conducted at weeks 0 (baseline), 4, 8, and 12, including TmQHI and Sulcus Bleeding Index (SBI) evaluations, GCF collection, and plaque-stained photographic documentation. Patients were randomly assigned to the experimental group or control group by the envelope method. The control group (n = 40) used a negative control toothpaste, while the experimental group (n = 40) used the Bletilla striata-Litsea cubeba toothpaste. Both cohorts performed twice-daily brushing for 3 min using the modified Bass technique throughout the 12-week intervention. Toothpaste packaging was identical across groups to maintain participant blinding. This double-masked study restricted allocation awareness exclusively to formulation designers, thereby mitigating assessment subjectivity. All clinical examiners demonstrated inter-rater reliability exceeding the predetermined calibration threshold (Kappa > 0.6), and the study protocol is outlined in Figure 2.
Fig 2 Flow chart of the experiment.

The efficacy evaluation referred to the Chinese-recommended health industry standard Efficacy Evaluation of Toothpaste (Document No. 25 [2010]). In each clinical trial using a negative or placebo control, the comparison of final values between the control and experimental groups must show statistical significance. A relative change rate (%) of endpoint value, that is
> 12%, and the experimental group must demonstrate a reduction rate of ≥ 15%, indicating the test product’s effectiveness in reducing gingivitis.

All patients in this study underwent four clinical efficacy evaluations, at 0, 4, 8, and 12 weeks after using the toothpaste from both groups. Each evaluation included measurements of the TmQHI and SBI.

After using a dental plaque disclosing agent, the TmQHI is recorded based on plaque coverage area: 0 indicates no plaque on the tooth surface; 1 indicates scattered plaque spots at the gingival margin; 2 indicates a continuous plaque band (≤ 1mm in width) at the gingival margin; 3 indicates plaque covering > 1 mm but < 1/3 of the tooth surface at the gingival area; 4 indicates plaque covering 1/3 to 2/3 of the tooth surface; 5 indicates plaque covering > 2/3 of the tooth surface.26,29

After probing the gingival sulcus, the bleeding situation was observed to evaluate the BI based on the presence and severity of bleeding. A score of 0 indicates healthy gums with no inflammation or bleeding; 1 indicates inflammatory colour change without bleeding; 2 indicates pinpoint bleeding after probing; 3 indicates bleeding spreading along the gingival margin; 4 indicates bleeding filling and overflowing the sulcus; and 5 indicates spontaneous bleeding.20

Four sterile paper points were placed in high-pressure steam-sterilised microcentrifuge tubes and numbered sequentially according to each patient’s name. The target tooth (right lower first molar) was dried with a sterile cotton ball to remove soft debris and saliva. New sterile dry cotton balls were placed on both the buccal and lingual sides of the alveolar ridge to isolate the area and prevent saliva contamination. Using forceps, paper points were inserted approximately 0.5 mm subgingivally at four sites of the target tooth (mesio-buccal, central-buccal, disto-buccal, and lingual), pressed against the tooth neck, and left in place for 30 s. Paper points with blood or saliva contamination were discarded. This process was repeated three times. The three GCF samples in microcentrifuge tubes were used for detecting IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α. The paper points were placed in microcentrifuge tubes, sealed, and immediately stored at –80°C. After GCF collection, clinical periodontal examinations were conducted to avoid contamination of the GCF with bleeding from probing.

Prior to detection, the samples were restored to room temperature. The absorbent paper points were removed from each microcentrifuge tube, cut into 1 cm segments using sterile scissors, and immersed in 200 μl of PBS buffer for 10 min. The microcentrifuge tubes were then placed in a benchtop high-speed centrifuge for centrifugation (4000 rpm, 10 min, 4°C), and 100 μl of the supernatant was collected for quantification. The levels of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α were measured using ELISA according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Statistical analysis was performed using SPSS Statistics 26.0 (IBM, USA). Data within the same group over time were analysed using analysis of variance (ANOVA), while comparisons between two groups at the same time point were conducted using an independent samples t-test. The significance level was defined as α = 0.05.
The clinical trial enrolled 80 eligible subjects, and no statistically significant differences were observed in baseline characteristics between the two groups (Table 2).

Within-group comparisons indicated significant differences between 4 and 8 weeks (p < 0.05) and 4 and 12 weeks (p < 0.001). Although the control group also showed a decreasing trend in TmQHI, the reduction was only significant at 12 weeks (p < 0.01), and the change from 4 to 12 weeks (p < 0.05) was smaller than in the experimental group. Intergroup comparisons (Fig 3b, Table 3) showed no baseline difference, but the experimental group had significantly lower TmQHI than the control at 8 weeks (p < 0.05), with a further increased difference at 12 weeks (p < 0.01). Representative plaque-staining follow-up images are shown in Figures 4 and 5. The experimental group demonstrated a greater reduction in TmQHI, declining by 35.97% from baseline at 12 weeks, compared to 20.36% in the control group. The between-group difference of 15.61% was statistically significant, with the experimental group showing a relative improvement of 18.40% at endpoint.

SBI results showed that the experimental group had significant differences from baseline at 8 weeks (p < 0.01), with further increase at 12 weeks (p < 0.001) (Fig 6a). Significant differences were also found between 12 weeks and both 4 and 8 weeks (p < 0.001, p < 0.01). The control group showed no obvious downward trend in SBI throughout the trial, with no significant differences at any time point compared to baseline. Between-group comparison (Fig 6b and Table 3) revealed no significant difference in SBI at baseline. By 12 weeks, the experimental group had a significantly lower SBI than the control group (p < 0.001). Compared to baseline, SBI decreased by 63.86% in the experimental group and 19.85% in the control group. The experimental group showed an endpoint reduction rate exceeding 15%, with a between-group difference of 44.01%. Endpoint comparison showed a statistically significant difference between the two groups.

IL-1β results showed a declining trend in both groups. In the experimental group, IL-1β levels in GCF decreased significantly from baseline at 8 weeks (p < 0.01) and further at 12 weeks (p < 0.001), with a significant difference between 4 and 12 weeks (p < 0.001). The control group exhibited a slower decline, showing a significant reduction only at 12 weeks compared to baseline (p < 0.01), and a smaller difference between 4 and 12 weeks (p < 0.05) (Fig 7a). Intergroup comparisons revealed no baseline difference, but significantly lower IL-1β concentrations in the experimental group at both 8 and 12 weeks (p < 0.05) (Fig 7b, Table 4). The reduction rate was 48.82% in the experimental group and 29.89% in the control group. Endpoint comparison showed a statistically significant difference (p < 0.05), with a relative change of 29.29%, an experimental group reduction exceeding 15%, and an intergroup reduction difference of 18.93%.
