cells.text: Methacrylic acid, ethyleneglycol dimethacrylate,2-hydroxyethyl methacrylate, silicon dioxide NPs
The osteogenic media increased the expression of RUNX2and ALP genes in PDLSCs. Dox-NPs increased the expression of the ALP gene and reduced the up-regulation of IL-1β.
Validation of in vivo therapeutic efficacy in large animals has not yet been accomplished, and no systematic in vivo biosafety evaluation has been conducted.
RAW264.7 cells,mBMSCs, a rat periodontal defect model
Balance immune microenvironment, enhance bone generation

In an environment with LPS-induced inflammation, nanoparticles could efficiently restore the M1/M2 ratio and scavenge ROS. The improved immune environment is highly proficient in promoting osteoblast differentiation while impeding the maturation of osteoclasts.

Validation of the osteogenic efficacy is currently limited to small-animal periodontal defect models, the long-term bone repair potential has not been systematically evaluated in large-animal models, and the implementation of such studies is restricted by economic factors.
L929 cell line, RAW 264.7 cell line

RSV@PPD NPs suppress macrophage M1 polarization, inhibit the NF-κB signaling pathway to regulate host immunity after scavenging ROS to promote M2 polarization. RES@PPD NPs can increase anti-inflammatory cytokines (IL-10, Arg-1, and TGF-β) and reduce pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α) in an animal model of periodontitis.
The immunomodulatory effects on preventing bone damage and restoring osteogenesis in the periodontal microenvironment should be further studied
Sericin,peanut oil, Span80, inorganic ions (CaCl2, SrCl2, and CuCl2) PEI/EGCG functional coatings
hPDLSCs, RAW264.7 cells, and SD rats
Balance the immune microenvironment, anti-inflammatory, and accelerate periodontal tissue repair

Se-CuSrHA@EGCG promotes polarization of macrophages to M2, inhibits M1-type macrophages, reduces pro-inflammatory factors, up-regulates anti-inflammatory factors, and regulates the immune microenvironment. It can upregulate the expression of angiogenic genes (VEGF, FGF2, CD31, and Pdgfb) and osteogenic genes (ALP, Runx2, and OCn).
It is challenging to ensure the consistency of ion release kinetics among different preparation batches.
Antibacterial, promote the formation of bone

The mHA/CS particles had an antibacterial impact on Fn and Pg and had a diameter of 2µm. In vitro, the mHA/CS loaded with 20µg/mL rhAm increased the expression levels of genes and proteins linked to osteogenesis and ALP activity. In vivo, it encouraged the development of tissue resembling cementum.
More examinations on the expression levels of genesand proteins related to cementogenic differentiation and animal model studies with extended time span are necessary for the further study.
CS/PLA nanofibers can enhance ECM mineralization and promote BMMSC osteogenic differentiation, and the expression of osteogenic marker genes, such as BSP, Ocn, COL-1, and OPN

The structural stability of the scaffold subjected to long-term high occlusal loading has not been systematically verified in large animal mastication models that mimic physiological chewing conditions.
CGA-PLGA@PVP nanomicelles could remove ROS, inhibit alveolar bone resorption, reduce proinflammatory cytokine overexpression, and prevent periodontitis from progressing.

Cumulative toxicity data associated with repeated local administration is currently absent, and the applicability of this therapeutic approach for high-risk populations including individuals with diabetic periodontitis has not been fully validated.
PV/Ag@IL4 can improve the oral mucosal immune milieu, change macrophages into the M2 phenotype, decrease alveolar bone resorption, and improve the prognosis of periodontitis.

Surface-loaded silver ions are associated with a well-documented risk of local burst release, and the bioactivity of IL-4 protein remains highly vulnerable to irreversible inactivation during long-term storage.
EVs derived from GMSC, PLGA, PVA, and MMP-sensitive peptides
C57BL/6 mice, Monocytic THP-1 cells, SD rats
Anti-inflammatory, improve regeneration of periodontal tissues

GMSC-SEVReduced pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion by T cells and monocytes/macrophages, induced Treg formation, and suppressed T cell activation, both in rat models of periodontitis and in vitro, can decrease the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines by monocytes/macrophages and T cells, prevent T-cell activation, and stimulate the development of Tregs. Microparticles treated with GMSC-SEV can greatly enhance periodontal tissue regeneration.

The GMP-grade large-scale extraction and purification workflow of mesenchymal stem cell exosomes features remarkable complexity and extremely high production costs, and its therapeutic effect on deep biofilm removal has not been systematically assessed in large animal periodontitis models.
Anti-bacterial, anti-inflammatory, and promote bone regeneration
MDSCs-MV enhance the mineralization ability of osteoblasts derived from PDLSCs and exhibit anti-inflammatory effects through suppressing T cells via the CD73/CD39/adenosine pathway.
Ethical implications, constant storage condition, exorbitant cost

Clindamycin was released from the noisome formulations; the clindamycin-loaded niosome gel showed similar effectiveness to positive controls against oral pathogens, including Candida albicans and Staphylococcus aureus (cheese isolate).

Validation of the material’s function is currently restricted to in vitro antibacterial performance tests, and no systematic in vivo therapeutic efficacy evaluation has been conducted in either small or large animal models.
RAW264.7 cells, L929 cells, human vascular endothelial cells (HUVEC), BALB/c female mice

Lipo-RSV reprogrammed the M1 phenotype of inflammatory macrophages to M2 by downregulating phosphorylated STAT1 (p-STAT1) and activating phosphorylated STAT3 (p-STAT3). Additionally, Lipo-RSV decreases the levels of ROS and pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-12) while increasing the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10.

Given that the anti-inflammatory effect has only been confirmed in mouse models at the current stage, the local retention ability of the material in the complex dynamic flow environment of the periodontal pocket has not yet been subjected to targeted evaluation.
Reduced inflammation,The number of osteoblasts inhibits the alveolar bone.loss

At one week, the LPS group experienced more bone loss than the control and LPS+NP groups. The CXCR3 antagonist treatment (LPS+NP) dramatically decreased bone loss compared to the LPS group at six weeks.

The osteoprotective performance has only been verified in periodontitis models constructed on healthy mice, while the specificity of target blockade remains unvalidated in disease models with concomitant systemic immune dysregulation.
Suppressing the inflammatory activation, reduced bone loss
Nanogluttons can effectively regulate the prolonged opening of mPTPs by “glutting” Ca2+ around and inside mitochondria and significantly inhibit the inflammatory activation of macrophages.
Further optimize the biomaterial design and concentrate on the phenomenon in stem cells and other immune cells are needed. Safety and effectiveness will also be tested for a longer period.
DPPLM NPs exhibited potent antibacterial activity, reduced inflammation and ROS generation induced by AGE in vitro, reduced alveolar bone loss, and promoted the expression of osteogenic genes.

It has not fully xplored the underlying therapeutic mechanism by which the drug-loaded nanoparticles regulate inflammation metabolism and oxidativestress. It did not consider the general condition of thewhole body in DM.
Trisodium phosphate, Calcium nitrate tetrahydrate, octadecylamine, anhydrous ethanol, nitric acid,sodium selenite, linoleic acid, PAMAM-G3

G3@SeHAN Scavenged cell-free DNA, increased TGF-β, BMP-2, and IL-10, while reduced TNF-α 08and IL-6, in RAW 264.7 macrophages induced by the saliva of periodontitis patients. Moreover, it promotes a greater percentage of the M2 macrophage phenotype over the M1 phenotype by controlling the mononuclear phagocyte system in the periodontitis environment.

The anti-inflammatory effect has only been validated in mouse periodontitis models, and the potential cation-related local inflammatory reactions have not been evaluated in long-term experiments lasting more than 180 days.
Raw 264.7 cells, MC3T3-E1 cell, male C57BL/6J mice

MT-Cds can effectively regulate intracellular ROS, inhibit the production of inflammatory mediators, and maintain the homeostasis of the mitochondrial environment. MT-Cds considerably decreased inflammation and osteoclast activation, delayed the deterioration of alveolar bone, and contributed to the regeneration of damaged tissues.

The long-term in vivo metabolic clearance pathway of carbon dots has not been fully elucidated, and there are still unknown risks regarding the potential accumulation toxicity after long-term and large-dose administration.

sections.title: Inorganic Nanoparticles
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

sections.title: Glass Nanoparticles
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: Bioactive glass (BG) is an inorganic substance that adheres strongly to cells and protein molecules and has a significant specific surface area. It promotes the surface deposition of bone-like apatite. in a bodily fluid environment and has good biocompatibility.105

Hu developed composite icariin-loaded BGNs (IR-BGNs) with tissue regeneration, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory properties through loading icariin onto bioactive glass nanoparticles (BGNs).106 The diameter of the particles was measured to be between 20 and 60 nm. Cell experiments showed that IR-BGNs were non-cytotoxic. At 8 and 24 hours, the IR-BGN group had significantly higher RAW-264.7 cell migration rates than the control group. Anti-inflammatory effects of IR-BGNs on RAW264.7 cells were better than those of using irisin and BGNs alone. IR-BGNs may affect macrophage polarization and the release of growth factors, significantly reducing the in-vitro induced immune response of macrophages. In comparison to the negative control, human periodontal ligament cells (hPDLCs) induced by IR-BGNs expressed more markers related to osteogenesis, ALP activity, and mineralization ability. Yang prepared a mesoporous bioactive glass loaded with Quercetin (Quercetin/MBG). This mesoporous nano-drug delivery system altered the bone immune microenvironment by reprogramming macrophages via the miR-21a-5p/PDCD4/NF-κB pathway and restoring the osteogenic/angiogenic potential of PDLSCs.107

sections.title: Metallic Nanoparticles
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: The abuse of antibiotics to treat periodontitis has drawn more attention due to the issue of bacterial resistance. Metallic nanoparticles have become an ideal choice for inhibiting the growth of various microorganisms due to their great antibacterial properties and huge specific surface area.

Compared with antibiotics, gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) have special physical characteristics, including producing reactive oxygen species (ROS), directly interacting with the phospholipid bilayer, and the ability to bind to cytoplasmic proteins, which results in significant antibacterial action.108 Zhang studied the potential of AuNPs to encourage PDLCs to differentiate into osteoblasts.109 Chloroauric acid was the raw ingredient used in the chemical reduction process to produce AuNPs. The surface of AuNPs was modified by L/d-cystine. L-Cys-AuNPs increased the expression of osteogenic genes, such as RUNX2, OCn, ALP, and COL-1, and stimulated the development of human PDLCs. A significant amount of newly generated alveolar bone and periodontal ligament was observed in a rat model of periodontal deficiency treated with L-Cys-AuNPs. Metallic nanoclusters are materials having antibacterial properties that have a precise and simple structural composition and an extremely small size (~2 nm). Using a simple one-pot approach, researchers attempted to develop ultra-small gold nanoclusters (AuNCs), an ultra-small structure composed of 18 sulfate ligands and 25 gold atoms.110 AuNCs are approximately spherical, uniformly distributed, well-dispersed, and have a particle size between 1.5 and 4.0 nm. The findings demonstrated that AuNCs considerably inhibited the growth of Fn and damaged the integrity of the cell wall at a concentration of 0.2 mM. Treatment with AuNCs seriously harmed the cell membrane and may have prevented the growth of bacteria by depolarizing the membrane. After culturing with AuNCs, the membrane potential decreased, and the red/green fluorescence ratio decreased by around 50%, indicating that AuNCs treatment can disrupt the biofilm induced by Fn and alleviate periodontitis and bone loss.

AgNPs can enter the interior of bacteria and continuously dissolve and release silver ions.111,112 Rams113 experimentally confirmed that silver diamine fluoride (SDF) has in vitro antibacterial activity against possible pathogens in severe periodontal lesions, can inhibit the pathogens of the red-orange complex in subgingival biofilms, and selectively retains streptococci associated with periodontal health, suggesting potential new applications of SDF in the management of human periodontal infections.

Zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) have been thoroughly studied since they have their remarkable antifungal, antibacterial, and photoelectrochemical characteristics.114 Drug carriers were chosen using polycaprolactone (PCL) nanofibers to load zinc oxide nanoparticles and oxytetracycline hydrochloride (PCL-OTCz).115 Actinomyces aggregans, Prevotella intermedia, Treponema, and Pg were the four Gram-negative anaerobic bacterial species chosen for mixed culture. Compared with oxytetracycline hydrochloride and zinc oxide nanoparticles, PCL-OTCz has stronger antibacterial activity.

Superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) have good biodegradability and an inherent superparamagnetic effect. They have immunomodulatory qualities, can encourage the osteogenic development of certain mesenchymal stem cells, and show promise as biocompatible nanomaterials for PDLSC modification. Xia116 used SPIONs to modify human periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSC-SPIONs). PDLSCs treated with 250 μg·mL−1 ferulic acid glyceride-like SPIONs demonstrated greater osteogenic differentiation ability and better cell viability when compared to unmodified PDLSCs. Magnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (MNPs) are biocompatible and exhibit minimal cytotoxicity. MNPs can be fixed near the target, penetrate the biofilm, destroy the EPS, and ultimately eradicate the biofilm by concentrating the magnetic field. Tong117 prepared Fe3O4 magnetic nanoparticles loaded with minocycline (FPM NPs) by a co-precipitation method, which have good biocompatibility and strong anti-biofilm activity. By targeting and delivering antibiotics into the biofilm to kill bacteria, sub-periodontal injection of FPM nanoparticles in conjunction with a magnetic field can successfully transfer magnetic nano-drugs to the deep part of the periodontal pocket to alleviate periodontal inflammation.

sections.title: Photothermal Nanoparticles
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: PTT converts light energy into thermal energy using photothermal agents. When exposed to near-infrared (NIR) laser radiation, producing local hyperthermia (usually >55°C) to disrupt the integrity of pathogens and kill bacteria.118 Compared with traditional antibiotic therapy, PTT is non-invasive, controllable, has broad-spectrum antibacterial ability, and strong penetration into periodontal tissues. Moreover, it is less likely to cause drug resistance in bacteria that cause periodontitis, which has attracted extensive attention from researchers.119,120 Lin synthesized an NIR-responsive photothermal material, Au nanobipyramids (Au NBPs).121 The surface of Au NBPs was modified using mesoporous silica (mSiO2) loaded with minocycline. A hybrid hydrogel (gel MA-AuNBPs@SiO2) was designed by combining Au NBPs@SiO2 with gelatin methacrylate. Under NIR irradiation, the antibacterial rate of gel MA-Au NBPs@SiO2 against Pg increases to 66.7% with increasing NIR irradiation power when compared to non-NIR irradiation.

With the continuous exploration of PTT in antibacterial applications, some emerging problems limit the potential of PTT in periodontal therapy. First, the short-term antibacterial effect of PTT cannot fully combat unique periodontal pathogens. Deep-seated pathogens in periodontal pockets that are not eliminated face the risk of reactivation and proliferation. Second, the antibacterial temperature of PTT. High temperatures may cause tissue damage, while reducing the temperature to a safe range may hinder antibacterial activity. Studies have found that mild PTT at an appropriate temperature (about 40–45°C), supplemented with additional persistent antibacterial components to ensure antibacterial performance, is expected to be an effective and safe periodontal antibacterial method. Li118 constructed a multifunctional photothermal nanoparticle (BR@C3G-Cu) by using free bilirubin as a raw material and applying a copper-ion-coordinated cyanidin-3-O-glucoside metal-polyphenol network (MPN) to bilirubin nanoparticles. Under safe and mild conditions, the synergistic effect of metal-dependent functions and the photothermal conversion properties of MPN helps to effectively and persistently eliminate periodontal pathogens, satisfying the various antibacterial needs of periodontitis. In addition, BR@C3G-Cu nanoparticles assisted by mild hyperthermia can change the polarization balance of macrophages by scavenging ROS and blocking the cGAS-STING pathway, thereby improving the periodontal pro-inflammatory bone immune microenvironment and reducing the osteogenic damage of periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSCs). In a mouse periodontitis model, BR@C3G-Cu nanoparticles exposed to NIR radiation can inhibit alveolar bone resorption and promote periodontal tissue remodeling.

PDT in the treatment of periodontitis uses a photosensitizer that generates ROS under light stimulation, disrupting the fragile lipid membrane and causing rapid oxidation of lipids in bacteria.122,123 Because of its high singlet oxygen output, great tissue penetration, and superior biocompatibility, chlorin e6 (Ce6) is frequently utilized in PDT treatment.124,125 Since the photosensitizer Ce6 is highly hydrophobic and cannot be effectively absorbed by periodontal pathogens, by promoting the interaction between Ce6 and the negatively charged cell wall, penetration, and cell membrane, Li developed a nanosystem to increase its bacterial adsorption and solubility.126 Ce6 was initially hydrophilically modified by combining it with the cationic cell-penetrating peptide TAT peptide (TAT-Ce6). After that, TAT-Ce6 was loaded with tinidazole (TDZ) to create self-assembling nanoparticles (TAT-Ce6/TDZ NPs). TAT-Ce6/TDZ NPs have a more compact internal structure and a regular spherical form, according to TEM pictures. The positively charged TAT peptide’s surface dispersion is confirmed by TAT-Ce6/TDZ NPs, which have a zeta potential of about + 40.1 mV and a particle size of around 146.2 nm. Following one hour of TAT-Ce6 therapy, Pg has a zeta potential that rises from −11.2 to +5.86 mV. Through the TAT peptide, TAT-Ce6 significantly improves the penetration of bacterial cell membranes. TAT-Ce6 and TAT-Ce6/TDZ NPs exhibit more antibacterial activity because they are more effectively absorbed by plaque biofilms through the TAT peptide.

Traditional PDT can produce a lot of ROS to destroy infections. However, the increase in ROS during antibacterial treatment may exert oxidative stress in periodontal pockets and cause irreparable damage to surrounding tissues. As a two-dimensional material, black phosphorus nanosheets (BPNs) have a folded layered structure where each phosphorus atom is covalently bound to three neighboring phosphorus atoms in the phosphorus monolayer. Nanoscale black phosphorus films exhibit a double-layer structure folded along the Z-axis in contrast to typical 2D nanomaterials. This folded structure gives BPNs a higher specific surface area, enabling them to effectively act as antioxidants to eliminate ROS. Li127 used BPNs, which can scavenge ROS to produce an antimicrobial effect while removing the adverse effects of ROS-based PDT. After BPN treatment, the levels of TNF-α, TGF-β, Arg-1, IL-6, IL-10, and IL-β mRNA expression were significantly reduced, confirming the in vitro anti-inflammatory effect of this nanomaterial. In addition, recurrent attacks caused by immune system disorders can also damage surrounding tissues.

sections.title: Mesoporous Material Nanoparticles
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: Currently, mesoporous calcium silicate nanoparticles (MCSN) and Mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSN) are two popular inorganic nanocarrier systems.128,129 Tan130 designed a drug carrier system of resveratrol-grafted mesoporous silica nanoparticles (MSN-RSV). The induction of MSN can eliminate the inherent cytotoxicity of respiratory syncytial virus to RAW 264.7 and improve the bioavailability of RSV. RSV and MSN can hinder the polarization of M1 and activate the M2 phenotype by positively regulating macrophage polarization, thus improving the regulatory function of the drug carrier. It can also improve diabetic periodontitis (DP) related to the regulation of macrophage polarization. The mechanism might be connected to the SIRT1/AMPK and NF-κB signaling pathways. Although it has no discernible impact on blood-glucose-related markers, local treatment of MSN-RSV as an adjuvant can also considerably lower insulin resistance (IR) in diabetic rats to a considerable degree. Since Au nanoparticles (Au NPs) require a smaller size and a high catalytic rate. Deng produced a carbon monoxide (CO)-enhanced multi-enzyme synergistic hybrid nano-platform (MSN-Au@CO) by coating ultra-small Au NPs in the form of multi-nanoenzymes on MSN and loading manganese carbonyl (MnCO). By catalyzing the oxidation of glucose into gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), Au NPs’ glucose oxidase-like activity kills bacteria by converting H2O2 into hydroxyl radicals (·OH) via peroxidase-like activity. In LPS-challenged macrophages, CO generated by the H2O2 reaction and Au NPs shows a synergistic anti-inflammatory effect. The underlying process may involve inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway to lower the inflammatory response and stimulating NRF2 to lower ROS.131

sections.title: Hydroxyapatite-Based Nanocarriers
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: As the main component of dental tissue and bone mineral, nano-hydroxyapatite (nHA) is characterized by its compatibility with the physiological environment. This non-toxic material, which is highly compatible with dental/bone tissue, is frequently utilized as an ingredient of fillers and supplements for bone repair. Wang132 developed an nHA in which a polycaprolactone-co-lactide (PCLLA) elastomer matrix included hydroxyapatite particles that make up traditional hydroxyapatite bone powder. Hydrogen bonds are formed by terminal hydroxyl groups on PCLLA arms and many surface hydroxyl groups on HA, which help to create a cross-linked network. In vitro, PCLLA-NanoHA increased macrophage polarization to the M2 phenotype. In vivo, PCLLA-NanoHA promoted alveolar bone repair like that of standard HA bone powder. In diabetic mice, PCLLA-NanoHA performed better at promoting bone tissue repair than the widely used HA bone powder. PCLLA-NanoHA regulates the M2 polarization of macrophages via activating the PI3K/AKT and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR) signaling pathways. As a result, a favorable local immunological milieu is created for bone regeneration and repair.

SPIONsPDLSCsHuman gingival fibroblast cells (hGFs)Anti-inflammatoryCompared to untreated PDLSCs, PDLSCs modified with 250 μgmL−1 ferumoxytol had a higher capacity for osteogenic development. Compared to PDLSC CM, PDLSC-SPION CM has a greater ability to reduce inflammation.Only in vitro cell assays wereperformed. Analysis of protein expression in the CM will be included in future studies when investigating the in vivo therapeutic effects of PDLSC-SPION CM.[116]
Fe3O4@PDA NPsMinoL929 cells, Male Wistar ratsAntibacterialFPM NPs demonstrated low systemic toxicity, great biocompatibility, and strong antibacterial activity against F. nucleatum, P. gingivalis, and S. sanguinis. Rat models treated with FPM NPs showed a good recovery in periodontal inflammation.It only used a rat periodontitis model in this study; further studies are required to develop a natural biofilm as a periodontitis model. Further research is required to optimize the size, shape, and surface of the nanoparticles to ensure effective targeting and drug release. Addressing potential toxicity concerns and regulatory issues in clinical practice warrants further investigation.[117]
Photothermal NanoparticlesMSNs, Au NBPs, gelatin methacrylateMinoL929 cellAntibacterialThe GelMA-Au NBPs@SiO2 hybrid hydrogels demonstrated good antibacterial properties and controlled mineral distribution.Under near-infrared light irradiation, the problem of uneven local temperature distribution is prone to occur, and excessively high temperature will damage the surrounding normal gingival tissues.[121]
UCNPs, mSiO2CAHuman gingival epithelial (HGE) cell line, human umbilical vein endothelial cell line (HUVECs), RAW 264.7 cells, and SD ratsAnti-bacteria, anti-inflammation, and immunomodulationUCMCs have particular anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and antibacterial properties, notably against anaerobic bacteria. Modulated the conversion of macrophages from M1to M2 type by the TNF, IL-17, and MAPK signaling pathways.The biofilm model using uncoated glass surfaces is not optimum for simulating the oral environment in periodontitis. The feasibility of UCMCs with NIR irradiation in vivo was verified in the most commonly used experimental periodontitis model of SD rats, whereas its application in other animals (rabbits and dogs) and deeper tissue depth remains for further research.[134]
BPNs, ICG/HGF-1 cells, SD ratsAntibacterial, anti-inflammatoryFollowing BPN treatment, the levels of TNF-α, TGF-β, Arg-1, IL-6, IL-10, and IL-β mRNA expression were significantly reduced and the levels of proinflammatory factors decreased.ICG/aPDT exhibited the antibacterial effect and the antioxidative ability of the BPNs.Black phosphorus nanosheets are extremely prone to degradation and inactivation in aqueous environments, making long-term preservation difficult. Besides, the local metabolic kinetics of phosphorus elements after material degradation have not been fully clarified.[127]
Mesoporous Material NanoparticlesMSNRSVRAW264.7 cells, SD ratsAnti-inflammatoryPreventing M1 polarization and triggering the M2 phenotype by triggering the SIRT1/AMPK signaling pathway and blocking the NF-κB signaling pathway.The complete in vivo degradation period of mesoporous silica exceeds 180 days, which may induce local chronic inflammatory responses and fail to match the time requirement for rapid clinical periodontal tissue repair.[130]
MSN, HAuCl4.3H2O, MnCO/RAW264.7 cells, Diabetic RatsAntibacterial, anti-inflammatory, and reduce bone lossInhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway to lower the inflammatory response and stimulating NRF2 to lower ROS. Demonstrating a reduction in periodontal bone loss and good biocompatibility in diabetic rats.The therapeutic efficacy has only been validated in in vitro cell experiments and diabetic rat models, and the stability of multiple enzymes loaded in the nanoparticles is difficult to maintain over a long period, making the system prone to enzyme activity loss during storage.[131]
Hydroxyapatite-Based NanocarriersHA, PCLLA/BMDMImprove immune microenvironment, promote alveolar bone regenerationPCLLA-NanoHA regulates the M2 polarization of macrophages via activating the PI3K/AKT and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPAR) signaling pathways. A favorable local immunological milieu is created for bone regeneration and repair.Since no long-term large animal experiments exceeding 12 months have been conducted, the local acidic microenvironment generated by the degradation of the implanted material may induce chronic inflammatory responses.[132]

cells.text: CeO2 NPs can reduce the excessive ROS induced by LPS and decrease inflammatory factors, reduce alveolar bone resorption, reduce osteoclast activity and inflammatory responses, block the MAPK-NF-κB signaling pathway, and promote the repair of damaged tissues.

The catalytic activity of nanozymes is extremely vulnerable to interference caused by non-specific protein adsorption in the complex local periodontal microenvironment. The catalytic performance varies drastically among materials with different particle sizes and component ratios, which imposes great challenges to the quality control during large-scale manufacturing.
BSA, PEG, TPP, MnO2 polycrystalline particles.

In addition to suppressing macrophage M1 activation and inflammatory factor release, MCBN can absorb excess electrons in the ETC, target the mitochondrial complexes of inflammatory macrophages, block the NLRP3 inflammatory vesicle activation and NF-kB signaling pathway, and convert the electrons to break down H2O2.
The therapeutic efficacy has only been validated in mouse periodontitis models, and the targeting efficiency cannot be guaranteed during subsequent clinical translation processes.
The multifunctional electrospun Janus nanofibers might restore alveolar bone damage by up-regulating the expression of osteo-Gene-related genes OCN, RUNX2, and ALP in a rat periodontitis model.

The ion release rate of ZIF-8 embedded in nanofibrous scaffolds is difficult to precisely regulate. Notably, the therapeutic performance of this system has only been preliminarily validated in rat periodontitis models.

PLN regulates the polarization of macrophages towards the M2 phenotype, significantly promoting the osteogenic differentiation and migration of BMSCs. PLN can prevent inflammatory bone loss in periodontitis and encourage bone regeneration.

Multiple immune-related pathways were affected by nano-topography; their effect needs to be investigated in future study. Besides, it is crucial to emphasize that urther validation of our findings in larger animal models is es-sential.
RAW264.7 cells, BMSCs, Male C57BL/6J mice

In addition to exhibiting a greater collagen content and a denser periodontal ligament structure, TS@BMP-2 increased the osteogenic potential, reduced the inflammatory levels in macrophages, and lowered the number of osteoclasts, all of which created an environment that was conducive to periodontal bone regeneration.
The intricate microenvironment of periodontitis requires acomprehensive investigation, potentially through clinical or large-animal studies, to better understand its complexities.
rBMSCs, L929, andRAW264.7 cells, SD rats
Anti-inflammation and accelerated bone defect repair

P@PCH polarizes macrophages toward a pro-healing (M2) phenotype by secreting more pro-healing and anti-inflammatory cytokines, stimulates the migration and differentiation of rBMSCs, and creates an osteoimmune environment that is conducive to the osteogenic differentiation and recruitment of stem cells.

The regeneration and repair of periodontal composite tissue are a very complicated process, including MSC recruitment, angiogenesis, osteogenesis and other biological behaviors,the system needs to be further optimized to meet the needs of various biological signals required for periodontal composite tissue.

PCL/LAP nanofiber membranes regulated inflammatory responses via increasing M2 polarization of macrophages, pro-remodeling N2 neutrophils, promoting the production of anti-inflammatory, and coordinating the immunomodulatory activities of PDLCs. In vivo, PCL/LAP nanofiber membranes promoted periodontal regeneration and the repair of calvarial defects in rats.

The vidence of the immunomodulatory effect of the PCL/LAP nanofibrous membrane in vivo is absent due to neutrophil and macrophage-involved regeneration pro-cesses, mainly occurring in the early stage. In addition,the particular mechanisms of the effects of PCL/LAP anofibrous membranes on PDLC-mediated periodontal regeneration remain unknown.
The mouse embryonic bone marrow MSC cell line (MC3T3-E1), Raw 264.7 cells, and SD rats

The osteogenesis of MC3T3-E1 cells in the inflammatory milieu and the M1-to-M2 transition of RAW264.7 were both triggered by the composite hydrogel. The composited hydrogel reduced local inflammation and improved the creation of new bone in situ in a rat model of periodontitis.
It need validation in larger animal models, and longer-term treatments are necessary to verify the potential for complete tissue regeneration.

C10-KR8@ZIF-8 nanoparticles promote the osteogenic differentiation of BMMSCs by enhancing the nuclear localization of YAP and activating the focal adhesion kinase/phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/AKT (FAK/PI3K/AKT) pathway.

The safe manufacturing and quality control f nanoparticles. further optimization f biomaterials is necessary to achieve effective therapeutic outcomes, as is the development of scalable mass-production solutions.

Excellent inhibitory effects on S. aureus, S. aureus, and E. coli biofilms were demonstrated by E-Au@H, which also promoted angiogenesis, improved BMSC aggregation, accelerated the development of calcified nodules, and supported bone regeneration.
Gold nanoparticles cannot be completely degraded in vivo, and their long-term local implantation may potentially induce chronic foreign body reactions in the surrounding periodontal tissues.
RAW264.7 cells, hPDLSCs, Male SD rats

In the hydrogel-treated PDLSCs, the hydrogel was able to increase ALP activity, modulate M1 macrophage polarization, and scavenge excess ROS. Its osteogenetic potency was explained by the activation of the Wnt/β-catenin cascade, while its anti-inflammatory properties resulted from its suppression of NF-κB signaling.

The ROS-responsive threshold of hydrogels is highly susceptible to interference from physiological fluctuations in the local periodontal microenvironment, which prevents the achievement of precise lesion-specific drug release. Notably, the therapeutic efficacy of this system has only been preliminarily validated in rat models.
The THP-1 cell line (TIB-202), Human lymphatic endothelial cells (HLECs), SD rats
Anti- inflammation, promotion of alveolar bone regeneration

In addition to promoting M2 polarization and lymphatic function, CH-BPNs-NBP shields human lymphatic endothelial cells and macrophages from ROS assault. CH-BPNs-NBP reduce inflammation and tissue damage and promote alveolar bone regeneration in vivo.
Black phosphorus nanomaterials suffer from intrinsically poor stability in aqueous environments, and their formulated preparations are prone to functional failure during long-term storage.

By controlling macrophage polarization through lipid metabolism and enhancing autophagy in periodontal ligament stem cells, BNP-PEDOT-PSF-AG hydrogel scavenged ROS for conductivity for bone formation and anti-inflammation.

The fabrication process of conductive hydrogels is highly complex, and it remains challenging to precisely control the dispersion uniformity of the incorporated conductive phases, which leads to an extremely high cost in large-scale manufacturing.
MOFs (comprisingMagnesium (magnesium and gallic acid), CMCS, DEX, and 4-FPBA
MC3T3 cells, RAW 264.7 cells, SD rats

In periodontitis, hydrogels and MOFs work in concert to promote bone repair, modulate the immune system, and have antibacterial action. By controlling M1/M2 polarization, CSBDX@MOF can stimulate alveolar bone repair and suppress the production of genes linked to inflammation and the CD206 gene.
For periodontitis is a chronic disease and bone regeneration takes a long time, the relative long-term osteogenic effect ofCSBDX and CSBDX@MOF system in vivo remains to beexplored.
AgNC and M2 EVs encapsulated within DNA hydrogel.
AgNC demonstrated strong antibacterial activity, while immunomodulatory M2 EVs had strong osteogenic effects on macrophages and anti-inflammatory effects.

DNA hydrogels exhibit extremely poor stability and are susceptible to rapid degradation by nucleases that are widely present in vivo. As a result, it is difficult for them to maintain sufficient structural integrity in the local periodontal microenvironment. Additionally, the bioactivity of M2-type extracellular vesicles cannot be easily preserved during long-term storage.

Because of its high drug loading, regulated and prolonged release, and intrinsic antibacterial qualities, CS-PA/CNP has strong immunomodulatory effects by preventing myeloid and lymphocyte aggregation.

sections.title: Nanozymes
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: With the latest advancements in nanomaterials, nanozymes have shown promising potential in metabolic regulation as enzyme mimics with adjustable catalytic activity. Nanoparticles doped with cerium (Ce), iron (Fe), platinum (Pt), manganese (Mn), and their oxides have been shown to play beneficial roles in infections, bacterial metabolic disorders, tumors, and neurodegenerative diseases because their metal active centers can mimic the redox processes catalyzed by natural enzymes.152 The primary biological mechanism by which activated macrophages eliminate phagocytosed microbes is the generation of ROS.177 However, too much ROS may cause macrophages to shift to the M1 phenotype, which would worsen inflammation.178 Cerium oxide (CeO2) is a nanozyme with catalase-like and superoxide dismutase-like properties that can efficiently scavenge H2O2 and O2•− by changing between Ce3⁺ (oxidized) and Ce3⁺ (reduced) forms.179 The CeO2 nanoparticles synthesized by Yu151 have activities similar to CAT and SOD and the capacity to scavenge •OH, which, in the inflammatory microenvironment, can scavenge ROS. Both in vitro and in vivo experiments revealed that CeO2 nanoparticles can reduce excessive ROS caused by LPS. By blocking the MAPK-NF-κB signaling pathway, CeO2 nanoparticles can also reduce inflammatory factors. Additionally, CeO2 nanoparticles have been shown to drastically reduce osteoclast activity, alveolar bone resorption, and the inflammatory response in a rat periodontitis model, all of which aid in the healing of injured tissues.

A mitochondrial complex biomimetic nanozyme (MCBN) composed of MnO2 polycrystalline particles coated with TPP, PEG, and bovine serum albumin (BSA) was developed by Ren.152 It has a nano-scale size and the biological characteristics of natural complexes. The prepared MCBN can target the mitochondrial complex of inflammatory macrophages, absorb excess electrons in the electron transport chain (ETC), and convert the electrons to decompose H2O2. By transforming existing free radicals, reducing the burst of ROS and ATP, and inhibiting the NF-κB signaling pathway and the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, MCBN efficiently suppresses the activation of M1 macrophages and the release of inflammatory factors. It also demonstrated markedly decreased alveolar bone loss and excellent inflammatory control in a ligature-induced periodontitis mouse model.

sections.title: Nanofibers
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: Novel antibacterial nanomaterials, like nanofibers, have been included in combined treatment approaches for antibacterial action and periodontal tissue regeneration in recent years. Zinc ions and 2-methylimidazole make up Zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8). ZIF-8 produces antibiotic properties by releasing Zn2⁺ and 2-methylimidazole in the acidic microenvironment of bacterial infections. Sun et al developed a multifunctional delivery system (PPZF JNF) that contained FK506 and ZIF-8 nanoparticles encapsulated in nanofibers.153 The nanofibers were fabricated via electrospinning using PCL and PVP as raw materials. After PPZF JNF treatment, Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli levels were significantly reduced. In BMSCs, osteogenic gene expression levels (RUNX2, ALP, and OCN) were increased. The CEJ-ABC distance in periodontitis-affected rats decreased by 21.8%. Additionally, bone volume/total volume and trabecular number increased by 25.7% and 34.5%, respectively, while trabecular separation decreased by 0.16-fold.

Electrospinning is a versatile method for producing tissue engineering scaffolds, producing nanofibers that mimic the ECM with excellent biocompatibility. He154 used surface-directed epitaxial crystallization to prepare Electrospun nanofibers made of strongly oriented, periodic lamellar poly(ε-caprolactone). In vitro studies, PLN was able to precisely regulate macrophage polarization toward the M2 phenotype. PLN-polarized macrophages markedly increased BMSC migration and osteogenic differentiation. The activation of Yes-associated protein (YAP), which in turn relied on the capacity of YAP to directly oppose the NF-κB signaling pathway and bind IKK-α, was necessary for the topographic signals regulating macrophage polarization. Subsequently, the same research team created TS@BMP-2, a hierarchically constructed nanofiber scaffold with a core containing bone morphogenetic protein-2 (BMP-2) and a nanoimprinted sheath. A BMP-2/PVA core and a PCL sheath were coaxially electrospun to generate the scaffold, which was then surface-directed epitaxially crystallized to produce cyclic nanolamellar relief on the sheath. In vivo experiments showed that the TS@BMP-2 treatment group significantly alleviated inflammatory conditions in periodontal tissues of C57/BL mice with periodontitis, demonstrating how local cues can effectively reduce inflammation. At four weeks, micro-CT images showed that the TS@BMP-2 group had higher collagen content and denser periodontal ligament structures than the control group. Furthermore, the TS@BMP-2 group had fewer osteoclasts, which improved the conditions for periodontal bone repair.155

sections.title: Nanoparticle Gels
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: Hydrogel systems with antibacterial and bone immunomodulatory effects represent a potential approach to the regeneration of periodontal tissue. They avoid the disadvantages of applying drugs directly, such as short half-lives180 and overlapping side-effects.181 Wang158 developed PF-127@DOX/ALG-MS@PA, a thermosensitive composite hydrogel composed of alginate microspheres and Pluronic F-127 (PF-127). The composite hydrogel can be injected locally because it has high gelling capabilities at body temperature and excellent dimensional flexibility in the liquid state. In an inflammatory environment, the composite hydrogel stimulates MC3T3-E1 cell osteogenesis and induces RAW264.7 cells to transform from the M1 to the M2 phenotype. According to in vivo studies, the composite hydrogel stimulates the growth of new bone in an SD rat model of periodontitis. The thermosensitive composite hydrogel PF-127@DOX/ALG-MS@PA, fabricated from Pluronic F-127 and alginate microspheres, enables temporally programmed dual-drug delivery. Doxycycline (DOX) undergoes rapid burst release within 0–24 h to eradicate pathogenic bacteria and suppress acute inflammation; alginate microspheres sustain drug release from day 3 to day 14 for immunomodulatory effects; starting from week 3, proanthocyanidins (PA) exert long-term pro-angiogenic effects to facilitate alveolar bone regeneration.

Wang159 coupled a C10 fatty acid with a recently created peptide KR8 (KRIWQRIK), a newly synthesized peptide, with a C10 fatty acid to construct C10-KR8@ZIF-8 (a zeolite imidazole framework-8 loaded with C10-KR8) nanoparticles, and developed an injectable gelatin-methacryloyl (GelMA) hydrogel incorporating C10-KR8@ZIF-8 nanoparticles for the continuous release of zinc and the C10-KR8 peptide. The pH-responsive hydrogel has a strong capacity for bone repair through the synergistic action of fostering osteogenesis in diseased circumstances and creating a dynamic immunomodulatory environment. It promotes the osteogenic differentiation of BMMSCs by enhancing the nuclear localization of YAP and activating the focal adhesion kinase/phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/AKT (FAK/PI3K/AKT) pathway.

Patients with DP face challenges in achieving complete periodontal tissue regeneration due to excessive oxidative reactions, immunoregulatory imbalance, and compromised mesenchymal stem cell performance. Fang163 used BSA nanoparticles to develop a polyphenol-mediated redox-active alginate/gelatin hydrogel known as BNP-PEDOT-PSF-AG hydrogel. It couples gas signals and endogenous electrical signals using an H2S sustained-release device and a conductive poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-assembled PDA-mediated silk microfiber network (PEDOT-PSF). The hydrogel has strong conductivity due to the poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene)-assembled PDA-mediated silk microfibers, which allow it to boost calcium ion influx, facilitate cell alignment, and transfer endogenous bioelectricity. Furthermore, the synergistic action of hydrogen sulfide gas-bioelectricity coupling stimulates bone production by controlling macrophage polarization through lipid metabolism regulation and increasing the autophagy of periodontal ligament stem cells.

sections.title: Nanocomposite Membranes
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis

blocks.text: Guided Bone Regeneration (GBR) mediated by barrier membranes has been recognized as an effective approach for repairing several kinds of bone defects, such as the alveolar bone.182 Membranes provide room for the formation of new bone by acting as physical barriers that stop soft tissue from developing into bone deficiencies. Most clinical barrier membranes, however, currently available (eg, Bio-Gide collagen membrane), only serve as space-makers and cannot effectively promote bone tissue regeneration.183 Liu167 used polylactic acid (PLA) and hydroxyapatite nanowires (HAP NWs) composites loaded with manganese dioxide nanosheets (MnO2 NSs) to create a barrier membrane for GBR. The HP@Mn membrane features asymmetric component distribution (PLA on one side and HAP@MnO2 on the other). Leveraging the catalytic activity of MnO2 nanozymes, these membranes efficiently decompose H2O2 into O2. Experiments conducted in vitro showed that HP@Mn membranes prevented H2O2-induced macrophage apoptosis, reduced intracellular oxidative stress, downregulated overexpression of inflammation-related genes/proteins, and suppressed M1 macrophage polarization. Nano-hydroxyapatite endowed osteogenic differentiation potential, while MnO2 NSs exerted a cooperative impact. Additionally, the barrier function played by PLA inhibited excessive proliferation of periodontal epithelial cells, establishing an environment that promotes the regeneration of periodontal tissue.
A comprehensive comparison of different nanocomposites is presented in Table 5 and Table 6.

sections.title: Other Treatment Strategies in Periodontal NDDS
heading_path: Nanoparticle-Based Drug Delivery Systems for Periodontitis
Other Treatment Strategies in Periodontal NDDS

blocks.text: TLR4, a key receptor for recognizing bacterial endotoxins in innate immunity, is essential for triggering immunological reactions during periodontitis.184 Through TLR4, innate immune cells identify endotoxins produced by initiate inflammatory signaling pathways and bacteria in the microenvironment. Furthermore, by attaching to endotoxins on the bacterial surface via TLR4, they can recognize and collect bacteria.185 Thus, TLR4 in immune-activated lesions represents a novel target for periodontitis treatment. Deng168 created a nanoplatform that expresses TLR4 and has biomimetic cell membrane characteristics. RAW264.7 cells with high TLR4 expression were created. via genetic engineering, and their cell membranes were extracted. After that, the functionalized membranes were manually extruded to cover the surface of minocycline-loaded silica nanospheres (SNs), forming the nanodelivery system MSNCs. MSNCs demonstrated excellent targeting ability in in vitro experiments toward E. coli and effectively released antibiotics to kill bacteria. Moreover, they neutralized endotoxins in the microenvironment and prevented macrophage inflammatory activation. MSNCs significantly reduced periodontal tissue inflammation and alveolar bone loss in a ligature-induced periodontitis mouse model, suggesting their promise as a novel approach for immunomodulation and targeted antibacterial therapy. In periodontitis, macrophage recruitment reduces the expression of microRNA-126 (miR-126). Cell Membrane-Camouflaged Nanodecoys (CNDs) are emerging delivery platforms with inherent biocompatibility. Lin169 developed multifunctional CNDs with targeted microbial toxicity and immunomodulatory capabilities for periodontitis treatment. A cascade catalytic system that combines hollow manganese dioxide (hMnO2) and L-amino acid oxidase (LAAO) was constructed. Mutual enhancement of catalytic efficiency accelerated O2 production in hypoxic microenvironments, disrupting metabolic processes of periodontal pathogens. Additionally, LAAO-hMnO2 CNDs scavenged overexpressed ROS, rebalanced the inflammatory microenvironment, and promoted M1-to-M2 macrophage polarization. Nanodecoys triggered nuclear translocation of NRF2 to reduce oxidative stress responses and rewire macrophage polarization, thereby promoting osteogenic differentiation. In vivo, alveolar bone regeneration was significantly enhanced following treatment.

In order to achieve the objectives of reducing inflammation and encouraging tissue regeneration, nanotherapy has become a viable approach in the last ten years to modify the periodontal microenvironment and reestablish immunological balance. Although many nanotherapeutic agents have demonstrated immunomodulatory, antibacterial, and regenerating qualities in animal models and in vitro, unfortunately, most current research remains in the preclinical stage. The use of nanoparticles to treat periodontitis has been the focus of several clinical studies. Only less than 20 clinical trials of nano-formulations for periodontitis treatment can be retrieved on ClinicalTrials.gov (Supplementary Material Table S1), such as “Perforated Collagen Membrane With Nano-hydroxyapatite for Intrabony Defects”, “Evaluation of Nano Bioactive Glass Combined With i - PRF Scaffold in Vital Pulp Treatments”, “Locally Delivered Whey Protein Nanoparticles Gel in Stage II Grade B Periodontitis”, “Antimicrobial Photodynamic Therapy With ICG-Loaded Nanoparticles for Periodontitis Management”, “Efficacy of Local Dox Gel Delivery Versus Dox Nanoparticles Prepared Gel in The Treatment of Stage II Periodontitis”, “Clinical and Biochemical Effect of Atorvastatin in Nano Particles Gel in Periodontitis Treatment”, and “Efficacy of Nano - Curcumin and Nano-Hyaluronic Acid as an Adjunct to Scaling and Root Planing in the Treatment of Periodontitis”. With these clinical trials, only two of them have publicly uploaded clinical results. This suggests that the shift from academic achievement to clinical application presents some difficulties.

First, the drug release concentration needs to be higher than the minimum inhibitory concentration in order to prevent bacterial growth utilizing nanoparticles or drug-loaded nanoparticles. To guarantee antibacterial efficacy during treatment, drug release rate and concentration must be controlled via nanomaterials. Despite the fact that several studies have evaluated the dispersing effect of nanoparticles on biofilms, clinical trials have not confirmed this effect.18

Second, the biosafety, toxicity, and long-term in vivo behavior of nanomaterials are crucial. When nanomaterials are applied to periodontal tissues, they must adhere to biosafety regulations to guarantee that they do not damage healthy tissue structures. Nanoparticles must have strong bioabsorbable qualities to be used in periodontal tissue regeneration. Patients may require a second procedure to remove any leftover material if the substance itself does not break down, which prolongs their suffering and recuperation period. To systematically assess chronic risks induced by nanoparticle accumulation in vital organs, multiple imaging techniques have been established to monitor long-term excretion and visceral retention of nanocarriers for chronic toxicity evaluation. Optical imaging represented by the IVIS small-animal in vivo fluorescence system utilizes NIR luminescent nanoparticles to dynamically track particle retention and clearance over long experimental windows.186 X-ray-based modalities including CT and SPECT enable quantitative tracing of radiolabeled nanocarriers; for instance, radionuclides such as Cu can be incorporated into gold nanoparticles for long-term biodistribution testing and semi-quantitative measurement derived from imaging signals.187 Supplementary monitoring tools include MRI, MPI and XPCS. In line with the Technical Guidelines for Nonclinical Safety Evaluation of Nanomedicines (Trial) issued by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), researchers are recommended to label nanoparticles with fluorescent or radioactive tracers, and utilize platforms such as IVIS and SPECT for in vivo tracking and semi-quantitative analysis of imaging readouts. Despite advances in monitoring methodologies, long-term toxicological profiles of most nanocarriers remain unclear. Therefore, it is necessary to study the long-term absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion behavior of NPs in the human body and conduct a thorough investigation of the potential toxicity of nanoparticles. This may be achieved by incorporating natural elements and optimizing degradation pathways. Understanding the mechanism of action of NPs and improving therapies will be made easier with the development of reliable strategies to monitor their distribution and assess their impact on the body.

Third, tissue regeneration, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial defense are all part of the cascade process that treats periodontitis. One-stage intervention could interfere with other stages. This complexity requires nano-therapy to have spatio-temporal and stage-specific regulation, including the late-stage resolution of tissue regeneration and inflammation, the mid-term recruitment of stem/progenitor cells, and the early removal of pathogens and necrotic tissues.188 For example, excessive host inflammation is linked to the degradation of periodontal tissue. By offering potent medication components, NPs can reduce this persistent inflammation and encourage tissue healing. A mild inflammatory reaction can encourage neovascularization, boost the local immune system, aid wound healing, and remove waste from the injured area.189 However, both the absence and excess of inflammation can have adverse effects on tissues.190 Therefore, creating and sustaining an ideal “ideal” level in the tissue environment to successfully fend off foreign invasion without seriously harming normal tissue structures is a challenge. The current targeting ability of nano-therapy is limited, and active targeting is the key to improving the specificity of nano-formulations. Additionally, it is necessary to maintain the pharmacological activity of nanoparticles after binding to the target. Therefore, enhanced specificity for the immune cell subsets t and distinct microenvironment in periodontal lesions is required, and this can be achieved by stimulus-responsive design and ligand-receptor engineering.191

In addition, issues such as large-scale production processes, control of key design features, and cost optimization also need to be resolved.8 Standardized processes for large-scale mass production have been established. For organic nanoparticles, continuous microfluidic synthesis platforms enable mass production at the scale of hundreds of liters by precisely controlling parameters such as two-phase flow rates, reagent ratios, and temperature within microchannels. This approach restricts batch-to-batch variations in particle size distribution, drug loading, and surface potential to within 5%, significantly outperforming traditional batch stirring methods, which typically exhibit variability exceeding 20%.192,193 For inorganic nanoparticles, continuous hydrothermal synthesis reactor systems ensure high batch consistency by programmatically regulating heating rates, pressure, and reaction duration.194,195 Furthermore, real-time quality control is achieved through online detection technologies, such as dynamic light scattering (DLS) and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), which screen and eliminate unqualified components. This integration greatly reduces unit production costs while ensuring batch uniformity.196,197 Currently, several medical nanomaterials have achieved mass production through these processes and have entered the stage of medical device registration and application.198,199

Periodontitis is a chronic inflammation triggered by subgingival pathogenic bacteria, progressively destroying periodontal supporting tissues and contributing to multiple systemic complications. Nanoparticle-based delivery systems enable localized controlled drug release, deep biofilm penetration, and targeted antibacterial action, while simultaneously modulating oxidative stress and macrophage polarization to promote periodontal tissue regeneration. These delivery systems address core limitations of conventional therapies, such as insufficient local drug concentrations, brief retention within periodontal pockets, systemic toxic reactions and emerging bacterial resistance, and they possess great translational potential for minimally invasive, targeted periodontal treatment.

However, multiple critical bottlenecks still impede their widespread clinical translation, including unclear long-term biosafety risks, variable biodegradation behaviors in acidic periodontal microenvironments, inconsistent batch-to-batch reproducibility during mass production, limited human clinical validation data, strict medical device regulatory restrictions and high manufacturing costs. The lack of quantitative evidence on periodontal retention, biofilm infiltration, and translational maturity for most nanocarrier categories represents a critical gap in current research.

Despite these challenges, we remain optimistic about the clinical prospects of periodontal nanomedicine. With sustained cross-disciplinary research continuously optimizing carrier design, biosafety, and scalable manufacturing processes, safe and effective nanoformulations are expected to become widely available in the future, transforming the treatment of chronic periodontal inflammation and offering new diagnostic and therapeutic hope for patients with periodontitis and related systemic inflammatory diseases.

blocks.text: In recent years, the prevalence of diabetes mellitus and periodontal disease has been on the rise, which has drawn scholars' attention to the association between diabetes mellitus and periodontitis.

Studies have demonstrated that a hyperglycemic microenvironment can notably increase the incidence of periodontitis and the severity of bone loss, impair the regenerative capacity of periodontal tissues, and thereby affect the therapeutic effect of periodontitis. This paper comprehensively reviews the latest research progress regarding the impact of diabetes mellitus on periodontitis and summarizes the current therapeutic strategies for diabetes complicated with periodontitis, including both traditional therapeutic methods and novel therapeutic approaches.

In conclusion, this review provides a systematic overview of the interaction between diabetes and periodontitis as well as related treatments, laying a foundation for subsequent clinical research and practice.

Diabetes mellitus and periodontitis exhibit a close bidirectional interaction: a hyperglycemic microenvironment worsens periodontal tissue damage, while periodontal inflammation further disrupts metabolic balance. This comorbidity has become a major global health issue, as its high incidence and complex pathology place a heavy burden on oral health and overall well-being (1–4). Hyperglycemia drives periodontal tissue destruction by disrupting immune responses, imbalancing bone metabolism, and impairing tissue repair. This forms a vicious cycle that complicates clinical treatment. Traditional therapies, focusing on glycemic control and mechanical debridement, have limitations such as insufficient tissue regeneration, potential drug resistance, and inability to address systemic-local interactions (5, 6). In recent years, innovative treatments integrating precision drug delivery, biological agents, advanced biomaterials, and physical adjuvants have shown great potential to overcome these challenges. This review summarizes the latest research on the pathological link between the two diseases, discusses the drawbacks of traditional therapies, and highlights cutting-edge treatment advances, offering insights into how multi-dimensional strategies can transform the management of this destructive comorbidit (7–9).

sections.title: Literature search methodology and scope definition
heading_path: Literature search methodology and scope definition

blocks.text: This narrative review searched PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus for literature published from January 2015 to June 2026. Search keywords included: (“diabetes mellitus” OR “hyperglycemia”) AND (“periodontitis” OR “periodontal disease”) AND (“pathogenesis” OR “immune” OR “osteoclast” OR “osteoblast” OR “stem cells” OR “therapy” OR “biomaterials” OR “regeneration”). Additional articles were identified from reference lists of included studies. Inclusion criteria were: (1) clinical studies; (2) animal models of diabetic periodontitis; (3) in vitro studies on periodontal cells under high-glucose conditions; (4) biomaterial and therapeutic strategies. Studies on obesity or metabolic syndrome without confirmed hyperglycemia, and non-periodontal diabetic complications, were excluded. Priority was given to randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and high-impact mechanistic studies; preclinical evidence was included when human data were limited. Unless otherwise specified, “diabetes” refers to type 2 diabetes; evidence from type 1 diabetes or animal models is included when it provides unique mechanistic insights and is clearly annotated.

Unlike previous reviews focused on individual mechanisms, this review offers a distinctive contribution in three aspects. First, we integrate local pathogenic pathways (AGEs-RAGE, oxidative stress, NLRP3 inflammasome) with cross-system mechanisms (gut-periodontium axis, inflamm-aging) within a unified framework. Second, we apply graded evidence assessment to distinguish clinically validated strategies from those at preclinical stages, and compare translational bottlenecks across different therapy types. Third, we identify key contradictions in the literature — for instance, while the AGEs-RAGE pathway is well-validated in animal models, targeted interventions have yielded inconsistent clinical benefits; and although stem cells and exosomes show promise, they lack standardized protocols and long-term safety data. Through this framework, this review provides a clear trajectory from mechanistic understanding to clinical translation, rather than a mere compilation of findings.

sections.title: Epidemiological characteristics of diabetes mellitus, periodontal disease and their bidirectional association
heading_path: Epidemiological characteristics of diabetes mellitus, periodontal disease and their bidirectional association

blocks.text: Latest epidemiological surveys indicate that the global number of people living with diabetes is on a steady rise, with the total number of patients exceeding 537 million currently. It is projected to grow to 783 million by 2045, representing an annual growth rate of approximately 3% to 4%. The International Diabetes Federation's Diabetes Atlas reveals that in 2021, 140.9 million people in China had diabetes, and this figure is expected to increase to 174.4 million by 2045, maintaining China's position as the country with the highest number of people living with diabetes worldwide (1, 10). According to the 2025 data from the World Health Organization (WHO), the number of severe periodontal disease cases exceeds 1 billion, and the prevalence rate among people aged 15 and above is approximately 19%. The prevalence of severe periodontal disease begins in late adolescence, peaks at around the age of 55, and persists into old age. Males and females are affected almost equally. Furthermore, Research has demonstrated that people with type 2 diabetes mellitus have a 2- to 3-fold risk of developing severe periodontal disease compared with non-diabetic individuals (11). Additionally, among people with type 2 diabetes with poorly controlled blood glucose, 68.52% are complicated with severe periodontal disease—a proportion significantly higher than that in people with optimal or well-controlled blood glucose (12). Meanwhile, the implementation of standardized periodontal disease treatment for such people with diabetes can reduce their glycated hemoglobin levels by an average of 0.4% to 0.6% (13). These sets of data fully confirm that there is a significant bidirectional association between diabetes mellitus and periodontal disease.
