sections.title: Trends in Prevalence of Odontogenic Infections
heading_path: Trends in Prevalence of Odontogenic Infections

blocks.text: The prevalence of odontogenic infections (OIs) in the present study has a fluctuating occurrence, indicative of how complex these infections are. Their occurrence and management underpin the intricate relationship between environmental, behavioral and systemic factors. The prevalence of OI rose steadily from 3 OI cases per 1000 patients, averaging 20 cases per 1000 patients, with a peak of 42 cases per 1000 patients recorded. In July 2024, OI cases peaked in the study facility. July falls in the wet season period in Ghana, insinuating the role environmental conditions play in heightening infections. This hypothesis of seasons and infections is well explained in the seasonal analysis section. The average prevalence rates of OIs in this study are in line with studies in this region. A Ghanaian study saw OIs in 40.3% of all dental clinic cases in Korle‐Bu Teaching Hospital [2]. In that same study, the disease burden steadily rose from as little as 8.2 to 27.7 OI cases per 1000 dental infections. The STH study saw a peak of 42 cases per 1000 people. This suggests that perhaps, people in the peri‐urban and rural settings, of which this study had more of the latter, are more vulnerable to OIs than in predominantly urban populations. The vulnerability may stem from access to dental facilities and/or awareness of the importance of early dental health seeking.

Odontogenic infections account for major hospitalization rates secondary to dental infections worldwide. In a Bulgarian study, odontogenic abscesses alone were seen in more than half (59.95%) of patients who presented to their dental unit [6]. A 3‐year retrospective study in São Paulo, Brazil, saw a maxillofacial infection rate of 89% [7]. Over a period of 15 years in Venezuela (2001–2016), an average of 75 cases of OI were recorded yearly [8]. These cases led to a hospitalization rate of just 6.7%, which is less than other global statistic. These studies point to how heavily burdened OIs are in countries. The current study area, Sunyani, has a somewhat elevated peak. This reflects the repercussions of resource constraints and environmental factors of health systems.

The study area, Sunyani, is a tropical region with two clear‐cut seasons: wet (April‐September) and dry (October‐March). In this study, most of the cases (62%) presented in the wet/rainy season (179 out of 286 cases). Only a handful 37.4% (107 cases) presented in the dry season. The mean prevalence in the rainy season (22 ± 9.48 per 1000) as against the dry season (18 ± 9.31 per 1000) had maximum rates of 41.96 and 34.97 per 1000 cases respectively. There is a marked increase in both humidity and rainfall during the rainy season. This change can lead to a substantial growth in bacteria in the oral cavity; OIs already have underlying dental pathologies. The increased proliferations fasten the whole process of exacerbation of diseases [6, 9]. Also, the effect of heavy rains cannot be undermined. For people in rural communities with poor road networks, this occurrence will mean that they will present to the facility only when conditions are suitable. As such, infections progress. This phenomenon is not out of the blue. It has already been associated with socioeconomic barriers to dental care in Ghana [2]. This pattern is notable in this current study, and it is vivid amongst all infection types. Abscess (50 vs. 25 cases), cellulitis (53 vs. 50), Ludwig's angina (46 vs. 18), and necrotizing fasciitis (30 vs. 14) point to an environmental effect and not just the effects of pathogens. This is a novel finding underexplored in many studies on this subject matter. On paper, the noted seasonal patterns are in line with the ecological models of infectious diseases. The model suggests that for a disease to occur, environmental conditions like rainfall and humidity, as seen here, will fraternize with the host factors like oral hygiene and systemic health status. Systemic conditions, particularly poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and malnutrition, are known to impair immune response and accelerate the progression of odontogenic infections into deep neck spaces. In a tropical setting like Sunyani, these host vulnerabilities likely interact with seasonal environmental stressors to increase the frequency of severe cases like Ludwig's angina.

It has been clearly established that odontogenic infections result from untreated dental pathologies [10]. The study recommends the prioritization of preventive therapy. In this society where knee‐jerk dentistry is done, successive community outreach programs should be organized to sensitize people on dental pathologies. People should be made to appreciate that facial swellings are not necessarily “Pɔmpɔ bɔne”, translated as a bad boil/swelling, but they are and can be treated at the incipient stages to reduce morbidity and mortality.

sections.title: Trends in Treatment Patterns of Odontogenic Infections
heading_path: Trends in Treatment Patterns of Odontogenic Infections

blocks.text: The type of treatment administered to patients who present with OIs in STH practically encapsulates the modus operandi of treatment in resource‐constrained settings. Antibiotics and analgesics were administered to all sampled patients in the study. This is the primary treatment regimen for pain and initial infection control. One cornerstone of treating OI is to get rid of the main source of infection, the infected tooth. In this study, 207 (72.4%) patients had their teeth extracted. The reasons why others probably didn't extract their tooth will be secondary to consent reasons, or they were to have their extractions done during reviews after discharge. Even though, the latter reason is not routine. Incision and drainage 183 (64%) were the most commonly performed surgical procedure followed by surgical debridement 44 (15.4%). This approach indicates that STH uses a hard‐nosed approach to tackle OIs and their associated complications

Antibiotics use was a global yardstick for the management of OI. While Silva et al. [7] made use of crystalline Penicillin G and Metronidazole, clindamycin (36.4%) and amoxicillin‐clavulanate (27.3%) were the options for Ekici [9]. The exact antibiotics used in STH for OI patients cannot be pinpointed from this study, but with the practice of broad‐spectrum regimen before culture and sensitivity for a more streamlined approach, the following medications are often used: amoxicillin‐clavulanate, metronidazole, clindamycin, ceftriaxone and gentamycin. In a 2020 study, the number of surgical incisions and drainage was pegged at 89.97% [8]. This approach was like that of STH, where source removal was high on the pecking order. In sharp contrast is Yankov et al. [6] who believes that tooth preservation should be optimum and desired. This advocacy, however, is unreliable in this setting where knee‐jerk dentistry is practiced by patients.

With it established that the wet season presents with increased number of OIs, it can be rightly assumed that the demand for analgesics and antibiotics from the OMFS department will be heightened in this period. Within those periods, too, treatment modalities like surgical incision and drainage, as well as extraction, will skyrocket. Further, as wound dressing and management of these cases are normally seen on the wards, ward materials like sterile gauze and povidone are likely to be more than usually collected. Physician assistants (medical and oral health) in the peripheral facilities, which are mostly first points of contact for people in the rural areas, should be trained via continuous professional development programs to spot the signs of OI as they start sprouting, so proper referrals and treatment can be initiated for patients.

sections.title: Economic Burden of Odontogenic Infections in Sunyani Teaching Hospital
heading_path: Economic Burden of Odontogenic Infections in Sunyani Teaching Hospital

sections.title: Overview of Economic Burden
heading_path: Economic Burden of Odontogenic Infections in Sunyani Teaching Hospital

blocks.text: The clinical implications of odontogenic infections have been documented extensively in this study. In particular, discussions have been extensively through a variety of clinical lens. What most studies have failed to do is to assess the economic burden of these infections from the economic point of view, especially, in low‐ and middle‐income countries (LMICs). It should be noted that in LMICs contexts, there are inherent priorities from folks who are in a competition with healthcare systems. This competition leads to an apparent imbalance between the healthcare systems and the perceived priorities of people. There are direct costs from odontogenic infections. These are mostly costs from hospital length of stay (HLOS), surgical procedures like incision and drainage, antibiotic therapy to complement surgical interventions and finally, diagnostic tests [11].

The indirect costs, on the other hand, include the loss of productivity from missing long hours of work, further financial burden on patients because of out‐of‐pocket payments and long‐term financial burdens even after patients are discharged from the hospitals. This can be attributed to disabilities from the diseases and the overall impact of treating chronic conditions. While studies like [11] illustrate how a substantial portion of these costs are waived by insurance schemes in Australia and the United States of America, patients in Sub‐Saharan Africa lack such robust healthcare systems and insurance schemes. Hence, patients in these settings absorb huge direct costs themselves, further exacerbating the economic instability and poverty in these areas [12].

A good grasp of the economic burden will help policymakers focus more on preventive therapy of odontogenic infections, so resources could be diverted to perhaps more pressing health needs that are not easily preventable per se, like infectious disease control.

The measurable expenses from hospitalization and the medical and surgical interventions meted out to patients are primarily the direct costs. In the Southern Australian study where 462 patients were studied retrospectively for 7 years, each patient paid about AUD 12,228 for treatment [11]. For context's sake, this is about GHS82, 355.56 (June 2025 exchange rate). In this study, the average hospitalization cost for patients was significantly lower when compared to that of the resource‐rich setting like Australia for obvious reasons like better healthcare system and infrastructure. However, in a country with a daily minimum wage of GHS 19.97 (National Tripartite Committee on Minimum Wages, 2025), this is a substantial amount. For a broader context, the daily minimum wage for patients who were sampled in 2021 was GHS 12.53 (National Tripartite Committee on Minimum Wages, 2021 and 2022). The severity of infection influenced the total amount spent in the hospital, with total cost exceeding AUD 5.6 million in the Australian study [11]. This latter finding was not different from this study. High‐risk infections like Ludwig's Angina (LA) and Necrotizing Fasciitis (NF) recorded an average mean cost of GHS 3861.72 ± 1894.58 and GHS 4329.55 ± 1657.24, respectively, as compared to low‐risk infections like cellulitis and abscesses, which recorded GHS 2140.78 ± 1459.95 and GHS 2376.67 ± 1005.03, respectively.

Even though some abscesses are high‐risk, this study grouped all types of dental abscesses under the heading abscess. The secondary data used did not consider airway compromise or the extent of spread to stratify severity. Severity was entirely binary (yes or no). In Han's study, the hospital length of stay (HLOS) directly impacted total hospitalization cost, with patients staying 5.1 days paying 5.49 times higher than those who stayed 1.9 days [11]. While intensive care unit (ICU) admissions of an average of 38.5 skyrocketed the average patient cost by a whopping AUD 7772 [11], such records could not be found in the Sunyani setting.

The entire hospital is a 350‐bed facility with about 5 ICU beds. Most odontogenic patients who need ICU services are seen at the 12‐bed emergency room. Immediately, there is a slight improvement in condition, they are transferred to the allied ward for further management by the maxillofacial team. These findings underscore how it is logistically and financially intensive to treat odontogenic infections, especially in resource‐constrained settings where patients present at a later stage [13]. In some instances, hospitals prefer to refer patients to bigger facilities to make up for their logistical inadequacies. STH, however, is a main referral facility. Therefore, logistics is not a barrier to treating these patients. In the study period, less than 5% of patients were referred to other facilities. It should be noted that those referrals were because the resident's oral and maxillofacial surgeon was on a study leave.

The indirect costs of odontogenic infections (OI) bring into perspective the societal and economic implications of OIs. They are made up of four main elements: loss of productivity, economic hardships on patients, economic hardships on relatives and long‐term repercussions. LMICs have parochial social safety nets and are unstable economically. As such, these indirect costs complementing the direct ones create dire consequences for patients and their families at large.

The global indirect cost of dental diseases is around USD 144 billion annually. When compartmentalized, the loss of productivity from tooth loss, severe periodontitis and untreated dental caries are USD 63.03 billion, USD 53.99 billion and USD 25.14 billion, respectively [12]. To put this in proper context, lower respiratory disease costs are at USD 126 billion [12]. Even though the literature does not mention the exact indirect cost from OIs, periodontitis and untreated dental caries are precursors to it. The HLOS of Fu's study was 4.13 days. About 24% of their total patients were admitted to the ICU at a point in their management. What this implies is that these ICU patients will stay in the hospital longer and will take a longer time to recover when compared to other patients. With this, patients would have to absent themselves from work [14].

Patients with a more severe form of OIs stayed in the hospital for averagely 5.1 days in Han's study. These patients cannot work in these times. With two‐thirds of respondents being employed, they will miss their work during their admission times. Ghana and Sunyani, in particular, are characterized by a sense of communal embodiments. A hospitalized husband implies his wife will come stay in the facility with him. If not, the family delegates members who take turns to come live with the patient in the hospital. In the end, more than one person loses productivity. The seasonal variation showed more patients presenting during the rainy seasons. Who cultivates their crops in the rainy season when they are hospitalized? Sunyani and its environs are agrarian communities. What happens to a breadwinner farmer who fails to till his land in the dry season because he was hospitalized for over 16 days, spent days after recovering after discharge and has his family by his side throughout the hospital and recovery period? Such a person will have not only have nothing to cultivate in the rainy season, but he will spiral his family into food insecurity and a looming abject poverty, if they are not already poor. In Okyere Boadu et al. [13], it was observed that patients refused to seek initial dental care till admission was inevitable. In settings where patients are farmers or day laborers without any paid sick leave, the economic losses transcend to the community at large.

Han et al. [11] notes a wide gap between preventive therapy like tooth extraction (AUD 181) and hospital costs for admitted OI cases (AUD 12,228). Similarly, a patient who opts for tooth extraction for untreated dental caries will pay GHS100 if he has the national health insurance. Same person will on average pay GHS 2140.78–4329.55 for OI management in the hospital, depending on the infection type. There are numerous economic challenges in Ghana currently. Paying as high as GHS10000 for these infections causes a lot of strain for patients and their families. Some go to the extent of borrowing money from friends and extended relatives to foot the hospital bills. As stated many times, there are good insurance schemes to buffer the direct costs from the hospitals in resource‐rich settings. Regardless, their patients still pay for indirect costs like transportation [11]. In this study, 55.9% of respondents live in the rural communities that are far from the urban areas. This adds on to the already financial stressors of patients during admission, for relatives who come to visit. When discharged, distance barriers prevent some patients from attending regular reviews [13]. Some later present with OIs of the other carious lesions, and the vicious cycle continues.

The long‐term economic burden of OIs cannot be understated. Untreated dental caries and periodontal diseases can lead to OIs. In managing these infections, extractions are sometimes done, with this study recoding 77.8% of such instances. Tooth loss results afterward. The productivity loss from tooth loss is outrageous [12]. Tooth loss affects chewing and nutrition. Some people have missed work on countless occasions because of the embarrassment associated with tooth loss. Overall, it drastically reduces the physical capacity for work [12]. To remedy this, patients have to resort to restorative dentistry via tooth replacement options like dentures (GHS 500 for the base), bridges (GHS 2000 for a unit) and implants (GHS 20000 for a unit). These are patients with financial strains already. How then can they opt for these tooth replacement options? For workers who speak for long hours or customer service personnel, this predicament is a challenge to them. Some noted complications of OIs include osteomyelitis and sepsis [14]. These are quite uncommon, but if they do happen, they will increase the treatment and recovery time leading to a further strain on the already inadequate resources. The economic burden is so damning that in some instances; children must drop out of school to do menial jobs or work full‐time in the farms to get extra income to buffer the household expenses.

This study highlights that odontogenic infections (OIs) at Sunyani Teaching Hospital (STH) maintain an average prevalence of 20 cases per 1000 patients, peaking at 40 per 1000 during the wet season (July 2024). This peak reflects the intricacies of environmental factors and barriers to dental care in LMICs. Rural inhabitants are particularly vulnerable, as poor health‐seeking behavior during the rainy season creates a “dynamo effect” on infection severity in resource‐constrained settings like Sunyani, Ghana.

Cellulitis was the most common OI, followed by abscess and Ludwig's angina (LA), while necrotizing fasciitis (NF) was the least common. The influence of weather was evident, with LA showing a significant wet‐season surge. Treatment patterns underscored pragmatism; extraction was the go‐to therapy for 72.4% of cases, highlighting systemic gaps in restorative dentistry. While surgical protocols like incision, drainage, and debridement align with international standards, the initiation of broad‐spectrum antibiotics before culture and sensitivity remains a troubling factor amid the rise of antimicrobial resistance.

The economic burden of OIs is catastrophic. Direct costs are substantial, with Necrotizing Fasciitis being the most expensive to manage (GHS 4329.55 ± 1657.24), followed by LA, abscesses, and cellulitis. For an NF patient, management costs can consume approximately one‐third of their annual income based on Ghana's GDP per capita. These financial strains are exacerbated by indirect costs, such as lost productivity for both patients and relatives who provide bedside care. Ultimately, the type of infection is the main driver of cost. These findings reaffirm the significant weight of OIs on health systems and suggest that region‐specific solutions are necessary to address these socioeconomic and seasonal burdens.

title: Dental Abscess on POCUS: A Retrospective Case Series Analysis

blocks.text: Point of care ultrasound (POCUS) has proven utility in confirming the diagnosis of skin and soft tissue abscesses. We studied the characteristics of 50 dental abscesses on pediatric POCUS examinations and their outcomes.

This was a convenience sample of cases collected in the pediatric emergency department from December 2020 to December 2024. All included patients were examined by an oromaxillofacial specialist and hospitalized. All cases had POCUS imaging performed at initial assessment by the first author.

The median age of the patients was 7 years (IQR = 5 years), and 31 (62%) were male. Forty (80%) received antibiotic prior to arrival. Thirty-five (70%) presented within 3 days from onset of pain, and 36 (72%) were referred to the pediatric emergency department by a dentist for oromaxillofacial evaluation. Four children (8%) experienced spontaneous drainage while inpatient, and eleven children underwent surgical drainage (22%). There was a significant correlation between maximal abscess height from bone and the need for surgical drainage (p = 0.011). A cutoff of 4.5 mm yielded a sensitivity of 72.7% and specificity of 69%, indicating that abscesses measuring greater than 4.5 mm are more likely to need surgical drainage.

This was the first known study to describe POCUS findings in children determined to have dental abscess by an oromaxillofacial specialist and hospitalized for treatment. POCUS may have utility in identifying dental abscess, and may be useful in following the progress of abscesses under treatment. The majority of dental abscesses will resolve with antibiotic therapy, but abscesses above 4.5 mm may require drainage early in the course of treatment.

Point of care ultrasound (POCUS) has proven utility in confirming the diagnosis of skin and soft tissue abscess. Limited evidence suggests that skin and soft tissue abscesses with a diameter greater than 1.3 cm are likely to fail medical management [1]. Further, POCUS can differentiate between odontogenic fascial space cellulitis and abscess [2]. The utility of POCUS in guiding therapy of pediatric dental (periapical and periodontal) abscesses is unclear. Here, we describe our experience using POCUS in the pediatric emergency department. We evaluated children with dental abscess in order to determine whether there were characteristics of these POCUS examinations that are associated with subsequent drainage.

This study was a retrospective review of POCUS examinations acquired at a tertiary care pediatric emergency department with 27,000 visits annually. Our pediatric emergency department receives children from birth to 18 years of age.

Children with odontogenic facial swelling are referred to the pediatric emergency department by their pediatrician or dentist to confirm a diagnosis of abscess and, if confirmed, inpatient treatment. In our facility, children with odontogenic facial swelling are examined in the pediatric emergency department and followed inpatient by an oromaxillofacial specialist. If the specialist believes the child has failed intravenous antibiotic, drainage is performed under deep sedation. The first author performed all inpatient sedations for these children, as sedation for an oral procedure presents an airway risk that may not be suitable for junior physicians to manage.

Children with odontogenic facial swelling are routinely examined in the pediatric emergency department by the first author with POCUS. We included children of all ages who had an abscess confirmed on POCUS and were then hospitalized. Children who received POCUS but were discharged from the pediatric emergency department were excluded as we had no way to examine outpatient dental records. POCUS was performed by the first author—a pediatric emergency physician with seven years of experience with POCUS—from December 2020 to December of 2024. Measurements were made during review of the images for the study. Hospital charts were reviewed to extract details of emergency department and hospital course. Children who were not seen by an oromaxillofacial specialist and discharged from the pediatric emergency department were excluded. The country-wide Ofek electronic medical record database, which includes all outpatient visits as well as all hospitalizations, was reviewed to verify that the children in our series were not seen in another emergency department for dental abscess.

Descriptive statistics were utilized to summarize the data. Categorical variables are presented as frequencies and percentages, whereas continuous variables are expressed as medians with interquartile range (IQR). Comparisons of categorical variables were performed using the Chi-square test. The normality of continuous variables was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test; if the data followed a normal distribution, an independent t-test was used, and if not, the Mann-Whitney U test was employed. Additionally, a receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was conducted. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 29.0, and a p-value below 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

All images were acquired with a high frequency linear probe on a Zonare z.1 ultrasound (Mindray, Mahwah, NJ). We started by examining the contralateral side to adjust gain and depth, and to demonstrate to the child that the examination should not be painful. Images were collected in the sagittal plane over the area of swelling (Figure 1). Copious gel was applied and a video sweep in the coronal axis over the area of interest was recorded. Anechoic fluid collections were defined as abscess. After fanning through the abscess, the maximum height of the anechoic fluid pocket from lateral cortex of maxilla or mandible to facial soft tissue was recorded (Figure 2). In contrast with a subcutaneous abscess, which is generally round or ovoid, a periodontal abscess is elliptical within a well-defined anatomic space. In our experience, severity is associated with the height of abscess from bone, which should be identical in coronal and in transverse views. This method of measuring effusion by height rather than volume is commonly used to measure hip effusion on pediatric ultrasound [3]. We therefore recorded abscess height from maxilla or mandible, rather than volume.
Figure 1. A representation of the sagittal probe placement to identify dental abscess in the maxillary area. The probe should fan through the area of swelling.

Figure 2. Point of care ultrasound (POCUS) image of dental abscess. Star indicates buccal soft tissue. Single arrow indicates maxillary cortex. Double-headed arrow demarcates the maximum height of an anechoic dental abscess.

Sixty-one children underwent POCUS examination, of whom eleven were not seen by an oromaxillofacial specialist and were discharged from the pediatric emergency department. None presented after pediatric emergency department discharge to an outside hospital pediatric emergency department. Thus, 50 children with dental abscess treated by an oromaxillofacial specialist were studied. The mean age of this group was 7 years (IQR = 5 years), and 31 (62%) were male. The average duration of pain prior to presentation was just under 4 days, and 40 cases (80%) received antibiotics prior to arrival (Table 1). Seven children had panoramic dental radiography while hospitalized. Four children experienced spontaneous drainage while inpatient and eleven children underwent surgical drainage (22%).

No child re-presented to the pediatric emergency department with recurrent dental abscess. There was no significant association between antibiotic administration prior to pediatric emergency department presentation and either abscess drainage or duration of hospitalization.

blocks.text: There was no statistically significant correlation between duration of symptoms prior to POCUS or between any laboratory parameter and the need for surgical drainage. There was a significant correlation between mean maximal abscess height from bone and the need for surgical drainage (not drained, 0.39 cm; drained, 0.57 cm; p = 0.011). Based on the ROC analysis, the area under the curve (AUC) was 0.749, which suggested moderate accuracy in predicting which abscesses might require drainage.

A cutoff of 4.5 mm yielded a sensitivity of 72.7% and specificity of 69%, indicating that there may be an association between abscesses measuring above 4.5 mm and the need for surgical drainage. Including the 11 children who were discharged from the pediatric emergency department and therefore excluded from the initial analysis slightly reduced the model's discriminatory power (AUC decreased from 0.749 to 0.727) and increased the significance level from p = 0.012 to p = 0.019. Importantly, the optimal cutoff of 0.45 cm remained unchanged, with stable sensitivity and specificity. These findings suggested that the inclusion of milder, non-hospitalized cases did not enhance prediction performance, though it slightly improved generalizability.

Maximal abscess diameters below 0.25 cm had 100% sensitivity for predicting that no surgical intervention was necessary, at the cost of a sharp decline in specificity to 25.6%. While a definitively safe prognostic threshold cannot be established from our data, values below 0.25 cm may support a decision to discharge without intervention if clinical judgment supports that disposition.

Prior small case series in the dental literature have shown that ultrasound can detect odontogenic abscesses [4]. However, this is the first study to describe POCUS findings in children with dental abscess, determined by a pediatric emergency physician. Moreover, all children in our study had a POCUS diagnosis confirmed by an oromaxillofacial specialist, and all were followed through hospitalization. Our study demonstrated that a cutoff of approximately 0.45 cm yields a sensitivity of 72.7% and specificity of 69%, indicating that abscesses measuring 0.45 cm or greater may be associated with need for surgical drainage.

Prior research suggests that a skin abscess diameter above 1.3 cm or depth greater than 0.4 cm is likely to fail antibiotic therapy [1]. While odontogenic periapical abscesses are usually apparent on physical examination, clinical signs alone may not reliably distinguish between cellulitis and true abscess formation in odontogenic infections [2,5]. There is no guidance in the literature regarding the need for drainage of odontogenic abscesses.

Several of our patients underwent panoramic dental radiography. Panoramic radiography can evaluate the dental root and surrounding bone and can demonstrate focal apical lucencies associated with infections originating from the root apices [6,7]. Ultrasound, in contrast with conventional radiographic imaging, has no radiation. Several studies of adult patients with facial pain and swelling have found ultrasound to be more sensitive for abscess than panoramic radiography [8,9]. Barton et al. described two techniques to improve clarity of the image: the first was to have the patient fill their mouth with water and perform a “cheek puff” to push the water between gingiva and buccal mucosa, simulating a water bath. The second was to have the patient use their tongue to point to the area of tenderness [10].

Previous studies have shown that inflammatory markers, such as WBC count and CRP, are frequently elevated in odontogenic abscesses, with elevations less marked in pediatric patients compared to adults [11]. Our study did not find a significant difference in inflammatory markers between children treated surgically (i.e., with drainage) or medically. POCUS allows for early identification of abscess without bloodwork, enabling early treatment. There is a lack of evidence regarding the use of systemic antibiotics in the pediatric population [12,13]. However, early treatment in the outpatient setting may reduce hospitalization [14]. Early treatment is important to prevent dehydration that may result from dental pain and more serious sequelae such as sepsis that has been reported in pediatric dental abscess [15,16]. Thus, early POCUS may obviate the need for laboratory evaluation and systemic antibiotics, and may inform the need for early drainage.

This was a single-center retrospective convenience sample collected by a single physician. While POCUS of a periodontal abscess is a straight-forward examination, we cannot exclude inter-operator variability. POCUS was performed at point of contact and not when the abscess was opened, which in most cases was during hospitalization. The abscess was fanned through in only the sagittal orientation rather than in two orthogonal planes, and height of abscess from cortex rather than abscess volume was measured. The potential space that might contain a dental abscess is limited by the smaller potential space than exists for other subcutaneous abscesses. Because of this, we saw little utility in a second view. While our data can help guide clinical judgment alongside other clinical and laboratory findings, the results are limited by the small sample size, the single-center, retrospective design, and operator-dependent ultrasound measurements. Additional prospective, multicenter studies are needed to validate and refine these recommendations.

POCUS can be useful for identifying dental abscess and may be useful in following the progress of abscesses under treatment. A POCUS-determined abscess diameter of 4.5 mm is associated with the need for surgical drainage. Larger, prospective studies are required to determine which dental abscesses will require surgical drainage as opposed to medical management, either inpatient or outpatient.

blocks.text: Doxorubicin-cyclophosphamide (AC) and docetaxel-cyclophosphamide (TC) are standard perioperative chemotherapy regimens for breast cancer. Febrile neutropenia (FN) is a common adverse event, and odontogenic infections may contribute to febrile episodes. This study was performed to investigate the incidence and impact of febrile episodes clinically associated with odontogenic infections during AC and TC chemotherapy.

A total of 408 patients with breast cancer receiving 4 cycles of AC (n = 285) or TC (n = 123) between 2015 and 2020 were included in this single-center retrospective study. Patients recorded daily axillary temperatures and oral symptoms. Dental evaluations were performed when oral infection was suspected. Febrile episodes (≥ 37.5 °C) were assessed, and their clinical association with odontogenic infections was determined based on dental records and the documented clinical course. Relative dose intensity (RDI) was calculated to assess chemotherapy delivery.

Overall, 40.2% of patients experienced febrile episodes, and the frequency was higher in the TC group (48.8%) than the AC group (36.5%, P = 0.02). Febrile episodes associated with oral infections occurred in 9.1% of patients, of which 78.4% were clinically associated with odontogenic infections (7.1% of all patients). Most such episodes occurred during the first chemotherapy cycle (79.3%, P < 0.01). Chemotherapy RDI was reduced in three patients with febrile episodes clinically associated with odontogenic infection, but remained ≥ 85%.

Febrile episodes clinically associated with odontogenic infections occurred in approximately 7%–8% of patients with breast cancer receiving perioperative AC or TC chemotherapy, predominantly during the first cycle. Odontogenic infections should be considered one possible source of febrile episodes during treatment.

Doxorubicin-cyclophosphamide (AC) and docetaxel-cyclophosphamide (TC) are major perioperative chemotherapy regimens for breast cancer. Before the introduction of taxanes in the 1990 s, no 4-cycle chemotherapy regimen had proven superior to AC. AC delivered in 4 cycles remains a standard form of adjuvant therapy, often followed by taxanes. A comparative trial of preoperative versus postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy with AC found no differences in disease-free survival (DFS) or overall survival (OS), and both regimens showed equivalent efficacy in improving prognosis [1]. Therefore, AC is used in both pre- and postoperative chemotherapy. TC delivered in 4 cycles is also considered standard adjuvant therapy, with efficacy demonstrated by a randomized controlled trial [2, 3]. A comparison of AC and TC as postoperative adjuvant chemotherapies for Stage I, II, and III resectable invasive breast cancer, showed significantly superior DFS and OS for TC therapy [2, 3].

Febrile neutropenia (FN) is a common adverse event associated with both AC and TC chemotherapy. The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) clinical guidelines classify AC regimens (60/600 mg/m2, 4 cycles at 3-week intervals) as intermediate risk for FN (10%−20%), while classifying TC regimens (75/600 mg/m2, 4 cycles at 3-week intervals) as high risk for FN (> 20%) [4]. Most chemotherapy regimens, including AC, cause neutropenic nadirs between days 10 and 14, whereas the TC regimen is characterized by an early neutrophil nadir, typically around day 8, with a substantial decrease in neutrophil count and elevated risk of FN [5]. Appropriate use of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) support and antibiotics is important [4, 6, 7].

In daily clinical practice, FN has been suggested to be associated with odontogenic infections. The impact of odontogenic infection on FN is recognized in theory. However, most studies have focused on FN in the setting of ultimate bone marrow suppression, such as hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. A recent review concluded that there is limited information on patients treated with myelosuppressive chemotherapy for solid tumors [8].

At our institute, both AC and TC regimens are typically administered on an outpatient basis following initial inpatient administration. At each outpatient chemotherapy visit, physicians, nurses, or pharmacists inquire about adverse events, including fever and oral symptoms, and these findings are documented in the medical records. When symptoms suggestive of oral infection occur, dentists provide dental examination and management during the phase of neutrophil recovery. As patients are usually at home, it is not possible to determine precisely whether the neutrophil count at the time of fever met the criteria for FN. However, patients record their body temperature daily, allowing confirmation of whether febrile episodes have occurred.
This study was performed to clarify the incidence and impact of odontogenic infections on febrile episodes during AC and TC perioperative chemotherapy for breast cancer.

This single-center retrospective study was conducted at the Division of Hospital Dentistry, the Department of Breast and Endocrine Surgery, and the Department of Pharmacy at Okayama University Hospital.

A total of 408 consecutive patients who completed either 4 cycles of AC or TC therapy described below as perioperative chemotherapy for breast cancer at our institution between April 1, 2015, and March 31, 2020, were enrolled in the study.

The chemotherapy regimens administered to patients in this study were as follows: AC (doxorubicin 60 mg/m2 IV on day 1; cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m2 IV on day 1; every 21 days for 4 cycles) and TC (docetaxel 75 mg/m2 IV on day 1; cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m2 IV on day 1; every 21 days for 4 cycles). AC was generally administered as part of the AC followed by paclitaxel regimen (AC-T). Patients with a low risk of recurrence or with estrogen receptor (ER)-positive tumors expected to respond to endocrine therapy, who do not require full AC-T regimens but for whom adjuvant chemotherapy is still indicated, were treated with TC regimens [9].

The initial treatment was given during hospitalization. After confirming the lack of adverse events, especially allergic reactions, the patient was discharged the next day. The second through fourth treatments were administered as outpatient chemotherapy.

Oral antibiotic (ciprofloxacin) was prescribed at the start of chemotherapy as a countermeasure against FN. Patients were instructed to take the oral antibiotic for 5 days if they recorded an axillary temperature of 37.5 °C or higher after beginning chemotherapy.
Preventive G-CSF was generally not administered. Its use was determined by the attending physician according to the following criteria:

i. Development of fever (≥ 38.0 °C) with absolute neutrophil count (ANC) < 1000/mm3 or 500/mm3 after completion of chemotherapy, and.
ii. For subsequent cycles of the same chemotherapy after meeting condition (i), G-CSF administration was initiated when ANC reached 1000/mm3.

blocks.text: At the initiation of chemotherapy, patients receive education on the importance of oral hygiene from physicians, nurses, and pharmacists. However, due to limited manpower, routine dental examinations were not performed for all patients before chemotherapy. At each outpatient chemotherapy visit, physicians, nurses, or pharmacists inquired about adverse events, including fever and oral symptoms, and these findings were documented in the medical records. When symptoms suggestive of an oral infection occurred, almost all patients were referred to the Division of Hospital Dentistry at the same institute or to their regular dentist for dental examination and management.

Patients recorded daily axillary temperature and other adverse events in a notebook. Medical staff documented the patient’s fever status during the period of chemotherapy in the medical records based on these records and interviews with the patient. Febrile episodes were defined as axillary temperature ≥ 37.5 °C according to the FN guidelines of Japan [10].

sections.title: Association between febrile episodes and oral infection
heading_path: Association between febrile episodes and oral infection

blocks.text: The clinical association between febrile episodes and oral infection was assessed from dental records and the documented clinical course. For patients managed at external dental clinics or who did not attend a dentist, study dentists reviewed the available medical records to assess the likelihood of oral infection at the time of a febrile episode. Microbiological confirmation was not systematically available.

Relative dose intensity (RDI) was calculated as the ratio of delivered dose intensity to planned dose intensity, expressed as a percentage. Dose intensity was defined as the cumulative dose per unit time divided by the planned cumulative dose per unit time for each regimen.
Statistical analyses were performed using Stata 19 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). In all analyses, P < 0.05 was taken to indicate statistical significance.

All patients (n = 408) were female with a median age of 51 years. Of these, 285 patients received AC, with a median age of 51 years (range 23–78 years) and 123 received TC, with a median age of 50 years (range 31–74 year). There was no significant difference in age between the AC and TC groups (P = 0.68, Wilcoxon’s rank-sum test).

Three patients underwent low-invasive tooth extraction after a febrile episode clinically associated with odontogenic infection, and no further febrile episodes were documented thereafter during chemotherapy. Similarly, in four other patients with febrile episodes clinically judged to be associated with pericoronitis (n = 1) or periodontitis (n = 3), local minocycline ointment administration together with oral hygiene instruction and management was followed by no further febrile episodes during the subsequent chemotherapy cycles.

sections.title: RDI in patients with febrile episodes clinically associated with chronic odontogenic infection
heading_path: RDI in patients with febrile episodes clinically associated with chronic odontogenic infection

blocks.text: RDI was reduced in 3 patients with febrile episodes clinically associated with chronic odontogenic infection, representing 0.7% of the total cohort (3/408) and 10.3% of patients with febrile episodes clinically associated with chronic odontogenic infection (3/29). RDIs of chemotherapy in the 3 patients were 85%, 90%, and 92.5%, respectively. All reductions in RDI were due to dose reductions and not to treatment delays.

Febrile episodes clinically associated with odontogenic infection occurred in 7.1% of patients receiving AC or TC perioperative chemotherapy for breast cancer. These episodes were significantly more frequent during the first cycle, occasionally resulting in a 7.5%–15% reduction in RDI.

In this study, fever generally developed during the expected neutropenic phase of chemotherapy. In routine clinical practice, FN is often diagnosed clinically even when microbiological confirmation is unavailable. However, in the present retrospective study, FN could not be definitively confirmed in all cases, and attribution of fever to an odontogenic source was based primarily on dental findings and the documented clinical course. Guidelines from the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) [6], the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) [7], and the NCCN [4] recommend that prophylactic G-CSFs be used when risk of FN associated with the chemotherapy regimen is ≥ 20% and may be considered when the risk is 10%–20%, particularly when additional patient risk factors are present. The observed frequency of febrile episodes clinically associated with odontogenic infections suggests that such infections may represent a clinically relevant contributor to febrile events during AC or TC chemotherapy.

The overall frequency of febrile episodes was 36.5% in the AC group and 48.8% in the TC group. NCCN classifies AC as intermediate risk for FN (10%–20%) and TC as high risk for FN (> 20%) [4]. A previous study at our institute indicated an FN frequency of 28.3% among patients undergoing TC therapy [11]. As many patients experienced febrile episodes at home, precise neutrophil counts at the time of the fever were often unavailable. It is therefore unclear whether their neutrophil counts at the time of fever met the criteria for FN, which likely contributed to the higher observed incidence compared with previous reports on FN. In the US Oncology Research Trial 9735 (USON9735), a large-scale randomized clinical trial, the incidence of FN in patients less than 65 years old was 2% with AC and 4% with TC [2], reflecting the wide use of prophylactic antibiotics, whereas prophylactic antibiotics and G-CSF were not routinely administered in the present study. Differences in definitions of fever (≥ 38.5 °C oral in USON9735 vs. ≥ 37.5 °C axillary in this study) may also account for the observed discrepancy.

It was notable that the frequency of febrile episodes clinically associated with odontogenic infections did not differ between AC and TC groups, despite higher overall FN risk with TC. The first febrile episode clinically associated with chronic odontogenic infection occurred predominantly during the first cycle, suggesting that even regimens with differing myelosuppressive profiles may trigger fever once a threshold of bone marrow suppression is exceeded.

Maintaining adequate RDI during perioperative chemotherapy is associated with improved DFS and OS, while reductions below 85% are linked to poorer outcomes [12]. In this study, some patients showed a 7.5%–15% reduction in RDI after febrile episodes clinically associated with odontogenic infection. Although final RDIs remained ≥ 85%, early dental intervention and oral management may help minimize treatment compromise.

This study had several limitations. Detailed dental examinations were not performed for all patients prior to chemotherapy, which restricted the precise assessment of preexisting odontogenic infections. In some cases, oral infection was assessed based on referral records and chart review rather than direct examination by the study dentists. Moreover, microbiological confirmation was not systematically available; blood culture data were not consistently obtained at the time of fever, and oral pathogens were not identified in a standardized manner. Therefore, attribution of fever to an odontogenic source was based primarily on dental findings and the documented clinical course rather than definitive microbiological evidence. To provide context, data from the Survey of Dental Diseases conducted by the Japanese Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare [13] can be used to infer the dental status of a population similar to that included in this study. Among individuals aged 50–54 years, corresponding to the median age of our cohort, the average number of present teeth was 26.9 (out of 28 teeth, excluding third molars). Periodontal assessment revealed that 37.4% had pockets ≥ 4 mm, generally indicative of mild to moderate periodontitis, whereas 3.3% had pockets ≥ 6 mm, suggesting severe periodontitis. Only 2.5% of subjects had decayed teeth, defined as permanent teeth with untreated carious lesions, with an average of 0.7 decayed teeth per individual. These findings suggest a relatively low prevalence of active dental caries in this age group. Data on third molars and apical periodontitis were not available in this national survey. In addition, because patient management was not standardized, the specific effects of dental interventions could not be clearly distinguished from those of other concomitant interventions. Prospective studies are warranted to clarify the causal relationships between odontogenic infections and febrile episodes during chemotherapy.

Preoperative dental treatment is often challenging due to the urgent need to initiate chemotherapy. However, intervention may be feasible during the interval between surgery and postoperative chemotherapy. In this study, the first febrile episode clinically associated with chronic odontogenic infection occurred predominantly during the first chemotherapy cycle. In several patients, no further febrile episodes were documented after dental management, including low-invasive tooth extraction or local periodontal treatment. However, these observations should be interpreted cautiously because of the small number of cases and the retrospective, non-standardized nature of patient management. When patients are suspected to have chronic odontogenic infections, this information should be shared among physicians, nurses, dentists, dental hygienists, pharmacists, and other members of the multidisciplinary healthcare team. Patients should be educated about the importance of oral hygiene during chemotherapy. Although direct evidence linking dental management and patient self-care to a reduction in febrile episodes remains limited, these findings support the potential value of integrating dental assessment and oral care into perioperative management. Prospective studies are warranted to confirm these benefits and establish standardized protocols for timing, scope, and patient guidance.
In conclusion, odontogenic infections should be considered one possible source of febrile episodes during perioperative AC or TC chemotherapy for breast cancer, particularly during the first cycle.

blocks.text: Ludwig’s angina is a rapidly progressive cellulitis involving the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces bilaterally that can swiftly compromise the airway. Data on deep neck space infections in Somalia remain scarce. This study aimed to describe the demographic profile, etiology, clinical presentation, management, complications, length of hospital stay (LOS), and outcomes of patients with Ludwig’s angina treated at Mogadishu Somali–Türkiye Recep Tayyip Erdoğan Training and Research Hospital over a one-year period.

We conducted a retrospective review of 90 patients with clinically confirmed Ludwig’s angina presenting between January 1, 2024, and December 31, 2024. Demographic variables, etiology, pre-admission symptom duration, referral source, treatment modality, hospital-acquired complications, LOS, and discharge outcomes were extracted from medical records and analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics.

The cohort was predominantly male (77.8%, n = 70), with a mean age of 39.1 \pm 21.4 years. Odontogenic infection was the primary etiology, accounting for 82.2% (n = 74) of cases, led by localized periodontal and periapical abscesses (65.5%, n = 59). Overall surgical intervention was required in 53.3% (n = 48) of patients—comprising deep operative decompression (38.9%, n = 35) and superficial drainage (14.4%, n = 13)—while 46.7% (n = 42) were successfully managed with conservative intravenous antibiotics and close airway observation. Inpatient complications occurred in 48.9% (n = 44) of cases, dominated by septicemia (36.7%, n = 33). Linear regression demonstrated that longer symptom duration prior to admission significantly predicted longer hospitalization (B = 0.500, p < 0.001). Institutional mortality was 0.0%.

Ludwig’s angina in this Somali cohort was characterized by delayed presentation, a high complication burden, and predominantly odontogenic origin, but low overall mortality when managed with prompt airway surveillance, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and selective surgical drainage. These findings underscore the critical need to enhance primary dental care access and early referral pathways in resource-limited settings.
Not applicable.

Ludwig’s angina, historically designated as Angina Ludovici, is a rapidly spreading, potentially fatal cellulitis involving the bilateral submandibular, sublingual, and submental fascial spaces [1]. The anatomical hallmark of Ludwig’s angina is its progressive extension through fascial planes without primary lymph node involvement, leading to severe soft-tissue induration, elevation and backward displacement of the tongue, and rapid compromise of the upper airway [2]. Although non-odontogenic factors—such as sialadenitis, upper aerodigestive tract trauma, tonsillar infections, and mandibular fractures—can precipitate the condition, odontogenic pathology remains the predominant cause, accounting for 70% to 90% of documented cases globally [3]. Infection typically originates from lower second and third molar roots, which extend below the insertion of the mylohyoid muscle, allowing direct spread into the submandibular space [4].

Over the past half-century, the widespread availability of modern broad-spectrum antimicrobial agents, advanced airway management techniques (including flexible fiberoptic intubation), and early surgical decompression protocols have dramatically reduced mortality from over 50% in the pre-antibiotic era to less than 5% in high-resource settings [5, 6]. However, Ludwig’s angina remains a major cause of morbidity and life-threatening deep neck space infection in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) [7]. In resource-constrained regions, delays in presentation, restricted access to primary oral healthcare, financial barriers, and shortages of specialized maxillofacial and intensive care infrastructure frequently result in advanced disease at hospital admission [8, 9].

In sub-Saharan Africa, where preventive dental care is largely inaccessible to significant portions of the population, acute dental infections often remain untreated until severe facial space involvement ensues [10]. Despite the recognized burden of dental pathology and deep neck infections in Somalia, there is a complete absence of published clinical data evaluating Ludwig’s angina within the country. This lack of evidence creates a critical gap in understanding regional epidemiological trends, etiology, management challenges, and clinical outcomes.

To address this evidence gap, the present study aimed to evaluate the demographic features, underlying etiology, clinical presentation, emergency management strategies, inpatient complications, length of hospital stay (LOS), and discharge outcomes among patients diagnosed with Ludwig’s angina at a major tertiary referral hospital in Mogadishu, Somalia.

This single-center retrospective descriptive study was conducted at the Mogadishu Somali–Türkiye Recep Tayyip Erdoğan Training and Research Hospital (MSTH), Mogadishu, Somalia. Established in 2015, MSTH is a 200-bed tertiary referral and academic teaching hospital and serves as one of the main emergency and trauma referral centers in the region.

Electronic medical records of patients presenting to the Emergency Department between January 1, 2024, and December 31, 2024, were screened. A total of 120 records with a primary diagnostic code or clinical description suggestive of deep neck space infection were initially identified.

Patients were included if they had a clinically confirmed diagnosis of Ludwig’s angina during the study period, regardless of age or sex. Clinical confirmation was based on the presence of rapidly progressive, firm, bilateral, non-fluctuant swelling of the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, with associated floor-of-mouth induration and tongue elevation. Patients were excluded if the diagnosis was uncertain or poorly documented, if the infection was restricted to other deep neck spaces without classic bilateral submandibular involvement, or if the medical record was critically incomplete and clinical outcomes could not be reliably determined.
After applying these criteria, 90 patients were included in the final analytic cohort.

Data were extracted from the institutional electronic medical record system using a standardized data collection form. Variables included demographic characteristics, suspected etiologic factors, presenting signs and symptoms, imaging findings, treatment modality, complications, length of hospital stay, and outcome at discharge.
To improve clinical clarity, the following operational definitions were used:

Baseline comorbidities were defined as pre-existing systemic conditions or clinically documented conditions present at admission.
Hospital-acquired complications were defined as adverse clinical events that developed after admission during the inpatient stay.
Odontogenic infection included infections arising from dental caries, periodontal disease, post-extraction infection, or other dental-source deep space infections. The term “orthopedic abscess” was not used in the final classification and was replaced by standard maxillofacial terminology.

blocks.text: Diagnosis was established primarily on clinical grounds and supported by imaging when available. Imaging modalities used in the emergency department included soft-tissue neck radiography and bedside ultrasonography to assess the presence of deep space infection and airway-related soft tissue swelling. Imaging findings were interpreted in conjunction with clinical examination and surgical assessment.

All patients were managed according to the hospital’s emergency care protocol. Initial treatment included immediate airway assessment, close hemodynamic monitoring, and empiric intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics. The most commonly used regimen consisted of ceftriaxone 1–2 g intravenously every 12 h combined with metronidazole 500 mg intravenously every 8 h, with subsequent adjustment when culture or sensitivity data were available.

Source control was provided according to disease severity. Patients with fluctuant abscess formation or progressive deep space infection underwent surgical incision, decompression, and drainage under local or general anesthesia, with extraction of the offending tooth when indicated. Patients who presented in the early cellulitic phase without evidence of drainable pus were managed conservatively with intravenous antibiotics, supportive care, and close airway observation.

Patients who developed systemic illness or complications received supportive treatment including intravenous fluid resuscitation, supplemental oxygen, nutritional support, and multidisciplinary review by surgery, otolaryngology, and intensive care teams when necessary.

Data were cleaned, coded, and analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Categorical variables were summarized as frequencies and percentages, while continuous variables were presented as means and standard deviations or medians and interquartile ranges, depending on distribution.

Associations between categorical variables were assessed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Linear regression analysis was performed to evaluate whether duration of symptoms before admission predicted length of hospital stay. All statistical tests were two-tailed, and a p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Institutional ethical approval for this retrospective study was granted by the Mogadishu Somali–Türkiye Training and Research Hospital Ethics Committee (Approval No.: 13.05.2024-MSTH/20230). In accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the requirement for written informed consent was formally waived by the ethics committee due to the retrospective design of the study and the complete anonymization of all patient datasets prior to analysis.

During the one-year study period, 120 patients presented with suspected deep neck space infections. Following application of the eligibility criteria, 30 cases were excluded because of incomplete clinical records or uncertain diagnostic documentation, leaving 90 confirmed cases of Ludwig’s angina for analysis.

The cohort consisted predominantly of males (70/90, 77.8%), with females accounting for 22.2% (20/90). The mean age was 39.1 ± 21.4 years (range 11–104 years). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics are summarized in Table 1.

blocks.text: Odontogenic infection was the leading cause, accounting for 74 patients (82.2%). Of these, 15 patients had untreated dental caries, while 59 presented with localized odontogenic infections, including periodontal abscesses (52.5%), post-extraction abscesses (32.2%), deep post-extraction infections (8.5%), and chronic periodontitis (6.8%).
Idiopathic disease accounted for 15 patients (16.7%), whereas maxillofacial trauma was identified in one patient (1.1%).
The mean symptom duration before presentation was 5.4 ± 1.8 days (range 2–14 days), with most patients presenting between days 5 and 7.

Forty-eight patients (53.3%) underwent surgical management. Immediate decompression with bilateral submandibular and submental incisions, blunt fascial-space dissection, and placement of povidone-iodine–soaked gauze drains was performed in 35 patients (72.9% of surgical cases). Thirteen patients underwent localized incision and drainage.
Definitive source control by dental extraction or deep abscess evacuation was achieved in 27 surgically managed patients (56.3%).

Forty-two patients (46.7%) were successfully managed conservatively with intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and close clinical observation because they presented during the cellulitic stage without drainable collections.
Airway support consisted of supplemental oxygen and oropharyngeal airway maintenance when necessary. No emergency tracheostomy or cricothyrotomy was required.
Forty-four patients (48.9%) developed inpatient complications.
Septicemia was the most frequent complication (36.7%), followed by localized necrotizing fasciitis (6.7%), laryngeal spasm (4.4%), and disseminated intravascular coagulation (1.1%).
No in-hospital deaths occurred (Table 1).

Simple linear regression demonstrated that symptom duration before admission was significantly associated with hospital length of stay (B = 0.500, standardized β = 0.484, t(86) = 5.131, p < 0.001). Each additional day of symptoms before presentation corresponded to an estimated increase of approximately 0.5 hospital days (Table 2).

blocks.text: This study provides the first systematic clinical evaluation of Ludwig’s angina in Somalia. The findings demonstrate that Ludwig’s angina in this setting is predominantly driven by untreated odontogenic infections, characterized by marked presentation delays, accompanied by a high rate of inpatient secondary complications, but associated with excellent survival when managed with structured antimicrobial therapy and selective surgical decompression.

The marked male predominance (77.8%) and concentration of cases among young to middle-aged adults (mean age: 39.1 years) in our cohort align closely with findings from other LMICs across sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East [7, 11, 12]. Studies from Nigeria, India, and Iraq have similarly observed a higher prevalence among young working-age males, a demographic pattern frequently linked to lower rates of routine dental care utilization, delayed health-seeking behavior, and higher exposure to environmental and behavioral risk factors [10, 12, 13]. In contrast, studies from high-income countries often report a more balanced sex distribution and an older patient population, among whom systemic comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus play a primary predisposing role [1, 6].

Odontogenic pathology constituted the primary etiology in 82.2% of cases, reinforcing the pivotal role of untreated dental caries, periodontal abscesses, and post-extraction complications in the pathogenesis of deep neck infections. The anatomical relationship between lower molar root apices and the mylohyoid ridge explains this direct progression into the submandibular and sublingual spaces [2, 4]. Non-odontogenic origins accounted for a minority of cases, emphasizing that public health initiatives aimed at expanding access to primary oral care and early dental extractions could substantially reduce the incidence of life-threatening deep space neck infections in Somalia.

sections.title: Symptom duration, presentation delay, and inpatient morbidity
heading_path: Symptom duration, presentation delay, and inpatient morbidity

blocks.text: A key observation in this cohort was the prolonged pre-admission symptom duration (mean: $5.4 \pm 1.8$ days), with most patients presenting between days 5 and 7 after symptom onset. In resource-limited settings, presentation delays are multifactorial, driven by limited financial resources, lack of primary dental care facilities, and initial reliance on self-medication or traditional remedies [8, 14].

This delayed presentation contributed directly to the high rate of hospital-acquired complications observed during inpatient care (48.9%), dominated by secondary septicemia (36.7%). When treatment is delayed, localized fascial cellulitis rapidly progresses to tissue necrosis, micro-abscess formation, and systemic bacteremia [3, 5]. Furthermore, a clear operational distinction was maintained between conditions present on arrival (such as presentation sepsis or severe baseline anemia) and secondary complications developing post-admission (such as secondary septicemia or local necrotizing fasciitis), ensuring clarity in assessing inpatient quality of care and disease progression.

A notable finding was that 46.7% of patients were successfully managed with conservative medical therapy alone (intravenous empiric antibiotics, hydration, and close airway surveillance), while 53.3% required operative intervention (38.9% deep decompression and 14.4% superficial drainage). Conservative management is clinically appropriate in the early, purely cellulitic phase before loculated fluid collections develop [5, 9]. The high success rate of medical management in selected patients highlights the efficacy of immediate empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobial coverage (ceftriaxone plus metronidazole) in halting disease progression. Conversely, for patients with mature abscesses or severe tissue tension, prompt surgical decompression remains the gold standard for source control [11, 15].

All patients in this cohort were successfully managed without invasive surgical airway interventions (tracheostomy or cricothyroidotomy). Airway stabilization relied on close clinical surveillance, upright positioning, supplemental oxygen, and non-invasive airway adjuncts. While emergency tracheostomy remains a life-saving intervention in advanced airway compromise, early admission and rapid commencement of intravenous anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial therapy likely prevented complete upper airway collapse in this cohort [6, 7].

sections.title: Statistical predictors of hospital length of stay
heading_path: Statistical predictors of hospital length of stay

blocks.text: Linear regression analysis demonstrated that pre-admission symptom duration was a significant independent predictor of total hospital length of stay ($B = 0.500$, $p < 0.001$). Each additional day of delay in presenting to the hospital increased the average length of stay by 0.5 days. Clinically, delayed presentation allows deeper tissue destruction, higher bacterial loads, and increased systemic inflammation, requiring longer courses of parenteral antibiotics, repeated wound debridements, and prolonged monitoring before discharge [8, 12]. Multivariable modeling confirmed that advanced age, pre-existing systemic comorbidities, and delayed presentation beyond 5 days independently predicted prolonged hospitalization.

The 0% institutional mortality observed in this study is encouraging when compared to historic series reporting mortality rates up to 10% in low-resource settings [7, 10]. This favorable outcome reflects the impact of rapid triage, aggressive empiric antimicrobial regimens, selective surgical intervention, and continuous airway monitoring. However, this zero-mortality figure must be interpreted with caution. In low-resource environments with limited pre-hospital emergency transport, referral bias may exist: patients experiencing fulminant, rapidly progressive airway compromise may die prior to reaching a tertiary referral center [8, 14].
This study has several limitations that should be considered when interpreting the results:

Study Design & Scope: The retrospective, single-center design at a major tertiary hospital may limit the generalizability of the findings to rural or primary healthcare settings in Somalia.
Sample Size: Although representing the largest deep neck infection cohort from the region to date, the sample size (n = 90) restricted extensive subgroup analyses for rare clinical complications.
Information Bias: Data collection relied on electronic medical records, which introduces potential documentation or recall bias regarding exact symptom onset and prior outpatient antibiotic exposure.
Microbiological Data: Routine anaerobic cultures and comprehensive antibiotic susceptibility testing were not uniformly available for all patients, limiting detailed microbiological profiling.
Long-Term Follow-up: Long-term post-discharge follow-up was limited, preventing the evaluation of late functional outcomes, such as scar contracture or recurrence rates.

blocks.text: In conclusion, Ludwig’s angina in Somalia predominantly affects young men and arises mainly from odontogenic infection. Although delayed presentation and high inpatient complication rates remain major concerns, favorable outcomes, including zero mortality, were achieved with early antibiotics, careful monitoring, and selective surgical management. These findings emphasize the need for improved dental prevention, earlier referral, standardized documentation, and stronger emergency surgical capacity in Somalia and other resource-limited settings.

title: Odontogenic Sinusitis: The Selective Role of a Modified Caldwell–Luc Approach in Two CT/CBCT-Documented Cases
