blocks.text: Halitosis is a common oral health concern with notable psychosocial consequences. Although psychological stress has been linked to various oral conditions, the specific mechanism through which perceived stress contributes to self-reported halitosis remains unclear. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of self-reported halitosis among university students and to evaluate the associations between perceived stress levels, oral hygiene behaviors, xerostomia, and self-reported halitosis, with a particular focus on the potential mediating role of xerostomia.

A cross-sectional study was conducted among 400 students from Çankırı Karatekin University’s Faculty of Dentistry and Faculty of Health Sciences, Department of Nursing, using a non probability voluntary response sampling method. Data were collected via a self administered online questionnaire (Google Forms) that included items on demographic characteristics, oral hygiene behaviors, and single item questions on xerostomia and self-reported halitosis. Perceived stress was assessed using the validated Turkish version of the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10). Associations were examined using chi square tests and binary logistic regression. The mediating role of xerostomia in the relationship between perceived stress and self-reported halitosis was evaluated through mediation analysis.

The prevalence of self-reported daytime halitosis was 18.5%, and 67.8% of participants reported xerostomia. Perceived stress was significantly associated with both self-reported halitosis and xerostomia. Mediation analysis revealed that xerostomia statistically mediated the association between perceived stress and self-reported halitosis (indirect effect = 0.653, 95% bootstrap CI [0.184, 1.122]). Xerostomia was a significant predictor of halitosis (OR = 3.249, 95% CI: 1.647–6.408, p = 0.001). Additionally, self-reported halitosis was significantly associated with brushing frequency, gingival bleeding, and smoking status. Statistically significant differences in perceived stress levels were observed based on gender and faculty of enrollment.

Perceived stress is associated with self-reported halitosis among university students, and this association is statistically mediated by xerostomia. These findings suggest that xerostomia may represent a potential mechanism linking perceived stress and self-reported halitosis. Future studies employing larger samples and objective clinical measurements, such as sialometry and volatile sulfur compound analysis, are needed to confirm these associations.
The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-09460-7.

Halitosis is commonly described as an unpleasant odor from the mouth, primarily caused by volatile sulfur compounds produced through microbial degradation of peptides in the oral cavity [1, 2]. Morning breath and odor associated with aromatic foods are considered physiological and transient, whereas persistent oral malodor is classified as pathological halitosis and may be linked to both intraoral and extraoral causes [3]. Common intraoral factors include tongue coating, poor oral hygiene, periodontal diseases, dry mouth, and oral candidiasis [2, 4].

Stress refers to the pressure experienced when a person perceives that environmental demands exceed his or her capacity to cope [5]. University students are exposed to stress related to examinations, heavy workload, and academic competition [6, 7]. Stress coping may involve avoidance or reward seeking behaviors [8], and smoking is often motivated by pleasure and stress relief [9]. Stress increases susceptibility to periodontal disease [10–12], and stress-related smoking may further compromise periodontal health [13, 14]. Oral hygiene habits may also deteriorate under stress, worsening periodontal status [15]. As a result, stress-related changes in oral hygiene and periodontal condition may contribute to the development of halitosis [2, 16].

Salivary output may temporarily decrease during periods of stress, nervousness, or anxiety [17]. Under stress, this reduction appears to occur primarily through central suppression of parasympathetic reflex activity rather than through direct sympathetic inhibition, as sympathetic nerve activity contributes only slightly to overall salivary volüme [18]. The sympathetic response instead mainly alters the protein composition of saliva as part of an adaptive mechanism [18]. Xerostomia, defined as the subjective sensation of oral dryness, may or may not be accompanied by a measurable reduction in salivary flow [19, 20]. Changes in salivary protein content have been reported to elicit a perception of dry mouth even when flow rate remains unchanged [21, 22]. It has been reported that increased saliva viscosity, or increased plaque accumulation due to reduced salivary flow and buffering capacity, can contribute to the development of halitosis [23], and that adequate fluid intake reduces the likelihood of halitosis [24]. A recent study among young adults found that those reporting halitosis and higher stress levels also reported more severe xerostomia [25]. Although these findings point to an association between perceived stress, xerostomia, and halitosis [26–30], whether xerostomia acts as a mediating factor in the relationship between perceived stress and self-reported halitosis has not been directly addressed.

The aim of this study was to determine the prevalence of self-reported halitosis among students enrolled in the Faculty of Dentistry and the Faculty of Health Sciences, Department of Nursing, at a Turkish university, and to evaluate the associations between perceived stress, oral hygiene behaviors, xerostomia, and self-reported halitosis. Specifically, we sought to test whether xerostomia mediates the association between perceived stress and self-reported halitosis.

This cross-sectional study was conducted during the final examination period in June 2025 among students enrolled at the Faculty of Dentistry and the Department of Nursing, Faculty of Health Sciences, at Çankırı Karatekin University. All registered students in both faculties were invited to participate (N = 829; Nursing: 325 female and 190 male; Dentistry: 186 female and 128 male). Participation was on a voluntary basis, constituting a non-probability voluntary response sampling method. A self administered online questionnaire was distributed to all students via Google Forms, and 400 students completed the survey, yielding a response rate of 48.3%.

The required sample size was determined a priori using G*Power software (version 3.1). Based on a chi-square goodness of fit test with an effect size of w = 0.20, an alpha level of 0.05, one degree of freedom, and a target power of 0.97, the minimum required sample size was calculated as 369 participants (actual power = 0.970). The final sample of 400 exceeded this threshold. Perceived stress was defined as the independent variable and self-reported halitosis as the dependent variable.

The study protocol was approved by the Health Sciences Ethics Committee of Çankırı Karatekin University (Meeting No: 18) and was carried out in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All participants provided informed consent electronically before completing the questionnaire.

Perceived stress was measured using the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) [31], which evaluates the degree to which respondents have found their lives unpredictable, uncontrollable, and overloading during the past month. Each item is rated on a 5-point Likert scale (0 = never, 4 = very often). The Turkish adaptation of the PSS-10 has demonstrated acceptable reliability and validity [32, 33].

Demographic characteristics, oral hygiene behaviors, xerostomia, and self-reported halitosis were assessed using a questionnaire adapted from previously published surveys [34–39], with additional items developed for the purposes of this study. The full questionnaire is provided as Additional file 1. Xerostomia was assessed using a single self-report question (Do you experience dry mouth? ) with three response options (never / sometimes / often). Participants responding ‘sometimes’ or ‘often’ were classified as having xerostomia, an approach consistent with previous epidemiological studies [38, 39]. In this questionnaire based study without clinical measurements, self-reported halitosis was assessed using two questions: ‘Do you feel that you have bad breath in the morning?’ and ‘Do you feel that you have bad breath during the day?’, each with four response options (never / rarely / occasionally / always). Since morning breath is generally regarded as physiological and transient [3, 40], only the daytime question was used to define the presence of self-reported halitosis. Following the methodology of a previous study [30], participants responding ‘occasionally’ or ‘always’ were classified as having self-reported halitosis, while those responding ‘never’ or ‘rarely’ were classified as halitosis free.

Only fully completed questionnaires were included in the analysis (n = 400; no missing data). The internal consistency of the PSS-10 was assessed using Cronbach’s alpha. Normality of continuous variables was evaluated with the Shapiro Wilk test.

Group comparisons were performed using independent samples t-tests or Mann Whitney U tests for two groups, and one way ANOVA or Kruskal Wallis H tests (with Dunn Bonferroni post hoc correction) for more than two groups, depending on data distribution. Categorical variables were analyzed using Pearson’s chi square test or Fisher’s exact test where appropriate.

Binary logistic regression was used to identify independent predictors of self-reported halitosis. To examine whether xerostomia mediates the association between perceived stress and self-reported halitosis, a mediation analysis was conducted using the PROCESS macro for SPSS [41], with 5,000 bootstrap resamples to estimate 95% bias corrected confidence intervals for the indirect effect. Mediation was considered present when the bootstrap confidence interval for the indirect effect did not include zero. The significance level was set at p < 0.05 for all analyses. All statistical procedures were carried out using IBM SPSS Statistics version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA).

Of the 829 students invited, 400 completed the questionnaire (response rate: 48.3%). The gender distribution of the study sample did not differ significantly from the source population (χ² = 2.70, p = 0.10). The PSS-10 demonstrated high internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = 0.831), and the mean perceived stress score was 2.23 ± 0.56.

Morning halitosis was reported by 27.25% of participants (n = 109). As morning breath is generally considered physiological and transient [3, 40], only daytime halitosis was used to define self-reported halitosis in the analyses. The prevalence of self-reported daytime halitosis was 18.5% (n = 74).

blocks.text: Female students reported significantly higher perceived stress scores than male students, and dentistry students scored higher than nursing students (Tables 1 and 2; p < 0.05). No significant differences were found in halitosis prevalence by gender, faculty, or academic term (p > 0.05). The prevalence of xerostomia was also similar between genders (68.7% (n = 180) in females vs. 65.9% (n = 91) in males; p = 0.575).

blocks.text: No significant associations were found between systemic diseases and either halitosis or stress levels (p > 0.05). Medication use was not associated with halitosis either; however, participants who reported using medication had higher perceived stress scores than non-users (24.53 ± 4.81 vs. 22.08 ± 5.56; p < 0.05).

Participants who reported xerostomia had significantly higher mean stress scores than those who did not (Table 4; p < 0.05). The prevalence of xerostomia was similar between genders (68.7% in females vs. 65.9% in males; χ² = 0.315, p = 0.575). Self-reported halitosis was significantly more common among smokers, individuals who experienced gingival bleeding, and those with xerostomia (Tables 5, 6 and 7; p < 0.05). Alcohol consumption and age were not associated with halitosis. Lower brushing frequency and shorter brushing duration were also significant predictors of halitosis (Table 8; p < 0.05). Mean perceived stress scores were higher in participants who reported halitosis compared to those who did not (Table 9; p < 0.05). No significant gender difference was observed in self-reported halitosis prevalence either.

blocks.text: To account for potential confounders, all variables that showed a significant association with halitosis in the bivariate analyses were entered into a multivariate logistic regression model (Table 10). In the univariate analysis, perceived stress showed a borderline association with halitosis (crude OR = 1.554, p = 0.050). blocks.text: The primary finding of this study indicates that the association between perceived stress and self-reported halitosis among university students is statistically mediated by xerostomia. Additionally, self-reported halitosis was found to be associated with smoking, gingival bleeding, and lower tooth brushing frequency. The prevalence of daytime self-reported halitosis was 18.5%.

Following the methodology of a comparable study [30], participants reporting halitosis ‘constantly’ or ‘occasionally’ during the day were categorized as having self-reported halitosis, whereas those reporting ‘never’ or ‘rarely’ were classified as halitosis-free. Morning halitosis was considered physiological and excluded from the analysis [3, 40]. While the prevalence of self-reported halitosis in the literature ranges from 2.4% to 55% [23, 40, 42], the relatively lower rate observed in our study (18.5%) may be attributed to our methodological decision to exclude morning halitosis from the analysis, as well as the health-related knowledge of our sample, which consisted of dentistry and nursing students.

Consistent with previous reports, no significant associations were observed between self-reported halitosis and age, gender, academic year, or faculty [43–45]. Overall, participants demonstrated relatively satisfactory oral hygiene behaviors. While dentistry students tended to brush their teeth more frequently, nursing students were more likely to utilize interdental cleaning aids, tongue scrapers, and mouthwash. Previous studies have documented low dental floss utilization, insufficient tongue cleaning, and minimal mouthwash use among dentistry students [46–48]. Conversely, a study conducted with final-year dentistry students observed higher floss use [49], suggesting that oral health awareness may increase in the later stages of academic training. Given that the questionnaire evaluated oral hygiene behaviors over the past month a period coinciding with final examinations the demanding preclinical and clinical workload of dentistry programs may have prompted students to prioritize basic brushing over more time consuming routines during this timeframe [50].

Self-reported halitosis showed a tendency to decrease with higher brushing frequency and longer brushing duration; however, no statistically significant association was found with interdental cleaning, tongue cleaning, or mouthwash use. Similar outcomes have been reported elsewhere [40, 51], and the relationship between brushing frequency and halitosis is well-documented [52–54]. Smoking was significantly associated with halitosis, whereas alcohol consumption was not, aligning with previous literature [55, 56]. Although the cross-sectional design of our study precluded a clinical diagnosis of periodontitis, 55.8% of the participants reported gingival bleeding during brushing. Self-reported halitosis was significantly more prevalent among individuals with gingival bleeding, which is consistent with the established link between gingival inflammation and halitosis [57–60].

The prevalence of xerostomia in our sample was 67.8%. While the reported rate of xerostomia in the literature varies between 0.9% and 64.8% [39, 61, 62], a study conducted at Ankara University reported a xerostomia prevalence of 54.6%, noting its common occurrence in young populations as well [63]. Given that only 7% of participants reported regular medication use and systemic diseases were not associated with halitosis, this high prevalence cannot be attributed solely to pharmacological factors. The rigorous nature of both curricula, combined with the fact that data collection coincided with the final examination period, may have contributed to elevated stress levels and subsequent xerostomia [6, 64, 65]. Health sciences students might also be more attuned to minor intraoral changes, rendering them more likely to report dry mouth symptoms. It is worth noting that self-reported xerostomia does not always correspond to an objectively reduced salivary flow rate [20, 66]. Although xerostomia can originate from various systemic etiologies [67], stress is widely recognized as a major contributor to oral dryness [26, 64], and our regression model confirmed perceived stress as a significant predictor of xerostomia. These findings align with large scale studies pointing to psychological factors as risk factors for self-reported halitosis [68, 69]. While we hypothesized that stress leads to xerostomia and subsequent halitosis, the reverse pathway is also plausible: individuals who perceive bad breath may experience social embarrassment and heightened anxiety, thereby elevating their stress levels. Likewise, the sensation of dry mouth may reinforce negative emotions and stress perception. The cross-sectional design prevents us from determining the direction of these associations, and longitudinal studies are required to clarify their temporal sequence.

In line with the existing literature, perceived stress was higher among female students and dentistry students [70]. Furthermore, stress was not associated with oral hygiene habits, gingival bleeding, smoking, or alcohol consumption. While the literature regarding stress and oral hygiene remains mixed [71, 72], our results suggest that these students maintained their oral hygiene routines despite elevated stress, potentially due to social factors such as concern for personal appearance and peer relationships. The absence of an association between stress and gingival bleeding can likely be explained by the maintenance of adequate oral hygiene, as gingivitis is fundamentally driven by microbial plaque [73]. Smoking and alcohol use among university students may be more closely tied to social adaptation and peer influence rather than stress avoidance [74–76].

Although female students reported higher perceived stress, no significant gender differences were observed in the prevalence of xerostomia (68.7% vs. 65.9%; p = 0.575) or halitosis. This finding is consistent with our mediation model, indicating that perceived stress appears to be associated with halitosis only when accompanied by xerostomia. While cross-sectional data do not allow for establishing directionality, mediation analysis remains a useful approach for identifying potential intermediate variables that warrant further investigation in longitudinal designs [77, 78]. Because the stress xerostomia response may vary based on individual susceptibility [79], perceived stress does not inevitably culminate in xerostomia or halitosis.

Although evaluating all variables via self-report reports introduces the potential for common method bias, the observed associations remained specific to xerostomia and halitosis; perceived stress demonstrated no association with gingival bleeding or oral hygiene behaviors. This selectivity suggests that the findings are unlikely to be merely an artifact of a general tendency to over report symptoms under stress. Nonetheless, stressed individuals may possess a lower threshold for noticing oral dryness, and the perception of a dry mouth may, in turn, heighten attention regarding breath-related concerns. Future studies employing objective measures, such as sialometry and volatile sulfur compound analysis, would be valuable in distinguishing subjective perception from physiological alterations.

This study has several limitations. The cross-sectional design does not allow causal inferences. Both halitosis and xerostomia were assessed through self-report rather than objective measurements, which may introduce perception bias and misclassification in both directions. Xerostomia was assessed using a single question rather than a validated multi-item scale, which may have limited measurement sensitivity. The absence of intraoral clinical examinations meant that factors such as tongue coating or periodontal pocket depth could not be verified. Potential confounding variables including dietary habits, caffeine and water intake, sleep quality, and anxiety or depression symptoms were not assessed. The response rate raises the possibility of self-selection bias, as students with higher stress or more severe halitosis may have been less inclined to participate. Data were collected during the final examination period, which may limit generalizability to other academic periods. No stratified sampling was applied across gender or grade levels. As a single center study among healthcare students, these results may not be directly applicable to the broader young adult population. Multi center longitudinal studies with objective clinical assessments are needed to clarify these associations.

The sample size (n = 400) exceeded the power analysis requirement. Focusing on healthcare students allowed us to examine the stress oral health relationship in a group with relatively high oral health awareness. The validated PSS-10 enabled a standardized assessment of perceived stress. Data collection during the examination period allowed for assessment under conditions of naturally elevated stress. The use of a mediation model offers a perspective beyond simple correlational analyses, although the exploratory nature of this approach within a cross-sectional design should be taken into account when interpreting the findings.

This study found a high prevalence of both self-reported halitosis (18.5%) and xerostomia (67.8%) among dentistry and nursing students during the examination period. Perceived stress was not directly associated with self-reported halitosis; rather, this association was statistically mediated by xerostomia. These findings suggest that the association between perceived stress and self-reported halitosis may depend on the presence of xerostomia.

These findings point to xerostomia as a potential target for managing stress related oral health complaints in demanding academic settings. Strategies aimed at reducing stress and promoting adequate oral hydration may help improve oral comfort and quality of life among university students. Future research with objective measurements and longitudinal designs is needed to confirm these associations and to explore individual differences in the stress xerostomia response.

blocks.text: Introduction: Halitosis is a common oral condition that may negatively affect social interactions, psychological well-being, and quality of life. However, evidence regarding its association with mental health and sleep quality remains inconsistent, particularly among university students. Aim: This cross-sectional study investigated the prevalence of objectively measured halitosis and its association with tongue coating, sleep quality, and symptoms of anxiety, depression, and stress among university students from the metropolitan region of Santos, Brazil. Methods: Sixty-two Brazilian university students enrolled in health-related undergraduate programs participated in the study; most were in the first academic year (61.3%) and resided in the municipality of Santos (59.7%). Halitosis was assessed using a portable breath detector, tongue coating was evaluated using the Coated Tongue Index, sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were measured using the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21). Results: Objectively measured halitosis was identified in 25 participants (40.3%; 95% CI: 29.0–52.7%). The analyses did not provide statistically significant evidence of associations between objectively measured halitosis and tongue coating, sleep quality, or symptoms of anxiety, depression, and stress. Significant positive correlations were identified between stress and sleep disturbance, anxiety and sleep disturbance, and depression and sleep latency, daytime dysfunction, and overall sleep quality. Tongue-cleaning habits were significantly associated with the presence of halitosis, whereas oral mucosal desquamation was less frequent among participants with halitosis. Conclusion: The study did not provide statistically significant evidence of associations between objectively measured halitosis and tongue coating, sleep quality, or psychological symptoms in this population. Significant positive correlations were identified between stress and sleep disturbance, anxiety and sleep disturbance, and depression and sleep latency, daytime dysfunction, and overall sleep quality. These findings highlight the importance of objectively assessing oral malodor in epidemiological studies.

Halitosis is a common oral condition characterized by an unpleasant odor originating from the oral cavity that may negatively affect social interactions, psychological well-being, and quality of life [1,2,3]. Its psychosocial impact may be particularly relevant among young adults and university students, who are exposed to intense social interactions, academic demands, psychosocial stressors, and lifestyle changes [1,2,3,4]. The relationship between halitosis and psychological factors is complex, as clinically detectable oral malodor may contribute to psychological distress, whereas emotional factors may also influence the perception of breath odor [1,2,5,6].

The etiology of halitosis is multifactorial, although approximately 80–90% of cases originate within the oral cavity. Oral malodor is primarily associated with the microbial degradation of organic substrates and the production of volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs). Tongue coating, periodontal conditions, oral hygiene, salivary characteristics, microbial composition, and behavioral factors may contribute to the development and persistence of halitosis [2,7,8,9,10,11,12].

Growing evidence indicates that psychological factors may influence both the perception and manifestation of halitosis. Anxiety, depression, stress, and social anxiety disorder have been associated with self-perceived and clinically diagnosed halitosis [2,6,9,10,13]. Individuals reporting halitosis frequently experience embarrassment, reduced self-confidence, social avoidance, and concerns regarding interpersonal acceptance, reinforcing the complex relationship between oral conditions and psychological health [3,14,15]. Importantly, previous studies have suggested that psychological distress may exert a greater influence on the perception of oral malodor than on objectively measured halitosis, which may partly explain the inconsistent findings reported in the literature [1,2,9,10,14].

Previous studies conducted among university students in Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia reported a prevalence of self-perceived halitosis of approximately 56% and 55%, respectively [3,4]. However, these estimates should be interpreted with caution because self-perception may be influenced by sociocultural context, including norms related to interpersonal communication, personal hygiene, social acceptability, and willingness to report a potentially embarrassing condition. Psychological characteristics, individual awareness, and oral health behaviors may also affect the recognition and reporting of oral malodor. Consequently, self-perceived halitosis does not necessarily correspond to clinically detectable oral malodor [8,9,10].

Sleep quality is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of physical and psychological health [16,17]. University students are particularly susceptible to sleep disturbances due to academic workload, irregular routines, lifestyle changes, and psychosocial stressors [16,17,18,19]. Poor sleep quality has consistently been associated with anxiety, depression, stress, reduced quality of life, and adverse health outcomes [19,20,21,22,23,24,25]. Furthermore, insufficient sleep has been associated with self-reported halitosis in adolescents, suggesting a possible interaction between sleep-related factors and oral malodor [11]. Proposed biological mechanisms include reduced salivary flow, alterations in the oral microbiota, mouth breathing, and behavioral changes associated with sleep deprivation, all of which may contribute to the production of volatile sulfur compounds [11,26,27].

Although increasing attention has been devoted to the relationships among oral health, mental health, and sleep quality, evidence regarding the interplay between objectively measured halitosis, psychological symptoms, and sleep disturbances remains limited, particularly among university students. Most available studies have investigated self-perceived halitosis or examined these conditions independently, resulting in heterogeneous and, at times, contradictory findings [3,4,14,15]. Moreover, relatively few investigations have simultaneously evaluated objectively diagnosed halitosis, tongue coating, sleep quality, and psychological symptoms within the same population. This gap limits the understanding of the complex interactions between oral and psychological health and highlights the need for multidisciplinary research using objective diagnostic methods.

Therefore, the present study aimed to investigate the prevalence of objectively measured halitosis and its association with tongue coating, sleep quality, and symptoms of anxiety, depression, and stress among university students from the metropolitan region of Santos, Brazil. We hypothesized that objectively measured halitosis would be associated with greater tongue coating, poorer sleep quality, and higher levels of anxiety, depression, and stress.

This descriptive, quantitative, observational, cross-sectional study was conducted using a non-probabilistic convenience sample of university students from the metropolitan region of Santos, São Paulo, Brazil. The study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee of Universidade Metropolitana de Santos (UNIMES) on 5 December 2023 (CAAE: 74442423.0.0000.5509; Approval No. 6.556.493) and conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki and its subsequent amendments. The study design and reporting followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) guidelines. The completed STROBE checklist is provided as Supplementary Material.

The objective of this study was to determine the prevalence of objectively measured halitosis and to investigate its associations with tongue coating, sleep quality, and symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress among university students from the metropolitan region of Santos, Brazil. We hypothesized that participants with objectively measured halitosis would present greater tongue coating, poorer sleep quality, and higher levels of depression, anxiety, and stress than participants without halitosis.

The study included university students aged 18 years or older enrolled in health-related undergraduate programs at the Universidade Metropolitana de Santos (UNIMES), located in the metropolitan region of Santos, São Paulo, Brazil. Students were recruited from different semesters of the courses in Medicine, Psychology, Nursing, Physiotherapy, and Pharmacy programs.

Students were excluded if they lived outside the metropolitan region of Santos, were younger than 18 years, had dentofacial anomalies, were undergoing orthodontic or orthopedic treatment, were receiving cancer treatment, had self-reported systemic conditions potentially associated with oral malodor, such as gastrointestinal, renal, or liver disease, or had used antibiotics in the month prior to data collection.

Data collection was conducted between 15 March 2024 and 30 June 2024 during previously scheduled sessions held at the participating university facilities. Assessments were conducted in classrooms for students enrolled in the Medicine, Psychology, Nursing, and Physiotherapy programs and in the clinical training facilities used by Pharmacy students.

Participants received standardized pre-assessment instructions regarding tongue-coating assessment and breath evaluation 24 and 48 h before the scheduled examination, with the aim of standardizing conditions before the clinical measurements. On the day of data collection, all participants received detailed information regarding the study objectives and procedures and provided electronic informed consent before participation. Participants subsequently completed an online questionnaire using their own mobile devices. The questionnaire was administered in Brazilian Portuguese using Google Forms and completed electronically by the participants. Questionnaires with incomplete responses were excluded from the final analysis. The estimated completion time was approximately 15 min. Immediately after completing the questionnaire, clinical assessment of tongue coating and breath analysis were performed by the same examiner, who had undergone practical training and procedural standardization in the study assessment protocol, including operation of the portable breath detector and assessment of tongue coating. No formal intra-examiner reproducibility coefficient was calculated. The participant recruitment and study procedures are summarized in Figure 1.

The questionnaire consisted of validated instruments (PSQI and DASS-21), together with a structured questionnaire developed by the research team to collect demographic characteristics, oral health habits, and general health information relevant to the study objectives. Sleep quality was evaluated using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), originally developed by Buysse et al. and culturally adapted and validated for the Brazilian population by Bertolazi et al. [28,29]. The PSQI evaluates sleep quality during the previous month through 19 self-administered items grouped into seven components: subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, sleep duration, habitual sleep efficiency, sleep disturbances, use of sleep medication, and daytime dysfunction. Component scores range from 0 to 3, resulting in a global score ranging from 0 to 21, with higher scores indicating poorer sleep quality. Global scores > 5 were considered indicative of poor sleep quality.

Symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were assessed using the Brazilian Portuguese version of the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21) [30,31,32]. The instrument comprises 21 items equally distributed across three domains: depression, anxiety, and stress. Responses are recorded using a four-point Likert scale ranging from 0 (“Did not apply to me at all”) to 3 (“Applied to me very much or most of the time”). Scores for each domain were calculated by summing the corresponding items, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.

Information regarding oral and general health was collected through a structured questionnaire addressing oral hygiene practices, tongue-cleaning habits, xerostomia, morning dry mouth, gingival bleeding, self-perceived halitosis, dental caries, gingival alterations, oral mucosal desquamation, smoking habits, mouth breathing, gastrointestinal complaints, and other self-reported health conditions potentially associated with oral malodor.

Tongue coating was assessed using the Coated Tongue Index proposed by Shimizu et al. [33]. The dorsal surface of the tongue was divided into nine anatomical areas. Each area received a score of 0 (absence of coating), 1 (coating with visible lingual papillae), or 2 (coating completely covering the papillae). The final index was calculated by summing the scores, dividing the total by 18, and multiplying the result by 100, yielding a percentage ranging from 0% to 100%.

Halitosis was assessed using a portable KKCare (KKcare, China) breath detector according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. The device provides a semiquantitative assessment of breath odor using a five-point scale. No independent validation against a reference method was performed in the present sample; therefore, the device was used as a screening tool rather than as a reference diagnostic method. Participants were instructed to exhale continuously into the device for approximately 5 s. Breath odor was classified as 0 (good), 1 (normal), 2 (not very good), 3 (bad), or 4 (very bad). For statistical analyses, scores ≥ 2 were considered indicative of halitosis.

Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 28.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA). The Shapiro–Wilk test was used to assess the normality of continuous variables. Descriptive statistics were calculated, with continuous variables expressed as means and standard deviations and categorical variables expressed as absolute and relative frequencies.

Associations between categorical variables were analyzed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, when appropriate. For the statistically significant categorical associations identified in the exploratory analyses, crude odds ratios (ORs) with corresponding 95% confidence intervals were calculated from 2 × 2 contingency tables to provide an estimate of the magnitude and precision of the observed associations. Spearman’s correlation coefficient was used to assess correlations between halitosis levels, tongue-coating index, DASS-21 domains, and PSQI components, as this test is suitable for ordinal or non-normally distributed variables. To quantify the precision of the estimates, 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) for Spearman’s rho were estimated using a bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) nonparametric bootstrap procedure with 50,000 paired resamples. The 95% CI for the prevalence of halitosis was estimated using the Wilson score method. Due to the convenience sampling strategy and the exploratory nature of the study, an a priori sample size calculation was not performed. Post hoc statistical power was calculated for the statistically significant correlations to provide additional information regarding the robustness of the observed associations. Nevertheless, the relatively small sample size may have limited the ability to detect weaker associations and should be considered when interpreting the findings. The analyses were exploratory. Multivariable modeling was not performed because only 25 participants met the criterion for objectively measured halitosis and several potentially relevant covariates had low frequencies or sparse cells. Under these conditions, simultaneous adjustment for multiple covariates would result in a low number of outcome events relative to the number of parameters estimated, increasing the risk of overfitting, unstable regression coefficients, inflated standard errors, and separation. Restricting the model to a small subset of covariates selected post hoc was also avoided because this could introduce data-driven model-selection bias. Therefore, the analyses were intentionally restricted to exploratory bivariate associations. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Table 1 summarizes the demographic and academic characteristics of the 62 university students included in the study. Medicine students represented the largest proportion of the sample (35.5%), followed by students from the remaining health-related programs. Most participants were in the first academic year (61.3%) and resided in the municipality of Santos (59.7%). Stomach disorders were self-reported by 16.1% of the participants, whereas 12.9% reported current smoking.

The mean tongue-coating index was 46.4 ± 27.7, and the prevalence of objectively measured halitosis was 40.3% (25/62; 95% CI: 29.0–52.7%). Regarding oral hygiene practices, 71.0% of the participants reported using dental floss, 51.6% used mouthwash, and 46.8% performed tongue cleaning. Participants reported brushing their teeth an average of 1.7 ± 0.6 times per day. Additional oral health characteristics and factors potentially associated with halitosis are presented in Table 2.

The assessment of psychological symptoms using the DASS-21 revealed that stress had the highest mean score (9.2 ± 3.7), followed by anxiety and depression. Sleep quality, assessed using the PSQI, showed a mean global score of 7.8 ± 2.7. Among the PSQI domains, sleep latency presented the highest mean score (1.7 ± 0.7). Detailed results for the DASS-21 and PSQI domains are presented in Table 3.

sections.title: 3.4. Correlations Between Halitosis, Tongue Coating, Mental Health, and Sleep Quality
heading_path: 3.4. Correlations Between Halitosis, Tongue Coating, Mental Health, and Sleep Quality

blocks.text: Spearman’s correlation analysis did not provide statistically significant evidence of correlations between halitosis levels and the tongue-coating index, psychological symptoms, or sleep quality indicators (Table 4).

Significant correlations were identified between mental health indicators and sleep quality parameters (Table 5). The stress domain was positively correlated with sleep disturbance (rho = 0.418; 95% CI: 0.212 to 0.600; p = 0.001; 1 − β = 0.93). The depression domain was positively correlated with sleep latency (rho = 0.271; 95% CI: 0.013 to 0.492; p = 0.033; 1 − β = 0.57), daytime dysfunction (rho = 0.287; 95% CI: 0.031 to 0.504; p = 0.024; 1 − β = 0.62), and the global PSQI score (rho = 0.298; 95% CI: 0.060 to 0.509; p = 0.018; 1 − β = 0.66). The anxiety domain was positively correlated with sleep disturbance (rho = 0.366; 95% CI: 0.129 to 0.561; p = 0.003; 1 − β = 0.84). For the remaining comparisons, the analyses did not provide statistically significant evidence of correlations between the mental health domains and sleep quality components.

sections.title: 3.5. Associations Between Halitosis and Oral Health Variables
heading_path: 3.5. Associations Between Halitosis and Oral Health Variables

blocks.text: Associations between the presence of halitosis and oral health variables are presented in Table 6. A significant association was observed between halitosis and tongue-cleaning habits (p = 0.009). Participants with halitosis had higher odds of reporting tongue cleaning than those without halitosis (crude OR = 4.43; 95% CI: 1.49–13.12). Oral mucosal desquamation was less frequent among participants with halitosis (p = 0.038; crude OR = 0.11; 95% CI: 0.01–0.94).

The principal finding and main contribution of the present study is that objectively measured halitosis did not reproduce the pattern of associations with psychological symptoms and sleep quality frequently reported in studies based on self-perceived halitosis. Objectively measured halitosis was identified in 40.3% of the university students, but the analyses did not provide statistically significant evidence of associations with anxiety, depression, stress, sleep quality, or tongue coating. In contrast, tongue-cleaning habits and oral mucosal desquamation were associated with halitosis. These findings emphasize the importance of distinguishing self-perceived oral malodor from objectively detected halitosis when interpreting epidemiological associations.

Previous studies among university students have reported self-perceived halitosis prevalences of approximately 55–56% [3,4], whereas a study involving dentistry students reported self-perceived halitosis in 33.8% and objectively assessed oral malodor in 47.5% of participants [34]. Self-perceived halitosis may be influenced not only by oral conditions but also by psychological, cultural, behavioral, and social factors [2,9,10,14,15]. Consequently, associations identified in studies based on self-report may partly reflect factors related to the perception of breath odor rather than objectively detectable oral malodor itself. This distinction offers a plausible explanation for why the present findings differ from several previous reports.

The use of an objective assessment represents an important methodological feature of the present study. However, the portable sulfide monitor should be regarded as a screening tool rather than a reference diagnostic method. Although such devices provide a rapid and non-invasive assessment of oral malodor, they primarily detect total volatile sulfur compounds and do not differentiate individual gases or their oral and extraoral origins [7,8,35]. Moreover, the device was not independently validated against a reference method in the present sample, and its semiquantitative nature may have introduced some degree of measurement imprecision, potentially reducing the ability to detect weaker associations. These methodological characteristics should be considered when comparing the present findings with studies using organoleptic assessment or gas chromatography.

The analyses did not provide statistically significant evidence of associations between objectively measured halitosis and anxiety, depression, stress, or sleep quality. This contrasts with reports linking halitosis to psychological distress and social anxiety [1,2,10,13], although much of this evidence concerns self-perceived halitosis, which may be influenced by emotional factors, self-esteem, body image, and social anxiety [2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10]. The distinction between self-perceived and objectively measured halitosis may therefore partly explain the different pattern observed in the present study. The limited sample size may have also provided insufficient statistical power to detect weak associations, while the relative homogeneity of students enrolled predominantly in health-related programs may have restricted the range and variability of psychological measures.

In contrast, significant correlations were identified among the psychological and sleep variables themselves: stress was positively correlated with sleep disturbance, anxiety with sleep disturbance, and depression with sleep latency, daytime dysfunction, and overall sleep quality. These correlations were weak to moderate and should be interpreted cautiously given the exploratory design and limited sample size. Their direction is consistent with the established relationship between sleep and mental health in university populations [19,20,21,22,23,24,25,36]. In a recent IJERPH study involving 397 university students, Priede et al. [25] similarly found that poorer sleep quality was moderately correlated with depression, anxiety, and stress and proposed that such multidimensional evidence could inform student mental-well-being support programs. Taken together, these findings support a broader interpretation of student health in which sleep, emotional distress, health behaviors, and oral-health concerns may interact, even when objectively measured halitosis itself is not statistically associated with psychological symptoms. Biological mechanisms linking psychological stress and sleep disturbance may involve increased physiological arousal and alterations in neuroendocrine and inflammatory pathways [17,18,19,20,22,26].

Regarding oral conditions, the analysis did not provide statistically significant evidence of a correlation between the tongue-coating index and objectively measured halitosis. Volatile sulfur compound production depends not only on the amount of tongue coating but also on its microbial composition, substrate availability, salivary characteristics, oral hygiene, and other individual clinical factors [5,7,8,12,27,37]. Similar variability has been reported in specific populations, including mouth-breathing children [38]. Thus, tongue coating should be interpreted as one component of the multifactorial etiology of halitosis rather than as an isolated determinant.

An unexpected finding was the significant association between tongue-cleaning habits and halitosis. Because of the cross-sectional design, this association should not be interpreted as evidence that tongue cleaning increases the risk of oral malodor. A plausible alternative explanation is reverse directionality: individuals who are already aware of or concerned about their breath may be more likely to adopt tongue cleaning in an attempt to control it.

Oral mucosal desquamation was less frequent among participants with halitosis. Although previous reports have suggested that epithelial desquamation may contribute to the availability of organic substrates for bacterial degradation [39], the mechanisms underlying this finding remain uncertain. Salivary flow, mucosal integrity, oral microbiota, and local inflammatory conditions may influence both epithelial turnover and volatile sulfur compound production [40]. Therefore, this association should be regarded as exploratory and hypothesis-generating rather than as evidence of a protective effect.

Several limitations of the present study should be acknowledged. First, the cross-sectional design does not permit determination of the temporal sequence of the observed associations or establishment of causal relationships. Second, the study used a non-probabilistic convenience sample recruited from a single university, predominantly comprising students enrolled in health-related programs. This relatively homogeneous sample may limit the generalizability of the findings and may also have reduced the variability of some investigated characteristics. In addition, self-selection bias cannot be excluded, as students who agreed to participate may have differed systematically from those who did not participate.

Halitosis was assessed at a single time point using a portable sulfide monitor. Although this approach provided an objective, rapid, and standardized screening assessment, the device was not independently validated against a reference method in the present sample, measures total volatile sulfur compounds, and does not differentiate individual gases or their oral and extraoral sources [7,8,35]. A comprehensive periodontal examination was not performed, and potentially relevant factors such as salivary flow and composition, dietary intake, medication use beyond the exclusion criterion for recent antibiotic therapy, and the microbiological composition and metabolic activity of the tongue biofilm were not comprehensively assessed or controlled.

Furthermore, several oral and general health variables, including xerostomia, gastrointestinal complaints, dental caries, gingival alterations, and other health conditions, were based on participant self-report rather than comprehensive clinical confirmation. Misclassification or reporting bias therefore cannot be excluded. Because multivariable modeling was not considered statistically reliable given the small number of participants with halitosis and the sparse distribution of several candidate covariates, the reported associations remain unadjusted, and residual confounding cannot be excluded. Finally, multiple statistical comparisons were performed without adjustment for multiplicity, increasing the possibility of false-positive findings (type I error). The results should therefore be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating and require confirmation in larger, longitudinal studies with more comprehensive clinical assessments.

Overall, the findings reinforce the importance of distinguishing objectively detected oral malodor from self-perceived halitosis when interpreting associations with psychological and behavioral factors. From a broader student well-being perspective, the observed interrelationships among stress, anxiety, depression, and sleep suggest that these domains should not be considered or addressed in isolation. Recent multidimensional research has similarly emphasized the use of combined mental-health, sleep, and behavioral evidence to inform student support programs [25].

Although coping strategies and quality of life were not directly assessed in the present study, evidence from university populations indicates that stress intensity, coping patterns, psychological well-being, and quality of life are interconnected [41]. A recent scoping review also highlighted the diversity of coping strategies used by university students and the importance of developing student-informed and context-sensitive approaches to stress prevention and management [42]. Furthermore, systematic reviews of resilience and mindfulness-based interventions suggest that institutional programs may contribute to reductions in stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms and may support some dimensions of student well-being, although the effectiveness varies according to the intervention and outcome assessed [43,44].

From a proactive public-health perspective, universities may therefore benefit from integrated and non-stigmatizing support pathways combining stress-management and adaptive-coping resources, sleep-health education, psychosocial support, and access to oral-health assessment. Future longitudinal and mixed-methods studies should jointly evaluate coping strategies, quality of life, sleep, psychological symptoms, and objectively measured oral conditions to clarify their temporal relationships and identify modifiable targets for student support.

Objectively measured halitosis was identified in 25 of the 62 university students (40.3%), and the analyses did not provide statistically significant evidence of associations with tongue coating, psychological symptoms, or sleep quality. Tongue-cleaning habits and oral mucosal desquamation were associated with halitosis, whereas psychological symptoms were correlated with specific sleep-quality components. Given the cross-sectional design, limited sample size, and multiple statistical comparisons, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory and require confirmation in larger longitudinal studies.

blocks.text: Obesity has become one of the leading health concerns in the world. There has been limited data on the effect of obesity on oral health in children and no research has specifically examined the impact of obesity on halitosis in this population. The aim of this study was to evaluate the potential effects of obesity on oral health parameters including dental caries, periodontal health, and halitosis in children.

A total of 295 children aged 10–13 years were included in the study. Height, body weight, and waist circumference were measured, and body mass index (BMI), z-scores, and percentile values were calculated using the WHO AnthroPlus 2007 program. Participants were classified into obese and non-obese groups. The obese group consisted of overweight/obese children, whereas the non-obese group comprised underweight/normal weight children. Oral health status, including the presence of halitosis, was assessed. In addition, a questionnaire was administered to the parents. The collected data were statistically analyzed using the chi-square test, Fisher’s exact test, Mann–Whitney U test, and multivariable logistic regression analysis (p < 0.05).

The obese group consisted of 111 children (37.6%), whereas the non-obese group comprised 184 children (62.4%). No statistically significant differences were observed between the obese and non-obese groups regarding DMFT/DMFS, dmft/dmfs, ICDAS II, plaque index, or gingival index scores. However, a statistically significant difference was found in the prevalence of halitosis between the groups. The frequency of halitosis was significantly higher in the obese group (24.3%) than in the non-obese group (14.7%) (p = 0.038). Furthermore, the association between tongue coating and halitosis was statistically significant in the non-obese group (p = 0.049), but not in the obese group (p = 0.790). Multivariable logistic regression analysis also identified overweight and obesity as potential risk factors for halitosis (OR = 1.847, 95% CI: 1.006–3.389).

In addition to the well-known causes of halitosis, overweight and obesity may also be considered potential risk factors in children. Parents should be informed that overweight and obesity may be associated with bad breath, which can lead to embarrassment and anxiety in children.
The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08893-4.

Obesity has been considered as one of the most important health problems affecting not only adults but also children and adolescents. According to the Global Burden of Disease Study, the prevalence of childhood obesity doubled from 1980 to 2015 in both developed and developing countries [1]. The growing problem has led to an increase in studies investigating the effects of obesity on both general and oral health in all over the world. It is known that obesity, which has a multifactorial and complex etiology, has negative effects on many systems such as endocrine, cardiovascular, respiratory, digestive and immune systems [2]. Regarding oral health, obesity has also been considered as one of the important risk factors for dental caries and periodontal health [3].

In the literature, there have been studies reporting a positive relationship between obesity and periodontal disease in both adults and children [4]. In a systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2017, it was reported that childhood obesity is associated with bleeding on probing, visible plaque index, subgingival calculus, probing depth and decreased salivary flow [5]. Although the exact reason for the decrease in salivary flow rate is not known, it is thought that proinflammatory cytokines released from adipose tissue cause a low level of chronic inflammation in the salivary glands [6]. In addition to the decreased flow, changes in the composition may also trigger periodontal disease. Increase in salivary bacterial population, sialic acid, protein concentration and TNF-α levels along with decrease in phosphorus and peroxidase activity were reported in obese individuals [7]. In a systematic review and meta-analysis published in 2019, it was reported that the increased salivary TNF-α level may be a helpful criterion for the diagnosis of obesity [7]. Moreover, it was also found that there was an increase in salivary immunoglobulin A (IgA) levels in obese children [6]. These alterations in periodontal status and salivary composition may also affect the oral microbial environment and contribute to the production of volatile sulfur compounds, thereby increasing the risk of halitosis [8].

Halitosis, also known as bad breath, is defined as an unpleasant breath odor originating from the mouth or outside the mouth. Causes of bad breath may include dental problems, dry mouth, infections, medications, or systemic diseases [9]. Halitosis is mainly classified as true or pseudo halitosis. While true halitosis is categorized as physiological (temporary) and pathological, pathological halitosis can be oral or extraoral, depending on the source of the odor. Physiological halitosis can occur due to temporary conditions such as dry mouth, hunger, smoking, certain foods and stress. Pseudo halitosis refers to the perception of bad breath without clinically detectable odor [10].

In the evaluation of halitosis, organoleptic evaluation, gas chromatography and sulfur monitoring are used. Organoleptic evaluation is a subjective method in which the physician scores the bad breath perceived on the patient [11]. In the sulfur monitoring method, measurement is made with a halimeter device that detects the amount of volatile sulfur compounds (VSC) in ppb (parts per billion) units. The method is easy to use, inexpensive, rapid, portable and reproducible. However, the compounds other than VSC cannot be detected with the device [12].

Regarding the association between halitosis and oral health in children; studies evaluated the effect of tongue coating, plaque index, dental caries and mouth breathing [8, 13, 14]. On the effect of obesity on oral health in children, caries and/or periodontal health were investigated [15]. The association between obesity and halitosis, however, has been carried out in limited studies concerning adults [16, 17]. To the best of our knowledge there has been no study on the effect of obesity on halitosis in children. Therefore, the aim of the present study is to investigate the effect of obesity on oral health and halitosis in children. The null hypothesis was formed as ‘There is no difference in terms of halitosis between obese children and non-obese children’.

In the present study, considering that there will be at least 20% difference in the prevalence of halitosis between obese and normal weight children, the minimum patient number required was calculated as 282, at 80% strength and 5% type I error levels. According to the studies investigating the prevalence of overweight and obesity among children in Turkey, the rate of overweight ranged from 9.2% to 22.4%, while the prevalence of obesity ranged from 1.6% to 10.3% [18–20]. According to these studies, the combined prevalence of overweight and obesity was determined as 32.7%. Therefore, in the present study, it was decided that at least 32.7% of the planned sample size would consist of overweight and obese individuals, with the remaining participants being of normal weight. The study protocol was approved by the Local Ethics Committee of Hacettepe University (Decision No: GO 18/477 − 17). The study was conducted in the Department of Pediatric Dentistry at Hacettepe University, Faculty of Dentistry and lasted for 16 months. A total of 295 children aged 10–13 years referred to the Department of Pediatric Dentistry were included in the study. This age range was selected to correspond to the early adolescence period. Adolescence is characterized by rapid growth and development, increased caloric needs, and lifestyle changes such as reduced physical activity and unhealthy dietary habits, alongside social, environmental, and psychological influences that may contribute to obesity. Therefore, the lower age limit was set at 10 years, corresponding to the onset of adolescence according to the World Health Organization, and the upper age limit was set at 13 years, based on the upper age of patients attending this department.

Written informed consents were obtained allowing data collection and the clinical procedure, after explaining the study protocol to the parent and child in detail. Inclusion criteria for the study were defined as being healthy and 10–13 years of age who were willing to participate. Before starting the study, a pilot study was conducted to determine the exclusion criteria. Exclusion criteria for the patients included: (a) systemic diseases, upper respiratory tract (tonsillitis, sinusitis), or gastrointestinal disease; (b) regular medication usage; (c) using antibiotic for the last month; (d) mouth breathing; (e) current orthodontic treatment; (f) dental caries cavities, prominent tongue coating, acute gingivitis and periodontitis or oral lesions. These exclusion criteria were applied to minimize potential confounding factors that could influence halitosis and to improve the internal validity of the study.

A questionnaire consisted of two parts was designed to collect information about the parents and their children. The questionnaire was administered in person to the parents of children participating in the study at the dental clinic. The first part focused on information of the parents, including their age, educational status, occupation, income, smoking habits, body weight and height, presence of any chronic diseases, oral hygiene habits and oral health status. In the second part, the information of the children, including their age, number of siblings, birth weight, oral hygiene and oral health, eating habits, mouth breathing and sleep apnea, were recorded. The questionnaire was developed for this study and presented as an attachment. The questionnaire was used as a descriptive data collection tool and did not aim to generate a score. Therefore, formal validation analyses were not performed. It was developed based on an extensive review of the literature and evaluated by a multidisciplinary team consisting of a pediatric dentist, a dietitian, and a statistician, ensuring content relevance, clarity, and suitability of the items.

Anthropometric measurements including body weight, height and waist circumference were taken. The body weight and height of the children were measured by a stadiometer (Seca, model: 7671321009, Germany) without shoes and thick clothes. During the measurement, it was ensured that the child was in an upright position and his/her feet were parallel to each other. Body weight was recorded in kilograms and height in meters. All anthropometric measurements were performed by one calibrated pediatric dentist (F.D.B.) who conducted the intraoral examinations using standardized procedures, following prior calibration on a subset of children to ensure consistency.

The waist circumference of the children was measured using a 150 cm long tape in the middle of the distance between the lowest rib and the iliac bone prominence. Items such as loose and thick clothes and belts that prevented the measurement were removed. The child was asked to stand in an upright position, hands and arms at both sides, feet close to each other. During the measurement, the child was asked to breathe normally, not to hold his/her breath and not to squeeze himself/herself, and the tape measure was not kept loose or applied excessive pressure. Measurements were made to the nearest millimeter (with an accuracy of 0.1 cm) and the detected value was recorded in cm.

After taking the measurements, body mass index (BMI), z-score and percentile values for the children were calculated with the WHO ANTRO Plus 2007 program. Using the growth reference values published by WHO for children and adolescents in the 5–19 age group in 2007, children were divided into two groups. The distribution of participants according to z score values was shown below:

Severe thinness: z score < -3 SD.
Thinness: -2 SD < z score < -3 SD.
Normal: -2 SD < z score < + 1 SD.
Overweight: +1 SD < z score < + 2 SD.
Obesity: +2 SD < z score < + 3 SD.
Morbid Obesity: z score > + 3 SD.

blocks.text: Oral health status of the children was evaluated using DMFT/DMFS, dmft/dmfs and ICDAS II indices, plaque index, gingival index and tongue coating by one calibrated pediatric dentist (F.D.B.). Prior to the study, examiner calibration was conducted through repeated assessments of a subset of children under standardized conditions. For the plaque index assessments, the labial (buccal), palatal (lingual), mesial, and distal surfaces of the teeth were scored using a periodontal probe according to the index developed by Silness and Löe. For the gingival index assessments, the labial (buccal), palatal (lingual), mesial, and distal surfaces of the teeth were scored using the periodontal probe according to the index developed by Löe and Silness.

The Winkel Tongue Coating Index (WTCI) was used to evaluate tongue coating. According to the index, the dorsum of the tongue was divided into six regions (three anterior, three posterior) and scored as follows: 0: No coating, 1: Mild tongue coating, 2: Severe tongue coating [21]. The total WTCI scores of the children were calculated and children with a total WTCI score of less than 6 were included in the study.

In the evaluation of halitosis, a portable “Halimeter” (Interscan Corp. Chatsworth, US & Canada) device was used in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions to measure the VSC in the mouth. The children were asked to refrain from eating, drinking, brushing, tongue cleaning and chewing for 2 h before the evaluation. Halimeter measurements were performed prior to periodontal examination in order to avoid any potential influence of mechanical stimulation on salivary flow and volatile sulfur compound levels. In the measurement, the children were asked to breathe only through the nose and keep their mouth closed for 3 min. This time is necessary for the formation of VSC in sufficient concentration. At the end of the 3-minute period, a disposable pipette attached to the halimeter device was advanced 2.5–5.0 cm into the child’s mouth and placed on the posterior dorsal part of the tongue. While the device was measuring, the child continued to breathe through the nose with his lips closed. The largest value obtained from the measurement is expressed numerically in ppb on the screen. The measurement was repeated three times and the average of the three measurements was recorded as the amount of VSC in the child’s breath. According to the manufacturer’s recommendations, VSC values of 150 ppb or higher were considered halitosis [12].

All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 23.0 (SPSS Inc. Released. SPSS for Windows, Version 23.0) package program. Number, percentage, mean standard deviation, median, minimum and maximum values were used as descriptive statistics. Chi-square, Fisher’s exact, and Mann-Whitney U tests were used to evaluate whether there was a statistically significant difference between categorical variables. Spearman correlation coefficient was used to determine whether there is a linear relationship between two numerical measurements, and if so, to assess the direction and severity of the relation. The factors associated with halitosis were identified using multivariable logistic regression analysis. Variables associated with halitosis in univariate analyses were considered for inclusion in the multivariable logistic regression model. In addition, plaque index and gingival index were included a priori as clinically relevant confounding variables based on previous evidence indicating a strong association between periodontal health and halitosis. Other potential confounding variables, including snack consumption and oral hygiene habits (tooth brushing frequency, flossing, and mouthwash use), were also evaluated in univariate analyses; however, no statistically significant associations were found between these variables and halitosis, and therefore they were not included in the final model. The level of statistical significance was set at p < 0.05.

A total of 295 patients (136 boys,159 girls) with a mean age of 11.63 ± 1.05 years, participated in the study. The children were further classified in two main groups according to their BMI and z-score as “obese group” and “non-obese group”. The distribution of the children according to BMI groups was shown in Table 1. Obese group constituted of 111 children (37.6%) with overweight, obesity and morbidly obesity whereas non-obese group constituted of 184 children (62.4%) with underweight and normal weight.

blocks.text: The children were also categorized as “halitosis group” and “no halitosis group” according to the presence or absence of bad breath. No halitosis group comprised 241 (81.7%) children, while halitosis group comprised 54 children (18.3%).
With respect to gender, the obesity was more common in boys compared to girls (p = 0.018). However, there was no statistically significant difference in halitosis between boys and girls (p = 0.975).

Most of the obese children (41.1%) were 12 years old. Nevertheless, there was no statistically significant relationship between age and BMI (p = 0.801). The rate of halitosis was 15.6% in the 10 and 11 years, 21.1% in the 12 years and 19.3% in the 13 years old children. There was no statistically significant relationship between age and halitosis (p = 0.769).

In comparison of the BMI of the parents (calculated according to their self-reported data) with the BMI of their children revealed a positive relationship (p < 0.001). It was found that 46% of the obese parents had also obese children.

heading_path: a. Comparison of the BMI groups in terms of chronic disease, birth characteristics, and oral hygiene habits

blocks.text: One hundred fourteen parents, (38.6%) reported chronic diseases in their families being 41.2% of them endocrine disorders such as diabetes and hypothyroidism. Twenty-seven children (57.4%) with a family history of endocrine disease were obese. The presence of endocrine disease in the family showed a significant difference between obese and non-obese groups (p = 0.010). Among the children with a family history of diabetes and hypothyroidism 52.5% and 85.7% were obese, respectively. The relationship was statistically significant for obesity and family history of hypothyroidism (p = 0.013).

In regard to the comparison of the obese and non-obese groups with the children’s birth characteristics, significant difference was found for the birth weight (p < 0.001). No significant difference was found between obese and non-obese groups for the time of birth or mode of delivery (p = 0.383, p = 1.000).
The children’s oral hygiene habits were shown in Table 2. There was no statistically significant difference in tooth brushing frequency between the obese and non-obese groups (p = 0.065).

blocks.text: The most common site for tongue coating was the middle posterior region (P2 area), and the least common site was the anterior right region (A1 area). In 204 children (69.2%) mild tongue coating (score 1) was observed in the P2 area and in 7 children (2.4%) in the A1 area.
The distribution of the children for total Winkel index scores of 0,1,2,3,4 and 5 were 84 (28.5%) 136 (46.1%), 31 (10.5%), 21 (7.1%), 22 (7.5%), and 1 (0.3%), respectively.

The halitosis group had higher tongue coating than no halitosis group (p = 0.004). No statistically significant relationship was found in obese and non-obese groups with respect to the total Winkel index score or the presence of tongue coating (p = 0.439 and p = 0.872, respectively).

The frequency of tongue coating by halitosis in obese and non-obese groups are showed in Table 6. In the non-obese group, halitosis was associated with the presence of tongue coating (p = 0.049), while in the obese group, halitosis was not associated with the presence of tongue coating (p = 0.984).
